Inception - possibly a ShinyHunters reboot - claims seven victims in a week

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Whatever they call themselves these days: be on the lookout for voice phishing attempts.
  • In a recent development, don't mind the recent arrests.
  • It has been revealed that shinyHunters is the brash cybercriminal group that, most recently, breached rival gang Clop before hacking the FBI, resulting in at least three arrests of key suspects in September and October.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Whatever they call themselves these days: be on the lookout for voice phishing attempts.

In a recent development, don't mind the recent arrests. The ShinyHunters extortion gang may still be operating, just under the latest name of Inception, according to Okta's threat intelligence group.

It has been revealed that shinyHunters is the brash cybercriminal group that, most recently, breached rival gang Clop before hacking the FBI, resulting in at least three arrests of key suspects in September and October. The crims - and their old data leak site - have since gone dark.

“While this threat cluster has changed their brand affiliation, the operators remain active in targeting organizations with voice phishing attacks and account takeovers resulting in data theft and extortion,” Okta threat hunters Moussa Diallo and Katie Nickels said on Monday.

Okta tracks this threat cluster as O-UNC-053 - the “O-UNC” prefix stands for an Okta Uncategorized cluster, and it uses this label before formally attributing the activity to a named threat group.

While Okta hasn't formally confirmed O-UNC-053 to be the same crime crew as ShinyHunters, the identity and access management provider’s researchers note that it does use nearly identical social engineering tactics: voice phishing, during which the scammers trick targets into entering credentials into phishing pages and approving multi-factor authentication (MFA).

Recent findings suggest that plus, they note: O-UNC-053 operators change the themes of their phishing domains about every four to six weeks, and they also post claimed victims on ShinyHunters’ data leak site. In November, however, organizations targeted by O-UNC-053 began appearing on a new data leak site branded as Inception and not ShinyHunters.

Industry observers note that the first five - Advanced Micro Devices, Cigna Healthcare, Paychex, PepsiCo, and Henry Schein - appeared November 17 on the site, and all were marked “leaked.” Soon after, security maven Dominic Alvieri questioned if Inception was linked to ShinyHunters. “ShinyHunters are not all in jail,” he wrote on social media.

It has been revealed that on November 19, AutoZone appeared on the site, with Inception again claiming to have leaked the auto-parts retailer's files. On Saturday, EV technology firm Lucid Group joined the claimed victims.

Industry observers note that none of the seven companies have confirmed breaches, and none responded to The Register’s inquiries. We will update this story when we receive more information.

Okta Threat Intelligence “is unable to validate if published data is authentic,” the researchers stated in response to our questions.

In the Monday report, the Okta team does note that Inception’s new data leak site listings “included multiple targets for which Okta Threat Intelligence previously observed O-UNC-053 infrastructure registration.”.

The infrastructure was registered between six and 19 days before Inception listed the companies on its leak site, and this gap “is consistent with prior shifts from Com-affiliated actors,” Diallo and Nickels added.

Sources indicate that the Com (short for community) is a loosely knit network of online groups whose young members participate in a range of illicit activities including hacking, swatting, digital extortion, real-life shootings, and other physical violence. Many security researchers consider ShinyHunters to be connected to The Com, along with groups such as Scattered Spider and LAPSUS$, with overlapping memberships and shared infrastructure.

Industry observers note that “Before and after the change in DLS publication, O-UNC-053 maintained consistent infrastructure and TTPs, leading us to assess that the cluster has very likely changed their brand affiliation,” the Okta researchers wrote. “We cannot currently make a high confidence assessment as to whether O-UNC-053 is operating the DLS themselves or is partnering with another extortion actor.”.

Regardless, members of the group formerly known as ShinyHunters and/or O-UNC-053 are still roaming the internet, looking for new victims, and conducting voice phishing attacks to steal data and then extort victims' companies for exorbitant sums of money. Consider yourself warned - and turn on phishing-resistant MFA.®.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News PostgreSQL 19 Released with Online Table Repacking and Query Planning Controls.
  • Nov 22, 2026 2 min read.
  • Sources indicate that the PostgreSQL Global Development Group released PostgreSQL 19, introducing changes to database maintenance, query planning, replication, and application development.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News PostgreSQL 19 Released with Online Table Repacking and Query Planning Controls.

Nov 22, 2026 2 min read.

Sources indicate that the PostgreSQL Global Development Group released PostgreSQL 19, introducing changes to database maintenance, query planning, replication, and application development. The release focuses on reducing administrative overhead and improving performance, with new tools for reorganizing tables without downtime and controlling query aims.

One of the main additions is REPACK, which reclaims unused table space and can reorder data to match an index. Its CONCURRENTLY option allows the operation to run without blocking reads or writes, making it a potential replacement for common uses of VACUUM FULL and CLUSTER. PostgreSQL 19 also introduces pg_plan_advice and pg_stash_advice, extensions that let administrators influence query plan selection and apply stored advice to queries by identifier, without changing application code.

According to recent reports, other maintenance improvements include parallel index vacuuming, changes to autovacuum prioritization, and additional monitoring views. EXPLAIN ANALYZE and related logging now report asynchronous I/O activity and WAL generated for full-page images. PostgreSQL also reports that changes to foreign key checks made bulk inserts nearly twice as fast in testing. Query planner improvements include more efficient anti-joins for eligible NOT IN clauses and eager aggregation before joins.

Sources indicate that the release adds several features for replication and application development. Logical replication now supports sequence values, and PostgreSQL automatically raises the effective WAL level to logical when the first logical replication slot is created. The upcoming WAIT FOR LSN command lets applications wait until a standby has replayed a specified WAL position before querying data, providing read-your-writes consistency. Developers also get INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO SELECT for get-or-create operations, JSON output from COPY, additional SQL/JSON string methods, and IGNORE NULLS support for window functions.

Security and compatibility changes include server-side TLS Server Name Indication (SNI), which allows a server to present different certificates based on the hostname used by the client. PostgreSQL 19 also warns after successful MD5 password authentication. MD5 was deprecated in PostgreSQL 18 and is planned for removal in a future release, with SCRAM recommended instead. JIT compilation is now disabled by default because its cost estimates proved unreliable, while LZ4 becomes the default TOAST compression method when supported by the build.

The release has also prompted discussion on Hacker News about whether production people should wait for PostgreSQL 19.1.

Another user recommended waiting for the first minor release on critical production systems:.

Personally, I would say, for critical production systems, it's still good to wait for the .1 release.

Industry observers note that postgreSQL 19 is available now. The complete list of changes is available in the official release notes.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If the AI can't explain what it's proven, are we actually any closer to understanding?

The leaders of the great model houses, Anthropic's Dario Amodei and OpenAI's Sam Altman, desperately want the world to believe AI is the skeleton key which will unlock the secrets of the universe.

But if the AI can’t explain what it’s “proven,” are we actually any closer to understanding anything, or have we simply built another black box?

Recent findings suggest that that question is top of mind among mathematicians and computer scientists this week after Anthropic researcher Levent Alpöge claimed to have solved a mathematical conjecture so elusive it's gone unproven for more than 150 years. The fact that this note came out one day after Anthropic's record-setting IPO is a coincidence, we're sure.

In a four-page post to his website, the researcher described how with the help of Claude, he believes he has proven the Riemann Hypothesis, one of seven Millennium problems so complex and so vital that the Clay Mathematics Institute has offered a $1 million prize to anyone who is successful in solving them.

The Riemann Hypothesis, conjectured by German mathematician Bernhard Riemann in 1859, contends that all nontrivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function – those with a real part between zero and one – have a real part equal to 1/2.

According to recent reports, confused? Don’t worry. We’ve linked to an explainer that goes into more detail here. What's important is that, if the Riemann Hypothesis is right, mathematicians can place tighter bounds on the difference between the actual distribution of prime numbers and mathematical estimates of that distribution.

Recent findings suggest that researchers have previously attempted to disprove the conjecture through computational brute force, and therein have shown the hypothesis holds to at least 10 trillion zeros. There’s reason to believe that the Riemann Hypothesis is accurate, but the possibility remains that over a sufficiently long series the pattern might diverge. And so, more than 150 years after Riemann published his hypothesis, it has remained just that.

Alpöge’s proof, if it can even be called that, is now the subject of great debate.

Recent findings suggest that the four pages in which Alpöge remarks on the discoveries he and Claude made aren’t exactly a proof, but rather 14 tarballs worth of Lean code totaling roughly 240 MB. Lean is an open source programming language commonly used to help validate mathematical proofs.

Sources indicate that the Clay Mathematics Institute, which oversees the seven Millennium Problems, has promoted the Riemann Hypothesis from “unsolved” to “active” status, but it is not yet considered solved. For Clay to consider the problem solved and award the prize, the proposed solution must be published in a qualifying outlet, remain available for scrutiny for at least two years, and receive broad acceptance from the mathematics community.

As it stands, Alpöge describes the 250,000 pages of text generated by the model for its written proof as a “massive unreadable travesty of ‘slop.’”.

Not long after Alpöge's remarks and Lean code were published, Stanford mathematician Ravi Vakil released a nearly 1,000-page draft proof by Alessandro Maria Masullo, who earned his PhD at Stanford in 2020. Masullo has reportedly spent more than a decade pursuing the problem.

Frameworks like Lean make mathematics a prime candidate for AI-assisted discovery for many of the same reasons that the technology has proven so successful in software development: code either compiles and runs or it doesn’t.

Code can also be audited and could, with great effort, be deciphered. But a proof written in Lean isn't a mathematical proof in the traditional, human-readable sense. Although its logical validity can be checked by a computer, understanding the reasoning behind it can be another matter. Traditional proofs ideally explain their arguments in a way that other mathematicians can follow. Cantor's Diagonal Argument offers a comparatively accessible example.

While the clock hasn’t even started for the Clay Math Institute, the Lean Focused Research Organization and Mathlib Initiative have already declared the Riemann Hypothesis solved.

Recent findings suggest that “We have full confidence that Alpöge's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement,” the orgs wrote in a joint statement. “We hereby certify that both the statement and the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis are correct.”.

Even if the code ends up being right, if we still don’t know why it’s true, have we really learned anything meaningful?

"At the minute, we don't even know why the theorem is true," Kevin Buzzard, professor of pure mathematics at Imperial College London, mentioned in a recent Al Jazeera interview.

Sources indicate that alpöge’s proof may simply be the product of a black box. To quote the late Arthur C Clarke, “any sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic.”.

Industry observers note that the implications of such a technology aren’t lost on researchers. Months ago, several prominent researchers called for greater scrutiny and oversight regarding the application of AI in mathematics.

“Mathematics produces not only a body of results, but also understanding, clarity, and judgment among the communities of mathematicians who have shaped them, often in the context of their own autonomously guided research,” the Leiden Declaration reads. “This expert knowledge is essential, both to effectively use mathematics, and to continue to articulate new and significant research questions.” ®.

Building the Hugging Face MCP Server

📅 10 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1435 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, TL;DR: The Hugging Face Official MCP Server offers unique customization options for AI Assistants accessing the Hub, along with access to thousands of AI applications through one simple URL.
  • We've learned many things about building a useful MCP server in the last month - we'll describe our journey here.
  • The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is fulfilling its promise of being the standard to connect AI Assistants to the outside world.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, TL;DR: The Hugging Face Official MCP Server offers unique customization options for AI Assistants accessing the Hub, along with access to thousands of AI applications through one simple URL. We used MCPs "Streamable HTTP" transport for deployment, and examine in detail the trade-offs that Server Developers have.

We've learned many things about building a useful MCP server in the last month - we'll describe our journey here.

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is fulfilling its promise of being the standard to connect AI Assistants to the outside world.

At Hugging Face, providing access to the Hub via MCP is an obvious choice, and this article shares our experience developing the hf.co/mcp MCP Server.

Recent findings suggest that the community uses the Hub for research, development, content creation and more. We wanted to let people customize the server for their own needs, as well as easily access thousands of AI applications available on Spaces. This meant making the MCP Server dynamic by adjusting users' tools on the fly.

We also wanted to make access simple by avoiding complicated downloads and configuration, so making it remotely accessible via a simple URL was a must.

According to recent reports, when building a remote MCP Server, the first decision is deciding how clients will connect to it. MCP offers several transport options, with different trade-offs. TL;DR: our open source code supports all variants, but for production we chose to go with the most modern one. This section goes through the different options in detail.

Recent findings suggest that since its launch in November 2024, MCP has undergone rapid evolution with 3 protocol revisions in 9 months. This has seen the replacement of the SSE Transport with Streamable HTTP, as well as the introduction and rework of authorization.

These rapid changes mean support for different MCP Features and revisions in Client applications varies, providing extra challenges for our design choices.

Here is a brief summary of the Transport Options offered by the Model Context Protocol and associated SDKs:.

Both STDIO and HTTP with SSE are fully bi-directional by default - meaning that Client and Server maintain an open connection and can send messages to each other at any time.

SSE refers to "Server Sent Events" - a way for HTTP Servers to maintain an open connection and send events in response to a request.

MCP Server Developers face a lot of choices when setting up the Streamable HTTP transport.

There are 3 main communication patterns to choose from:.

When using Request Scoped Streams with the official SDKs, use the sendNotification() and sendRequest() methods provided in the RequestHandlerExtra parameter (TypeScript) or set the related_request_id (Python) to send messages to the correct stream.

Recent findings suggest that an additional factor to consider is whether or not the MCP Server itself needs to maintain state for each connection. This is decided by the Server when the Client sends its Initialize request:.

The table below summarizes the MCP Features and their supported communication pattern:.

With Request Scoped streams, Sampling and Elicitation requests need a Stateful connection so that the mcp-session-id can be used for response association.

It has been revealed that the Hugging Face MCP Server is Open Source - and supports STDIO, SSE and Streamable HTTP deployment in both Direct Response and Server Push mode. You can configure keep-alive and last activity timeouts when using Server Push Streams. There's also a built-in observability dashboard that you can use to understand how different Clients manage connections, and handle Tool List change notifications.

The following picture shows our MCP Server connection dashboard running in "Server Push" Streamable HTTP mode:.

For production, we decided to launch our MCP Server with Streamable HTTP in a Stateless, Direct Response configuration for the following reasons:.

Stateless For anonymous customers we supply a standard set of Tools for using the Hub along with an Image Generator. For authenticated users our state comprises their selected tools and chosen Gradio applications. We also make sure that users ZeroGPU quota is correctly applied for their account. This is managed using the supplied HF_TOKEN or OAuth credentials that we look up on request. None of our existing tools require us to maintain any other state between requests.

You can use OAuth login by adding ?login to the MCP Server url - e.g. https://huggingface.co/mcp?login. We may make this the default once the claude.ai remote integration supports the latest OAuth spec.

Direct Response provides the lowest deployment resource overhead - and we don't currently have any Tools that require Sampling or Elicitation during execution.

It has been revealed that future Support At launch, the "HTTP with SSE" transport was still the remote default in a lot of MCP Clients. However, we didn't want to invest heavily in managing it due to its imminent deprecation. Fortunately, popular clients had already started making the switch (VSCode and Cursor), and within a week of launch claude.ai also added support. If you need to connect with SSE, feel free to deploy a copy of our Server on a FreeCPU Hugging Face Space.

In the future, we would like to support real-time Tool List Changed notifications when users upgrade their settings on the Hub. However, this raises a couple of practical challenges:.

In a recent development, first, users tend to configure their favourite MCP Servers in their Client and leave them enabled. This means that the Client remains connected whilst the application is open. Sending notifications would mean maintaining as many open connections as there were right now active Clients - regardless of active usage - on the chance the user updates their tool configuration.

Industry observers note that second, most MCP Servers and Clients disconnect after a period of inactivity, resuming when necessary. This inevitably means that immediate push notifications would be missed - as the notification channel will have been closed. In practice, it is far simpler for the Client to refresh the connection and Tool List as needed.

Unless you have reasonable control over the Client/Server pair, using Server Push Streams adds a lot of complexity to a public deployment, when lower-resource solutions for refreshing the Tool List exist.

Just before launch, @julien-c submitted a PR to include friendly instructions for users visiting hf.co/mcp. This hugely improves the User Experience - the default response is otherwise an unfriendly bit of JSON.

According to recent reports, initially, we found this generated an enormous amount of traffic. After a bit of investigation we found that when returning a web page rather than an HTTP 405 error, VSCode would poll the endpoint multiple times per second!

It has been revealed that the fix suggested by @coyotte508 was to properly detect browsers and only return the page in that circumstance. Thanks also to the VSCode team who rapidly fixed it.

Although not specifically stated - returning a page in this manner does seem acceptable within the MCP Specification.

The MCP Protocol sends several requests during initialization. A typical connection sequence is: Initialize, Notifications/Initialize, tools/list and then prompts/list.

Given that MCP Clients will connect and reconnect whilst open, and the fact that customers make periodic calls, we find there is a ratio of around 100 MCP Control messages for each Tool Call.

Some clients also send requests that don't make sense for our Stateless, Direct Response configuration - for example Pings, Cancellations or attempts to list Resources (which isn't a capability we presently advertise).

Sources indicate that the first week of July 2025 saw an astonishing 164 different Clients accessing our Server. Interestingly, one of the most popular tools is mcp-remote. Approximately half of all Clients use it as a bridge to connect to our remote server.

MCP is rapidly evolving, and we're excited about what has already been achieved across Chat Applications, IDEs, Agents and MCP Servers over the last few months.

We can already see how powerful integrating the Hugging Face Hub has been and support for Gradio Spaces now makes it possible for LLMs to be easily extended with the latest Machine Learning applications.

Here are some great examples of things people have been doing with our MCP Server so far:.

We hope that this post has provided insights to the decisions that need to be made building Remote MCP Servers, and encourage you to try some of the examples in your favourite MCP Client.

Take a look at our Open Source MCP Server, and try some of the different transport options with your Client, or open an Concern or Pull Request to make improvements or suggest newly introduced functionality.

Let us know your thoughts, feedback and questions on this discussion thread.

Cisco and OpenAI pitch eBPF kernel plugins as the way to tame the patchpocalypse

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (453 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Theregister

💡 Key Takeaways
  • ‘Shirudo’ project promises to whip up compensating controls in a hurry.
  • Cisco and OpenAI have released an open-source tool called Shirudo to implement compensating controls in Linux, potentially improving security for users who can’t quickly patch newly discovered software flaws.
  • Shirudo relies on eBPF, the technology that makes it possible to run sandboxed programs in the Linux kernel.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

‘Shirudo’ project promises to whip up compensating controls in a hurry.

Cisco and OpenAI have released an open-source tool called Shirudo to implement compensating controls in Linux, potentially improving security for users who can’t quickly patch newly discovered software flaws.

Shirudo relies on eBPF, the technology that makes it possible to run sandboxed programs in the Linux kernel. eBPF programs are effectively kernel plug-ins but don’t get unrestricted access to system resources.

Developers have mostly used eBPF to create network functions that enable things like the open source Kubernetes observability and security tool Cilium, a Cloud Native Computing Foundation project.

Cisco and OpenAI think eBPF can help organizations cope with the flood of 100,000-plus software flaws reported this year, many after the debut of AI-powered bug finders.

Industry observers note that the increased volume of flaws, and patches to fix them, is a problem for many organizations which already struggle to test fixes or find change windows in which to implement them. That problem has seen greater interest in “compensating controls” – changes to applications or infrastructure that harden them against flaws or malware, without requiring a patch.

With Shirudo, Cisco and OpenAI are suggesting two things:.

The privileges eBPF programs enjoy make them a fine way to implement compensating controls for Linux;.

Agents should scan your infrastructure for vulnerabilities, then use tools like OpenAI’s Codex to write compensating controls as eBPF programs at machine speed.

“Shirudo” is apparently the Japanese word for “shield,” so Cisco and OpenAI have called the eBPF programs the tool creates “shields.” The two companies envision humans checking every shield Shirudo creates before putting it into production.

Shirudo is open source and available here. The two companies say they’ve already demonstrated it could mitigate the recently discovered flaws in Java without requiring downtime for an Elasticsearch implementation.

Cisco and OpenAI are not alone in advocating for compensating controls. Third-party software maintenance outfits like Rimini Street have used them for years to protect software when their clients no longer have the right to access patches. VMware has introduced “virtual patching.” Palo Alto Networks and Rapid 7 also like this approach, and offer automation to develop controls.

Where Cisco and OpenAI differ is their decision to make Shirudo open source, and their ambition that other players adapt and advance it.

That offer is not entirely altruistic, as if Shirudo takes off it could create more demand for Codex. Cisco’s angle comes from the fact it owns Isovalent, an early champion of eBPF and the creator of both Cilium and the Tetragon sub-project on which Shirudo is based. Switchzilla is using eBPF in other products, so normalizing its use through an open source project can’t hurt. ®.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News QCon San Francisco 2026: The Harness Is the Newly introduced Operating System.

Nov 22, 2026 4 min read.

At QCon San Francisco 2026, Manju Rajashekhar, founder and CEO of Mad Labs, opened the conference with the keynote "The Harness Is the Newly introduced Operating System.".

Industry observers note that rajashekhar argued that the harness around an AI model, rather than the model itself, decides what an agent can do and how safely it does it. Each part of a harness, the keynote proposed, maps onto a job that operating systems already perform.

It has been revealed that rajashekhar began with a split that shaped computing history. Applications encoded behavior, while operating systems abstracted the hardware beneath them, and that separation made portable, composable software possible.

It has been revealed that AI agents break that arrangement because they generate behavior at runtime. Software therefore needs a fresh layer that makes that behavior useful, reliable and repeatable, and Rajashekhar called that layer the harness.

In Rajashekhar's framing, model plus harness equals agent, and the harness is "everything in an agent that isn't the model." It supplies the tasks, context, tools, state, permissions, feedback loops and a definition of done.

Industry observers note that the simplest agent is a model running in a loop that the harness controls. But "a loop isn't enough. Every iteration has to count," and Rajashekhar described four parts of the loop that make each iteration count.

Context works like virtual memory. The harness assembles what the model needs for its next decision inside the hard limit of the context window, and the advice was to "give the model a pointer, not the whole thing.".

The interface works like system calls and "puts a ceiling on the agent's effective capability." Rajashekhar pointed to the SWE-agent paper, in which GPT-4 Turbo resolved 11.0% of SWE-bench Lite issues through a plain shell and 18.0% through an interface designed for agents.

In a recent development, execution works like processes and permissions. The harness enforces boundaries through isolation and scoped credentials, such as a test database with no production access, because "instructions guide. Boundaries enforce.".

It has been revealed that feedback works like return codes. The harness keeps "tests failed," "could not run" and "outcome unknown" apart, so the model does not have to guess what happened.

Industry observers note that that matters because errors compound. On a 20-step task with a 95% chance of each step going right, the whole job succeeds 36% of the time, and catching 80% of errors lifts that to 82%.

Recent findings suggest that when an agent goes in circles, Rajashekhar said, most engineers swap the model. A better first step is to keep the model and change the harness.

DeepSeek's model card for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash reports the same model scoring from 65.5% to 74.2% on DeepSWE across eight harnesses. The minimal harnesses scored highest, which Rajashekhar read as a sign that more harness is not automatically better.

In a second study, Qwen3.8-27B passed 66.8% of 100 hard LiveCodeBench problems with a single call. Inside a manager-worker scaffold with a shared ledger, it passed 92.4%.

Rajashekhar made a related point on LinkedIn earlier this year. Frontier models are forgiving, the post noted, while "open-weight models are less forgiving. They make you think deeply about the harness and how it aligns to the model.".

In a recent development, the harness also determines what an agent is allowed to affect. Rajashekhar contrasted an agent that fixes failing tests with one that deletes the tests so they pass, observing that "the difference isn't ability. It's authority.".

The example offered was the July 2026 incident in which OpenAI evaluation agents on a capture-the-flag benchmark reached the internet through an open code sandbox. They held admin access on Hugging Face's internal clusters for about two and a half days.

In a recent development, human approval alone is a weak gate, Rajashekhar argued, citing Anthropic's work on Claude Code auto mode, which InfoQ covered in May. People approve the large majority of permission prompts, and "a tired gatekeeper is a rubber stamp.".

According to recent reports, the keynote extended a talk Rajashekhar gave at QCon AI Boston 2026. That talk argued that production agents "are just distributed systems in disguise" and proposed the actor model as their runtime.

In the Boston design, each agent task owns its state, receives events through a mailbox, writes each state change to a durable store and runs under a supervisor. The talk closed with a variation on Greenspun's tenth rule, suggesting that any sufficiently complicated agent loop contains half of an actor system.

In a recent development, the San Francisco keynote widened the lens from the runtime to everything the model sees, calls and runs inside. Rajashekhar brings a systems background to that question, having led caching systems on Twitter's early engineering team, which open-sourced twemproxy.

The talk arrives as "harness" has become the common term for everything around the model. Thoughtworks Distinguished Engineer Birgitta Böckeler described it in a February memo as covering "the tooling and practices we can use to keep AI agents in check.".

Rajashekhar closed on why a harness design is never finished. Every component "encodes an assumption about what the model can't do," and those assumptions expire as models improve.

Anthropic's harness for long-running apps needed context resets because Claude Sonnet 4.5 highlighted "context anxiety" near its context limit. That behavior largely disappeared with Opus 4.5, as InfoQ reported in April.

In a recent development, the reverse also holds. LangChain moved checks the model kept skipping into the harness and lifted GPT-5.2-Codex from 52.8% to 66.5% on Terminal-Bench 2.0 without changing the model.

It has been revealed that rajashekhar asked attendees to open an agent they already use and read its system prompt and tool list. Then, on a task where it struggles, change one part of the loop and rerun what already worked.

Developers interested in learning more can watch InfoQ in the coming weeks for video of the keynote and can view the keynote abstract and resources here.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that TL;DR Robotic policies are increasingly bulky, and predict chunks of future actions rather than a single next action.
  • Get started with async inference by following our tutorial.
  • Sequential inference (first) versus async inference (second).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that TL;DR Robotic policies are increasingly bulky, and predict chunks of future actions rather than a single next action. This results in the robot being idle while awaiting fresh actions to perform, introducing noticeable lags at execution, and lacking responsiveness. Asynchronous inference tightens the control loop, removing lags at runtime and resulting in more adaptive control by decoupling action prediction from action execution. In this blog post, we cover the basics behind async inference, and how it can be used to improve the performance of robotic policies in the real-world.

Get started with async inference by following our tutorial.

Sequential inference (first) versus async inference (second). Allowing for replanning and a tighter control loop, async inference results in (1) attempts at recovery, and (2) a ~2x speedup in task completion. Sequential inference keeps acting out the current action chunk even after failure to grasp the object, while async inference can replan and act the fresh action chunk. Both setups use the same policy!

Sources indicate that with async inference, we decouple action execution from action prediction. This is particularly relevant considering the tendency of currently popular models like [ACT], [OpenVLA], [PI0], and [SmolVLA] to be outputting chunks of actions at:t+Ha_{t:t+H}at:t+H​ rather than single actions ata_tat​ given an observation oto_tot​. Convince yourself of this by running all these models using LeRobot.

Using chunks sequentially results in (1) lags at runtime, impacting task execution time and (2) lack of responsiveness, due to acting widely open-loop. Asynchronous inference mitigates both these limitations by decoupling action prediction from action execution. We introduced asynchronous inference in SmolVLA, and found it to result in a ~2x speed-up in task completion time with comparable task success rate.

In particular, we design a 2-component system where policy inference and action execution are performed in two different processes, possibly on two different machines connected through the network:.

Communication between PolicyServer and RobotClient relies on gRPC, which guarantees ~5× faster performance than a comparable REST API. The result of all of this is a robot that never waits for inference.

Asynchronous inference, highlighting: (1) The client sending the first observation for inference, receiving the first chunk shortly after; (2) The client sending another observation for processing while it has not yet exhausted the current chunk; (3) The client receiving an updated action chunk, which it aggregates with the remainders of the one it was previously executing.

Suppose a policy π \pi π maps the current observation ot o_t ot​ to a sequence of H H H future actions. Formally, π:O  ↦  A,At=(at,at+1,…at+H)=π(ot)\pi : \mathcal{O} \;\mapsto\; \mathcal{A}, \mathbf{A}_t = \begin{pmatrix} a_{t}, & a_{t+1}, & \dots & a_{t+H} \end{pmatrix} = \pi(o_t)π:O↦A,At​=(at​,​at+1​,​…​at+H​​)=π(ot​).

A traditional control loop would therefore consist of the following steps:.

Recent findings suggest that during step 2 the robot is idle. The latency grows with the model size (and models tend to be increasingly bulky over time), and can swiftly dominate interaction time (which is typically around 1/fps), as shown in the video below (coming from our Discord community 🤗):.

This directly results in (1) reduced performance in terms of task completion time---the robot needs to be waiting for the next action chunk to be computed---and (2) reduced responsiveness, due to (2.1) acting widely open-loop while actions are available and (2.2) complete idleness while waiting for the next action chunk.

(Left)Sequential inference with highlighted idle periods. (Right)Time to select an action showing spikes when inference is triggered due to local queue exhaustion (inference latency is around ~100ms---~3 frames at 30fps---using an ACT model on a 2021 MacBook Pro).

Our system removes the idle period by overlapping computation and execution:.

The key idea is that the robot already knows what to do for the next few timesteps, so it can keep moving while fresh actions are being computed on the server.

Asynchronous inference overlaps in time the execution of the current action chunk with the computation of the next one, by decoupling these two processes, possibly running them on entirely distinct machines connected through the network.

In a recent development, this results in a tighter control loop, and a robot that never waits for inference. In turn, this results in ~2x speedup in task completion time with comparable task success rate, and more adaptive control coming from a tighter loop (see video below).

Because gRPC is HTTP/2-based and uses protocol buffers, it achieves low-latency binary messaging and bidirectional streams out of the box, which in turn helps us maintain a tighter control loop and sub-100ms round-trip latency (on our local network, and hosting SmolVLA on a NVIDIA RTX 4090).

Industry observers note that the RobotClient runs on-board, and streams observations to the PolicyServer through gRPC. The PolicyServer prepares the observations received for inference, and sends back to the RobotClient an action chunk.

From the client's perspective, observations are streamed to the server according to the local queue status. Incoming chunks are aggregated on overlapping portions with the currently available action queue.

It has been revealed that the RobotClient maintains a local action queue and follows a simple yet effective strategy: send a new observation when the queue length drops below a configurable threshold (\(g\) in the SmolVLA paper, chunk_size_threshold in the code). This threshold value, expressed as a fraction of the maximum chunk size, acts as a trigger condition that balances computational load with responsiveness.

The client streams observations to the server, according to the local queue status.

From the client's perspective, the process unfolds as follows:.

Queue monitoring: The client continuously monitors its action queue length against a chunk size threshold parameter. When the queue drops below this threshold, it signals that a new observation should be sent for processing.

Observation streaming: Once the threshold condition is met, the client captures the current observation and streams it to the PolicyServer via gRPC. Crucially, observations are streamed rather than being sent via a unary RPC because they typically exceed the maximum message size of 4MB (multiple camera captures at high resolution result in this).

Action chunk aggregation: When a new action chunk arrives from the server, the client merges it with any remaining actions in the current queue over the overlapping portion. This is where custom aggregators come into play, handling overlapping sections between the current and incoming chunks differently. As of now, we support flexibly aggregation between the chunks via the specification of a custom aggregate_fn(chunk1: torch.Tensor, chunk2: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor function, which is called for each overlapping timestep and can be user-provided. The overlapping portions (shown in light blue in the diagram) require careful handling. We can design different aggregation strategies:.

According to recent reports, this system is highly configurable, as the chunk size threshold can be tuned based on network latency, model inference time, and desired responsiveness. A lower threshold means more frequent updates (and higher computational cost), while a higher threshold reduces communication overhead at the expense of potential queue starvation. Lastly, we typically receive actions from PolicyServer in a thread, and perform them in another one. This keeps the client listening for incoming chunks in a separate thread, without blocking execution and always consuming the current chunk until a fresh one becomes fully available.

It has been revealed that upon receiving observations from the RobotClient, the PolicyServer receives observations from the RobotClient, and performs the necessary observation cleaning to make received observations ready for inference. This process is illustrated in the image below:.

The observation cleaning pipeline running on the server, highlighting the three main steps related to (1) Keys matching (2) Preprocessing and (3) Preparation for inference.

Recent findings suggest that once the observation has been prepared, it is compared with the last observation used for inference. This avoids collapsing into a loop whereby very similar observations are processed, thus triggering unnecessary inference and similar actions being executed (which in turn, result in very similar observations being processed again). We compare observations in terms of their joint-space similarity, which provides us an approximate and quick way of measuring changes in the robot. Clearly, this metric is not adaptive to dynamic changes in the environment (an object changing its position, or disturbances being applied), but we found it to be a good trade-off for the majority of the cases, and to be very effective in avoiding unnecessary inference and state collapse. Critically, the RobotClient retains control over whether a given observation must be processed, to avoid deadlocks. Observations sent by the client and tagged with must_go=True are processed regardless of the similarity metric.

The policy workflow, in which incoming observations are compared to the last one used for inference, and processed only if different enough, or `must_go`.

Lastly, to ensure the PolicyServer always processes the latest available observation, we block incoming observations until the previous one has been successfully processed. In this, we leverage queues on the PolicyServer to ensure incoming observations are not enqueued until the server is ready to process them (see below).

The client pings the server every 1/fps seconds, but observations are not enqueued for processing until the previous one has been successfully processed.

For all practical purposes, in async inference there are two time-scales that matter:.

Importantly, the ratio c=environment_dtinference_time c = \frac{\texttt{environment\_dt}}{\texttt{inference\_time}} c=inference_timeenvironment_dt​ results in different behaviours:.

Recent findings suggest that critically, ccc influences the number of available actions in the queue at any given time. To avoid the aforementioned sequential limit control, one can:.

Experiments (see plots below) show that g≈0.7g\approx0.7g≈0.7 offers a good trade-off when observations sent are not filtered out (they are all must-go). We recommend setting g=0.5g=0.5g=0.5 and following our documentation to tune this parameter to your needs.

It has been revealed that the number of available actions in the queue at any given time, as a function of g. Larger values of g result in more frequent updates, and more computational cost. Values of g closer to 0 reproduce sequential inference (empty queue, wait). We found g~0.7 to be a good trade-off in our experiments.

It has been revealed that async inference is a simple yet effective way to improve the performance of robotic policies. In our experiments using SmolVLA, async inference results in a ~2x speedup in task completion time with comparable task success rate, and more adaptive control coming from a tighter loop.

Industry observers note that to run your policy using async inference, you just need to follow our tutorial with your own custom parameters (e.g., the policy path or the chunk size threshold). Async inference comes with support for policies supporting action chunking!

In a recent development, we have introduced async inference, a simple yet effective way to improve the performance of robotic policies. In our experiments using SmolVLA, async inference results in a ~2x speedup in task completion time with comparable task success rate, and more adaptive control coming from a tighter loop.

We are excited to share this work with the community, and to see how it can be used to improve the performance of robotic policies. We welcome PRs to improve and extend the async inference framework at huggingface/lerobot, and are available to discuss this further in our Discord community, 🤗.

Came across this while I was working on something similar. Good work.

I built Inferential to handle multi-robot inference orchestration on Ray Serve. Deadline-aware scheduling scores requests across cadence urgency (EMA-tracked), robot-reported priority, anti-starvation age, trajectory progress, and static priority. ZMQ ROUTER/DEALER transport with protobuf+numpy wire format -- under 1ms serialize-transmit-deserialize vs ~100ms over gRPC. Request TTL, overflow policies, automatic disconnect detection, dispatch retry.

Tech Report: Kimina-Prover: Applying Test-time RL Search on Large Formal Reasoning Models

📅 10 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2389 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that we're excited to announce the release of Kimina-Prover-72B, our state-of-the-art theorem proving model trained with the Kimi k1.5[1] RL pipeline based on Qwen2.5-72B [2].
  • Test-Time Reinforcement Learning Search: A trainable agentic proving framework that enables the model to recursively discover, combine and apply multiple lemmas to construct complex proofs, building on a novel lemma-enabled pattern.
  • Error-Fixing Capability: Kimina-Prover can read and interpret Lean’s error messages and propose targeted fixes, demonstrating significantly higher sample efficiency compared to regenerating proofs from scratch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that we're excited to announce the release of Kimina-Prover-72B, our state-of-the-art theorem proving model trained with the Kimi k1.5[1] RL pipeline based on Qwen2.5-72B [2]. Alongside it, we are also releasing two distilled variants: Kimina-Prover-Distill-8B and 1.7B (based on Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-1.7B[3] respectively).

Test-Time Reinforcement Learning Search: A trainable agentic proving framework that enables the model to recursively discover, combine and apply multiple lemmas to construct complex proofs, building on a novel lemma-enabled pattern.

Error-Fixing Capability: Kimina-Prover can read and interpret Lean’s error messages and propose targeted fixes, demonstrating significantly higher sample efficiency compared to regenerating proofs from scratch.

These advancements enable Kimina-Prover to solve challenging mathematical problems and surpass prior methods. As shown in Figure 1, on the widely used miniF2F benchmark, Kimina-Prover achieves a state-of-the-art pass rate of 92.2%.

We focus on automated theorem proving (ATP) in the Lean 4 language, aiming to automate the construction of formal mathematical proofs. Recent advances in neural theorem proving have significantly improved the ability of AI systems to assist with or automate this process. Notable progress includes AlphaProof[4] from Google DeepMind, which demonstrated strong performance on problems at the level of the International Mathematical Olympiad. Open-source systems such as DeepSeek-Prover-V2[5], which incorporates reinforcement learning, have also achieved state-of-the-art results. In addition, neuro-symbolic agentic approaches like DSP+[6] have shown that competitive performance is possible without large-scale training by leveraging off-the-shelf models in a modular framework.

Sources indicate that our earlier work of Kimina-Prover Preview[7] introduced a large language model for formal theorem proving in Lean, establishing a new performance baseline on the miniF2F benchmark. Trained with a large-scale reinforcement learning pipeline, the model adopted a reasoning-driven exploration paradigm and demonstrated that larger models can serve as stronger formal reasoners. Its structured reasoning pattern enabled efficient proof search and emulated human-like problem-solving strategies.

Following this initial success, we continued to improve the model through further iterations of reinforcement learning. However, single-step reasoning remains insufficient for solving complex problems that require long, multi-stage proofs. To address this limitation, we introduce the Test-Time Reinforcement Learning (TTRL) search framework, which enables the model to discover, combine, and reuse multiple intermediate lemmas autonomously. This framework supports deeper, long-horizon reasoning by decomposing hard problems into reusable subcomponents.

According to recent reports, A key ingredient of TTRL search is the lemma-enabled pattern, which allows the model to identify and apply intermediate lemmas as part of its proof construction process. This structured reuse of intermediate results significantly expands the model’s problem-solving capability beyond single-step generation.

To further enhance robustness, we also integrate an error-fixing mechanism that interprets Lean’s error messages and proposes targeted corrections. This allows the model to refine its outputs through iterative feedback, improving proof reliability and overall sample efficiency.

According to recent reports, as the combination of the proposed techniques results in significant improvements in formal theorem proving performance. On the miniF2F benchmark, Kimina-Prover achieves a pass rate of 84.0% with pass@32 and 86.4% with the addition of a single round of error correction. With pass@1024, the pass rate reaches 87.7%. Applying the full Test-Time Reinforcement Learning (TTRL) search framework yields a final pass rate of 92.2%, with an estimated pass upper bound of approximately 42,000. However, this pass budget can be substantially optimized in future versions, as a large portion of the current sampling is spent on proving unhelpful or redundant lemmas.

In a recent development, notably, these results indicate a shift in the scaling behavior of the prover. While earlier versions exhibited approximately linear improvements in log scale with increasing sampling budget, the current system demonstrates diminishing returns beyond pass@1024. This suggests that further gains are less dependent on increased sampling and instead require more sophisticated search strategies, such as those introduced by TTRL.

The lemma-enabled pattern is designed to equip the model with the ability to identify and utilize useful lemmas provided in the input. To support this capability, during reinforcement learning (RL) training, a random subset of one to three formal lemmas is prepended to the problem context, exposing the prover to potentially useful intermediate results that can aid in constructing the final proof. These lemmas are prepared through a two-step pipeline: (1) a general-purpose LLM generates candidate lemmas in natural language; (2) these are then translated into formal statements using our Kimina-Autoformalizer-7b.

Initial observations highlighted that the model had a low tendency to incorporate the provided lemmas. To address this, we introduced a preference-based reward shaping strategy within the RL framework. When a theorem could be proven through multiple trajectories, solutions that successfully leveraged a provided lemma were assigned a higher reward, while those that did not were penalized. This approach proved effective, increasing the lemma utilization rate to a stable 30–40% after training. Importantly, this method not only encouraged lemma usage but also promoted selectivity: the model learned to apply lemmas strategically when they were useful, while ignoring irrelevant ones, demonstrating more efficient and human-like reasoning behavior.

The lemma-enabled pattern allowed the model to incorporate pre-generated lemmas as intermediate steps in constructing proofs. However, we observed that randomly sampling and inserting lemmas was insufficient for solving complex problems requiring highly structured and deeply nested reasoning. To address this limitation, we developed the Test-Time Reinforcement Learning Search framework—a trainable, agentic approach that systematically organizes, filters, and composes a large set of candidate lemmas to build complete proofs. This framework transitions the process from random exploration to a more strategic, goal-directed search.

Industry observers note that as illustrated in Figure 2, we define the search scope of each problem as the problem itself along with its associated candidate lemmas. TTRL Search tracks a lemma utilization score within each search scope to measure how frequently and effectively each lemma contributes to the final proof. At the beginning of each RL training iteration, for each problem (i.e., search scope), we construct K = 10 input variants by prepending different combinations of lemmas. To balance exploration and exploitation, 60% of the inputs are built using the top-ranking lemmas—those with the highest utilization scores—focusing the model on the most promising proof paths. The remaining 40% are formed by including these top lemmas alongside one to four randomly selected additional lemmas, encouraging exploration of novel and potentially useful lemma combinations.

To ensure quality, a filtering mechanism prunes lemmas that consistently fail to contribute meaningfully: any lemma that fails to achieve a utilization score of at least τ=0.10 after 50 insertion attempts is removed from the search pool.

In a recent development, A key feature of TTRL is its recursive search mechanism. The search scope is not limited to the original theorem but is also maintained for each lemma, allowing the framework to recursively decompose the problem into smaller subproblems. A parallel sublemma generation process runs throughout, and whenever a theorem or lemma fails to find a proof after N = 128 attempts, latest candidate sublemmas are generated. This recursive strategy enables test-time scaling of reasoning depth, significantly extending the model’s effective problem-solving capability.

To maintain logical soundness, we address a failure mode wherein incorrectly formalized lemmas could lead to trivial or invalid proofs. In such cases, the model may exploit inconsistencies to construct seemingly valid but unsound solutions. To prevent this, we introduce a negation proving process: for each newly generated lemma, we attempt to prove its logical negation. If the negated statement is provable, it indicates that the original lemma is logically inconsistent and is immediately discarded. This step ensures the reliability and soundness of the overall proof construction process.

A critical limitation of recent advanced theorem proving models is their lack of the ability to correct proofs based on feedback from the proof assistant—capabilities that human customers routinely leverage. To address this gap, we developed a dedicated framework to integrate error-fixing capabilities into Kimina-Prover.

It has been revealed that SFT Data Generation for Error Correction. General-purpose large language models exhibit a low success rate when interpreting Lean’s error messages and proposing valid corrections. To overcome this, we constructed a specialized Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) dataset tailored for error correction. This dataset consists of triplets in the form of (incorrect proof, Lean feedback, correct proof). To enrich the supervision signal, we prompted Claude 3.7 sonnet[8] to synthesize step-by-step reasoning chains explaining how the incorrect proof can be transformed into the correct one using the provided feedback. The result is a high-quality dataset that includes not only the initial and corrected proofs but also the intermediate reasoning, facilitating more effective learning.

Industry observers note that batched Failure Replay Strategy. Integrating error correction directly into the reinforcement learning (RL) loop initially proved ineffective due to the low success rate (~1%) of the SFT model in fixing errors, resulting in sparse rewards and unstable training. To address this, we designed the Batched Failure Replay strategy. Rather than attempting to correct errors immediately during an RL iteration, all failed proof attempts from iteration N are collected. In the subsequent iteration N+1, the training batch is composed of a fixed-size union of these prior failures (e.g., 500 samples) and standard problems from the prompt set (e.g., another 500 samples). This ensures consistent and high-volume exposure to error correction tasks in each training step, enabling the model to gradually learn effective error-handling behaviors in a stable and data-efficient manner.

Industry observers note that this training approach led to measurable improvements in the model’s ability to recover from failure. The model advanced from correcting basic syntax errors to resolving complex logical mistakes and, eventually, discovering alternative proof strategies when initial attempts failed. Crucially, this capability improved sample efficiency. As shown in Table 2, we compared different strategies under fixed computational budgets. The 16+16 attempt-and-fix strategy—consisting of 16 initial proof attempts, each followed by one error-fixing attempt—achieved a success rate of 35.6%, outperforming the 32×1 brute-force baseline, which reached 28.8% with 32 independent attempts. Further increasing the sample budget to 32+32 with error correction yielded a success rate of 44.1%. These results demonstrate that enabling the model to correct its own errors is a more efficient use of computational resources than repeated trial-and-error.

In addition to our core TTRL search and Error fixing, we developed several other novel techniques to enhance the model's learning process and problem-solving capabilities.

Industry observers note that prompt Set Curation and Iteration. Effective data curation is critical for reinforcement learning (RL) efficiency. Our initial prompt set of over 300K problems was refined to a competition-focused subset of approximately 90K, with an emphasis on problems from sources such as the olympiads-ref subset of NuminaMath 1.5[9]. During RL, we applied dynamic filtering: problems with consistently high success rates were removed to maintain challenge, while persistently difficult problems were decomposed into simpler subproblems or variations using a general-purpose LLM. The final prompt set combines auto-formalized statements for broad coverage, human-annotated problems for quality, and augmented variations for targeted skill development. The curated prompt set will be open-sourced.

Continuous Pre-training on Lean Data. To address the limited Lean proficiency in most base models, we applied Continuous Pre-training (CPT). A 6-billion-token CPT dataset was constructed from multiple sources: 260M tokens from online platforms such as GitHub, 5.5B tokens of compiler-validated rollout data from our RL pipeline, and additional structured data in state–tactic–state and state–tactic–error formats to enhance diversity. These structured data supplements the base model with additional domain knowledge.

Random Proof Cut Data Augmentation. To better utilize high-quality, human-annotated proofs that lack intermediate reasoning steps, we developed the Random Proof Cut technique. This method augments such data using two variations:.

This strategy allows the model to learn how to extend existing lines of reasoning and to fill in logical gaps, effectively integrating human-generated content into the training process.

Sources indicate that non-proof Problem Solving. Many problems are presented in the form of requiring a final answer, which cannot be naturally framed as a traditional proof task. Inspired by the CombiBench[10] evaluation methodology, we introduced a capability for non-proof problem solving to unify answer generation with proof construction. In this setting, the model is given a problem with the final answer field left blank. It performs a two-stage process within a single inference: it first deduces the correct answer and then generates a complete formal proof to justify that answer. This approach ensures the model’s reasoning is explicitly conditioned on reaching the correct solution.

Here we provide some proof cases found by our newest Kimina-prover model. The complete list of solved miniF2F problems is available on GitHub.

The system recursively decomposed the problem into four layers of lemmas using a TTRL search approach, ultimately generating a 520-line formal proof. During this recursive proving process, initially, only one lemma, sum_cexp_div_pow_ne_zero, remained to be solved. While this conclusion seems straightforward to prove informally, it would still require a lot of steps to prove it rigorously in Lean 4. Our system recursively generated two extra layers of lemmas and obtained a 260-line formal proof for sum_cexp_div_pow_ne_zero. This proof is valid under Mathlib v4.15.

Recent findings suggest that in the following example, the initial proof timed out because directly applying simp to ((Real.sqrt 3 / 2 : ℂ) + (1 / 2) * Complex.I) ^ 12 resulted in excessive search complexity. Breaking down the proof by step-by-step calculating intermediate powers like $z^3$, then $z^6$, and finally $z^{12}$ significantly reduced the computational burden on the compiler.

How Escambia County Uses Miovision’s AI to Investigate Traffic Signal Complaints

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Escambia County, Florida, is using Miovision’s AI Studio to help investigate complaints about traffic signals.
  • The release follows the introduction of Mateo, Miovision’s traffic engineering assistant, in April.
  • According to Miovision, county staff previously had to pull signal controller records and compare timing plans and traffic volumes by hand.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Escambia County, Florida, is using Miovision’s AI Studio to help investigate complaints about traffic signals. In results released November 23, Miovision remarked the county could pull an initial analysis together in about five minutes, down from 30 to 45 minutes under its previous workflow. The improvement was in investigation time, not the number of complaints or the amount of time drivers spent waiting at red lights.

The release follows the introduction of Mateo, Miovision’s traffic engineering assistant, in April. The newer results show what one traffic team is doing with it in daily operations. They also illustrate why access to the right data is more vital here than an AI model’s ability to give a confident-sounding answer.

According to Miovision, county staff previously had to pull signal controller records and compare timing plans and traffic volumes by hand. They now use AI Studio to ask for a view that brings those records together. The AI Studio product page describes how a natural-language request can be turned into an interactive workspace that draws on sources including signal performance data and telemetry. That is useful when an engineer needs to compare the same junction over multiple hours or find out whether a pattern appears across several locations.

Sources indicate that one example is a split failure: vehicles are still waiting when their green phase ends. Miovision’s traffic performance software monitors this alongside measures such as arrivals on green. Escambia already used this kind of data. A separate case study of a corridor project in the county describes how existing controllers and field detectors supplied timing and detection records for earlier before-and-after analyses. In the new workflow, the assistant helps assemble and compare the records; the traffic engineer still decides what the patterns mean.

That review matters because a split failure can have different explanations. A recurring queue during an expected peak, an unusual surge and a detector that is not reporting reliably can all warrant different responses. An initial chart gives staff a place to look, but it is not a basis on its own for changing a signal blueprint. A five-minute investigation also does not mean the underlying problem was fixed in five minutes.

Agencies evaluating a similar workflow can separate three measures: time to gather the records, time to reach a decision and time to resolve the complaint. A tool that improves the first step could be worthwhile even if a field visit or an equipment replacement still determines how long residents wait for the glitch to be fixed.

The county also used AI Studio after a hurricane to prioritize checks of 343 network cameras across five partner agencies, Miovision mentioned. Staff built a tool that compared pre-storm pictures with post-storm views and paired the comparison with the cameras’ last communications. That helped separate views that had moved from cameras that were no longer reporting and gave maintenance teams lists to verify and act on. The 343 figure refers to the cameras audited, not the number destroyed or successfully repaired by AI.

Sources indicate that miovision reported roughly a week of manual inspection time avoided and nearly full camera functionality restored within 30 days. Those are vendor-reported results from one local deployment, not a controlled comparison. They do point to a practical use for AI in a public agency: make the relevant evidence easier to retrieve and review, while keeping decisions about signal timing and field repairs with the people responsible for the network.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that in January of this year, Hugging Face's Xet Team deployed a fresh storage backend, and shortly after shifted ~6% of Hub downloads through the infrastructure.
  • Today, more than 1 million people on the Hub are using Xet.
  • For one, the team came prepared with years of experience building and supporting the content addressed store (CAS) and Rust client that provide the system's foundation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that in January of this year, Hugging Face's Xet Team deployed a fresh storage backend, and shortly after shifted ~6% of Hub downloads through the infrastructure. This represented a significant milestone, but it was just the beginning. In 6 months, 500,000 repositories holding 20 PB joined the move to Xet as the Hub outgrows Git LFS and transitions to a storage system that scales with the workloads of AI builders.

Today, more than 1 million people on the Hub are using Xet. In May, it became the default on the Hub for latest users and organizations. With only a few dozen GitHub issues, forum threads, and Discord messages, this is perhaps the quietest migration of this magnitude.

Recent findings suggest that how? For one, the team came prepared with years of experience building and supporting the content addressed store (CAS) and Rust client that provide the system's foundation. Without these pieces, Git LFS may still be the future on the Hub. However, the unsung heroes of this migration are:.

Sources indicate that together, these components have allowed us to aggressively migrate PBs in the span of days without worrying about the impact to the Hub or the community. They're giving us the peace of mind to move even faster in the coming weeks and months (skip to the end 👇 to see what's coming).

In the early days of planning the migration to Xet, we made a few key design decisions:.

Driven by our commitment to the community, these seemingly straightforward decisions had significant implications. Most importantly, we did not believe owners and teams should have to immediately alter their workflow or download a new client to interact with Xet-enabled repositories.

If you have a Xet-aware client (e.g., hf-xet, the Xet integration with huggingface_hub), uploads and downloads pass through the entire Xet stack. The client either breaks up files into chunks using content defined chunking while uploading, or requests file reconstruction information when downloading. On upload, chunks are passed to CAS and stored in S3. During downloads, CAS provides the chunk ranges the client needs to request from S3 to reconstruct the file locally.

Sources indicate that for older versions of huggingface_hub or huggingface.js, which do not support chunk-based file transfers, you can still download and upload to Xet repos, but these bytes take a different route. When a Xet-backed file is requested from the Hub along the resolve endpoint, the Git LFS Bridge constructs and returns a single presigned URL, mimicking the LFS protocol. The Bridge then does the work of reconstructing the file from the content held in S3 and returns it to the requester.

In a recent development, to see this in action, right click on the image above and open it in a upcoming tab. The URL redirects from https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/documentation-images/resolve/main/blog/migrating-the-hub-to-xet/bridge.png to one that begins with https://cas-bridge.xethub.hf.co/xet-bridge-us/.... You can also use curl -vL on the same URL to see the redirects in your terminal.

Meanwhile, when a non-Xet-aware client uploads a file, it is sent first to LFS storage then migrated to Xet. This “background migration process,” only briefly mentioned in our docs, powers both the migrations to Xet and upload backward compatibility. It is behind the migration of well over a dozen PBs of models and datasets and is keeping 500,000 repos in sync with Xet storage all without missing a beat.

Every time a file needs to be migrated from LFS to Xet, a webhook is triggered, pushing the event to a distributed queue where it is processed by an orchestrator. The orchestrator:.

These migration workers then pick up the jobs and each pod:.

In April, we tested this system's limits by reaching out to bartowski and asking if they wanted to test out Xet. With nearly 500 TB across 2,000 repos, bartowski's migration uncovered a few weak links:.

Sources indicate that fixing this three-headed monster meant touching every layer - patching xet-core, resizing CAS, and beefing up the worker node specs. Fortunately, bartowski was game to work with us while every repo made its way to Xet. These same lessons powered the moves of the biggest storage users on the Hub like RichardErkhov (1.7PB and 25,000 repos) and mradermacher (6.1PB and 42,000 repos 🤯).

CAS throughput, meanwhile, has grown by an order of magnitude between the first and latest large-scale migrations:.

When we began replacing LFS, we had two goals in mind:.

Designing with our initial constraints and these goals allowed us to:.

Industry observers note that instead of waiting for all upload paths to become Xet-aware, forcing a hard cut-over, or pushing the community to adopt a specific workflow, we could begin migrating the Hub to Xet immediately with minimal user impact. In short, let teams keep their workflows and organically transition to Xet with infrastructure supporting the long-term goal of a unified storage system.

In January and February, we onboarded power people to provide feedback and pressure-test the infrastructure. To get community feedback, we launched a waitlist to preview Xet-enabled repositories. Soon after, Xet became the default for newly introduced users on the Hub.

We now support some of the largest creators on the Hub (Meta Llama, Google, OpenAI, and Qwen) while the community keeps working uninterrupted.

Starting this month, we're bringing Xet to everyone. Watch for an email providing access to Xet and once you have it, enhancement to the latest huggingface_hub (pip install -U huggingface_hub) to unlock faster transfers right away. This will also mean:.

According to recent reports, if you upload or download from the Hub using your browser or use Git, that's fine. Chunk-based support for both is coming soon. In the meantime use whichever workflow you already have; no restrictions.

Next up: open-sourcing the Xet protocol and the entire infrastructure stack. The future of storing and moving bytes that scale to AI workloads is on the Hub, and we're aiming to bring it to everyone.

If you have any questions, drop us a line in the comments 👇, open a discussion on the Xet team page.

This enables and strengthens our commitment to provide free public storage to the open source community. Of course, we're always evaluating ways to surface this transparently and support the community, so let me know if any of this is confusing.
