Lua for data representation

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1111 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Citrons

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • my major advocacy is that lua is a very good general purpose language.
  • lua’s syntax provides many niceties.
  • here is a function that for any string, creates the correct multiline string to represent it:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

my major advocacy is that lua is a very good general purpose language. this is not an opinion shared by all. lua’s major design goal was extending and embedding into existing programs. I think the simplicity and flexibility in design persued towards the end of that goal extends to make lua a very good language in general. that said, it does its job quite well as an embedding language, and one of its more interesting use cases (and actually, one of its oldest use cases) is as a data or configuration format.

lua’s syntax provides many niceties. for instance, lua has an infinite family of multiline strings: the most basic one starts with [[ and ends with ]]. however, any amount of equal signs can be put between the two square brackets: print([======[hello, world]======]). the only way to close a [===[ is with an accompanying ]===], not with a ]] or a ]==], or a ]====].

here is a function that for any string, creates the correct multiline string to represent it:.

local function stringize(str) local equal_signs = "" for e in str:gmatch("](=*)]") do if #e >= #equal_signs then equal_signs = e .. "=" end end return ("[%s[%s]%s]"):format(equal_signs, str, equal_signs) end of course, you can just use string.format with %q, but multiline strings usually provide nicer looking and more compact results. these strings are very good for representing lua code as strings in other lua code.

According to recent reports, anyway, download this file. if you want to consume massive amounts of memory and possibly crash your computer, run it in cpython. if you want to see “hello, world” printed 5 million times, run it in lua. lua’s parser is designed to handle massive files with stride, which is fairly unique and quite necessary if lua is to be used for this purpose.

design and implementation choices like these come together to suit lua for this purpose. I’ve seen 3 main styles of using lua code to represent data or configuration. I think lua manages to accomodate each of them well, and each have their appropriate use.

In a recent development, chunks are much like function bodies. they have return values. so, one thing that one can do is just return a big table from a lua program.

Recent findings suggest that return { foo = "bar", list = {1, 2, 3}, rule_of_thirds = true, } if you’re using this style, you can omit the return and then prepend it when you load the lua files. this makes any trailing statements syntactically invalid because the return statement must be the last statement in the block. keep in mind, though, that this does not prevent arbitrary code because function literals can be used instead.

return (function() arbitrary_code() end)() trying to strip out function literals to make this technique safer is fraught and defeats the general elegance of this technique. one can fairly readily use JSON instead.

what is often missed about lua is that it’s subtly full of metaprogrammability. for instance, lua globals are just stored in a table, and which table is used can be controlled by the code itself. this table is known as the “environment”. an environment may be passed to load as an argument. the way this can be used is that you can load a chunk with an empty environment and then capture the values it sets as globals.

-- config.lua foo = "bar" list = {1, 2, 3} rule_of_thirds = true then, you can get a table with all the configuration as simply as this:.

local config = {} assert(loadfile("config.lua", "t", config))().

lua has a bit of sugar that allows you to shed the parenthesis on function calls to make them look cleaner. an imperative style is a very suitable means to represent data in lua, and it’s very powerful.

path "/path/to/things" config { foo = "bar", list = {1, 2, 3}, rule_of_thirds = true, } lipsum [[ Voluptatibus laudantium et omnis ut debitis. Similique omnis molestias consequuntur. Praesentium corporis omnis nihil et quidem dolore. Veritatis fugiat eaque corporis eligendi officiis praesentium. Libero quo vero temporibus impedit sit inventore assumenda ]] programming in lua provides a real world example of this.

the major problem with using an entire programming language to represent data is that untrusted data can be readily crafted to be malicious. indeed, I would not use this technique for untrusted data. with that in mind, it is possible to solve or mitigate the potential vulnerabilities.

Industry observers note that the main technique for sandboxing lua is controlling the environment. when using lua for data representation, an empty enivronment is the most appropriate (or, an environment that only exposes data constructors). this prevents any I/O or access to the larger program’s state. preventing access to all standard library functions is safest. there are a few standard library functions that have consequences you might not expect.

another concern is denial of service. this is trickier to prevent. it’s fairly trivial to construct a lua chunk which does not return (while true do end). debug.sethook can mitigate this somewhat. even so, it’s probably possible to construct something that uses excessive amounts of memory. that said, denial of service is significantly less problematic than the vulnerabilities that are completely avoided by depriving the untrusted code of any standard library functions.

finally, make sure to reject lua bytecode. untrusted lua bytecode is not safe and may cause arbitrary nasal demons in the lua interpreter. load can accept both bytecode and lua source by default. however, passing "t" for the mode parameter prevents this.

clearly, it’s silly to bring in the entire lua interpreter where you would just use JSON or INI. where this use case of lua shines is when you’re already using lua for a project (and then you already have this powerful data description language), or when you need something with a lot of power or flexibility.

It has been revealed that these mini languages can be extended to arbitrary complexity and nuance. unlike JSON, you can add arbitrary type constructors, or anything at all. you can build any kind of language you want, and that’s how lua is designed to be used, and it’s actually approximately the story of how it was invented.

In a recent development, if you’re anything like me, this will sound a little familiar. indeed, many have said similar things about lisp and forth. both of those languages have very different approaches but reach the same conclusion of “inventing your own language”. I believe lua belongs in their pantheon.

In a recent development, python? js? ruby? what the hell are those? all I care about is LUA.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage Podcasts Simulation Can Tell You What Your Agents are Actually Doing: A Conversation with Zhou Yu.

Recent findings suggest that in this podcast, Michael Stiefel spoke to Zhou Yu about using dynamic simulations to evaluate AI agents. One particular focus was conversational agents where actions depend on prior responses, and the non-deterministic nation of LLMs means you cannot rely on static, reference-based benchmarks.You need to test them using dynamic simulations that incorporate different personas, goals, and corner cases. You can simulate how conversations shift based on moods, preferences, accents, or environmental conditions such as factory background noise. Rather than relying on simply binary pass or fail, the rule based task verifiers can measure whether the task was completed as well as threshold metrics for cost, efficiency, safety, and compliance.

According to recent reports, simulations can be used during the entire software lifecycle. Product managers can use them for prototyping and design. Engineers can use them for testing in CI/CD pipelines. They can also be used to test production for model drift or failure of third party tools. They can also be used to test compliance with the laws in different regions. Simulations can also be used with synthetic data to fine-tune models.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness.

Dr. Yu was named one of the Forbes 30 Under 30 and has extensive research and product experience in conversational agents, computer user agents and LLM model training. Her company enables automated quality assurance testing for AI agents.

Tech Report: Ettin Suite: SoTA Paired Encoders and Decoders

📅 16 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1059 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • What would happen if you took the ModernBERT recipe and applied it to a decoder-only model?
  • We introduce a new open-data training recipe to reproduce the encoder-only ModernBERT model (and actually beat it!).
  • This blog post introduces Ettin, the first suite of SoTA paired encoder-only and decoder-only models (17M-1B params) trained with identical data (2T tokens), architecture, and training recipes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What would happen if you took the ModernBERT recipe and applied it to a decoder-only model? Turns out, a state-of-the-art decoder language model that beats Llama 3.2 1B and SmolLM2!

We introduce a new open-data training recipe to reproduce the encoder-only ModernBERT model (and actually beat it!). We then apply the exact same recipe to decoder-only models. For the first time, we have two state-of-the-art models trained in the same setup but with two different training objectives: masked language modeling (MLM), and causal language modeling (CLM).

This blog post introduces Ettin, the first suite of SoTA paired encoder-only and decoder-only models (17M-1B params) trained with identical data (2T tokens), architecture, and training recipes. Ettin enables true apples-to-apples comparisons between architectures and delivers state-of-the-art performance for open-data models in both categories. We then further explore whether it is possible to get a competitive encoder starting from the decoder and vice-versa.

If you are interested in trying out the models, some boilerplates are available at the end of this blogpost!

Industry observers note that the LLM community has largely converged on decoder-only models like GPT, Llama, and Qwen. Their generative capabilities are impressive, but this focus is detracting attention from other categories, such as encoder-only models like BERT.

However, encoder BERT-like models remain the workhorses of production systems for classification, retrieval, and embedding tasks. They're faster, more memory-efficient, and often more accurate for discriminative tasks. The key difference lies in their attention patterns:.

Industry observers note that while decoder models have seen rapid innovation, encoder model development had stagnated – until recently, with efforts like ModernBERT modernizing them. But which architecture is better? Previous comparisons between encoders and decoders used different datasets, architectures, and training recipes, so it was hard to tell.

Named after the two-headed Norse giant, Ettin provides a controlled comparison by training with both architectures on identical data, identical model shapes, and identical training recipes. They only differ in attention patterns and training objectives!

It has been revealed that we build on the ModernBERT recipe, which borrowed modern techniques from decoder-only models and brought them to encoder training. This provides a strong base for training both architectures.

We train six different sizes, ranging from 17M to 1B parameters. This allows us to test the effects of scale, and provides a wide variety of models for you to use! No matter if you need a blazing fast on-device model or a powerful but slower model, we got you covered!

We use a comprehensive three-phase training approach to maximize performance:.

Phase 1 - Pre-training (1.7T tokens): We start with a diverse mixture of high-quality data sources, training on shorter contexts (1024 tokens) to establish strong foundational knowledge.

Phase 2 - Context Extension (250B tokens): We increase context length to 8K tokens using higher-quality filtered data, allowing models to understand longer documents and more complex relationships.

Phase 3 - Decay (100B tokens): We finish with premium data sources including scientific papers, textbooks, and curated content while gradually reducing the learning rate.

Our encoder models gain all the benefits of ModernBERT's speed, allowing them to be significantly faster than the previous generations of encoders.

Unlike ModernBERT, all our training data is public and reproducible:.

You can continue to train these models on fresh data or propose a new recipe to further improve results!

In a recent development, our encoder models outperform ModernBERT across all tasks and model sizes, while using completely open training data. Since we provide a large range of sizes, you can now use ModernBERT-style models in smaller sizes (great for on-device or for fast-inference), or power up with a 1B-sized encoder that crushes the competition.

Applying the same recipe to decoder models yields equally impressive results, with our models outperforming or matching established baselines such as Llama 3.2 and SmolLM2:.

The gains are particularly strong on knowledge-intensive tasks like SciQ, reflecting the benefits of our high-quality training data mixture. These results demonstrate that our training recipe creates genuinely strong models in both architectural paradigms.

For the first time, we can fairly compare encoder and decoder architectures trained with identical data and recipes. The results reveal fundamental architectural advantages that persist even when all other factors are controlled:.

The results show clear patterns:.

Industry observers note that encoders dominate classification and retrieval: On MNLI classification, even a 150M encoder (89.2) outperforms a 400M decoder (88.2). For retrieval tasks, the gap is smaller but still noticeable - especially when decoders are not trained with MNTP.

Decoders excel at generation: On generative tasks, decoders maintain consistent advantages, with the performance gap actually widening at larger model sizes.

Size doesn't always matter: A 400M encoder beats a 1B decoder on classification tasks, while a 400M decoder beats a 1B encoder on generation tasks.

Due to the lack of latest encoder models, works like LLM2Vec have proposed to continue pre-training decoders with MLM. We can now test the effectiveness of this strategy!

Sources indicate that we switched the objective and continued to train our models with the opposite objective for 50B additional tokens. This is what we found:.

This suggests the architecture choice matters fundamentally, not just the training objective.

With identical training data, we can study how different objectives affect learning. For example, analyzing gender bias using the WinoGender benchmark reveals:.

This opens doors for systematic studies of how training objectives influence model behavior beyond just accuracy metrics.

You can use these models with just a few lines of code!

For text generation tasks, use decoder models:.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Reuters reported on November 23, 2026 that about 160,000 Anthropic options contracts changed hands during their first hour of trading that day.
  • According to recent reports, the early activity placed Anthropic among the 25 most heavily traded names in the options market, according to Mercury Alerts, the options analytics service that supplied the figures.
  • Mercury Alerts projected that the opening pace would produce more than 600,000 contracts over the full session.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Reuters reported on November 23, 2026 that about 160,000 Anthropic options contracts changed hands during their first hour of trading that day. The launch added a listed instrument for hedging the AI manufacturer’s shares or taking speculative positions following its initial public offering.

According to recent reports, the early activity placed Anthropic among the 25 most heavily traded names in the options market, according to Mercury Alerts, the options analytics service that supplied the figures. Volume was roughly evenly split between calls, which give holders the right to buy shares at a fixed price, and puts, which give holders the right to sell at a fixed price.

Mercury Alerts projected that the opening pace would produce more than 600,000 contracts over the full session. Anthropic shares were down 2% at $87.33 in early trading when Reuters published its report.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ayman Elhalwagy is Co-Founder and CEO of RootCause.ai, with a background in computer engineering, machine condition monitoring, and applied AI.
  • Recent findings suggest that rootCause.ai develops a causal inference and simulation platform for business and operational decisions.
  • It has been revealed that your PhD at Brunel focused on combining datasets and monitoring the condition of machines, before you went on to found AI consultancy Numvio.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that dr. Ayman Elhalwagy is Co-Founder and CEO of RootCause.ai, with a background in computer engineering, machine condition monitoring, and applied AI. His PhD at Brunel University focused on combining datasets and monitoring machinery. He later founded AI consultancy Numvio, where his work with enterprise data and forecasting systems helped shape his interest in causal models that explain business outcomes and support decisions.

Recent findings suggest that rootCause.ai develops a causal inference and simulation platform for business and operational decisions. It brings data from different systems into a shared ontology, builds causal models, and lets organizations test the potential effects of decisions before acting. In this interview, Elhalwagy discusses predictive versus causal AI, business digital twins, forecast validation, hidden variables, and the human oversight needed when simulations inform automated actions.

It has been revealed that your PhD at Brunel focused on combining datasets and monitoring the condition of machines, before you went on to found AI consultancy Numvio. What did those experiences reveal about the limitations of predictive AI, and how did they shape your decision to found RootCause.ai?

My PhD in computer engineering at Brunel University focused on combining datasets and monitoring the condition of machines, with the dataset work validated by NASA and the monitoring system used for mining equipment around the world.

Recent findings suggest that after that, I started Numvio, an AI consultancy, where we repeatedly saw the same problem: companies had years of dashboards and forecasts but still didn’t know what was causing the results. Predictions could tell them what was likely to happen, but not what to change, so finding answers often took months, by which time the decision had already been made. We founded RootCause.ai to make that work possible in days rather than months, and repeatable rather than a one off study.

Industry observers note that how would you explain the difference between predictive AI and causal AI to a business leader? Can you share an example where accurately predicting an outcome still fails to reveal how to improve it?

Put simply, predictive AI answers “what will happen” whereas causal AI answers “what happens if I do this”. For example, a global logistics company we worked with had 12,000 accident reports spread across six separate datasets, and dashboards on hundreds of variables. They could only see that accidents were happening, but they didn’t know what was causing them, therefore their only way to test ideas was to change a policy and wait months to see if the accident rate moved.

To solve this, we built a causal model across all six datasets, identifying that the main cause was driving more than 4.5 hours without a break, not the driving style or vehicle. Once the company knew the cause, they could effectively test in the model what enforcing breaks would do to accidents, and what it would cost in driving time.

Sources indicate that what research underpins RootCause.ai’s ability to identify cause and effect from existing business data? How do you account for hidden variables and distinguish causal relationships from misleading correlations?

According to recent reports, our causal discovery algorithm, SPARC-fast, identifies which variables influence others and runs around 1,000 times faster than standard methods on ordinary compute. It uses the tech giant’s ontology, or structured map of its data, to rule out implausible relationships and accounts for time delays to help establish whether a relationship is causal, since a cause must happen before its effect.

In a recent development, the algorithm has been benchmarked against public datasets with known causal relationships and can also detect hidden variables, or factors outside the available data that influence results. While it can’t identify what those hidden variables represent, customers can often recognise them. One customer, for example, identified a hidden variable as a promotion they had run but never recorded in their data. The result is a causal graph that people can read, edit and version, rather than a black-box result.

Recent findings suggest that what does a digital twin of a business actually represent? Could you walk us through how operational data becomes a model that can simulate decisions and their consequences across products, markets, and time?

Industry observers note that for us, a digital twin is a model of a business built from its own data, able to understand how different parts of the business affect one another, allowing you to change one variable and see the consequences across the rest of the business. We connect to the manufacturer’s existing data systems, automatically build an ontology to bring information from different sources into a consistent structure, and use SPARC-fast to identify the relationships between variables, including time delays and hidden influences.

Industry observers note that we then fit the model to the company’s data, accounting for differences across products and regions, and keep it updated as newly introduced data comes in. Companies can then simulate decisions such as changing prices, discounts, policies or tariffs to see their effects across products, regions and time horizons, or identify which single change would have the biggest impact on a particular business outcome. Results can be delivered through apps, APIs (Application Programming Interface), SDKs (Software Development Kit) or MCP (Model Context Protocol), allowing teams to use simulations within their existing systems.

It has been revealed that your team reports reducing forecast error at a publicly traded telecommunications company from 20% to 5%. How was that improvement measured, what baseline did you compare against, and how did it translate into better business decisions?

Industry observers note that one of our customers, a publicly traded telecom equipment manufacturer that builds equipment up to 18 months before resellers need it, makes accurate forecasting critical to avoiding over or understocking. Its existing in-house model, built by its own data team, had a weighted MAPE (mean absolute percentage error) of around 20%. We measured the improvement through backtesting against the same historical data, training the model on information available at different points and comparing forecasts with what actually happened. Across 2,086 product-region combinations and eight forecast horizons, covering 16,688 forecasts, weighted MAPE fell from around 20% to 5%.

The model also indicates which inputs are driving changes, translating into better business decisions by allowing the company to test pricing, discounts, bookings and reseller changes before setting its manufacturing plan. It is transparent about its limitations too: for brand latest products with no sales history, the company’s existing product family average still performs better.

In a recent development, the logistics example in your briefing identified prolonged driving without a break as a key factor in truck accidents. How did you validate that finding, and did changing break policies lead to a measurable reduction in incidents?

We analysed 12,000 incident reports and 10GB of telematics data across six datasets, covering tachograph violations, collisions and driving behaviour. We found that time since the driver’s last rest break was the strongest factor associated with accidents, with risk rising sharply after 4.5 hours of driving. Interestingly, it wasn’t the expected factors of speed, weather or driving style.

Sources indicate that the model highlights every relationship and its strength, allowing the customer to check how we reached that finding. We then simulated enforcing rest breaks, accounting for the additional driving time, and estimated savings of around $1 million per 2,000 trucks. This is a simulated estimate rather than a measured reduction in accidents following a policy change.

How reliable are simulations when businesses encounter conditions with little historical precedent? How does your platform communicate uncertainty and recognize when the evidence is insufficient to recommend an action?

Causal inference exists to answer questions history doesn’t contain, allowing companies to ask “what if something different happens”, rather than “what happened last time”. Companies such as Netflix, Amazon, Uber and Walmart use it, and it has only been accessible to those that can afford to build the capability.

Our digital twins are built on causal models. A pattern matching forecast can only repeat what it has seen, whereas a causal model captures the links between variables, allowing businesses to test values they have never encountered, such as a latest tariff level or inflation rate. The models are explainable, showing how each variable is calculated and how accurate it is. They can also identify hidden variables influencing results, so users know when vital information is missing rather than being handed a confident number.

We also automatically bring in external data such as inflation, interest rates, tariffs and weather to reflect conditions outside the business’s control. Customers can backtest the model against historical data, seeing how forecast accuracy changes across different time horizons. Forecasts are provided as a range rather than a single number, and the model retrains if predictions drift from reality over a sustained period. If the data is too limited or flat for a reliable forecast, we tell customers that too.

Which advances in AI are making causal modelling more accessible to smaller organizations? Where do large language models fit into your system, and what data and human expertise do customers still need?

Instead of using LLMs, our platform is hard statistics and applied mathematics, with LLMs not good at hypothetical scenarios, even when you give them good data. That is a limit of how they are built, as they learn patterns from what has happened. A “what if” question is about something that has not happened.

There is a view in AI research, Yann LeCun’s work among it, that feeding models more and more data will not on its own get them to reliable answers on this kind of question. We agree. That all noted, customers want to use their own agents to orchestrate our technology, so we have made the platform open to them. An agent can connect through MCP or API, run a simulation, and use the result as it goes about its work. The agent does the asking and the statistics do the answering.

It has been revealed that as AI moves from recommending decisions to executing them, what should remain under human control? What validation and safeguards would you require before allowing a causal AI system to act autonomously?

Today, a person decides which policy or action to take, while the system simulates the likely consequences. Once approved, that decision can be carried out through an API, SDK or MCP, but the technology does not independently decide what to do. Before enabling autonomous actions, we believe the model must be readable, editable and versioned, with backtested accuracy established for the specific decision and time horizon. Hidden variables must also be identified and understood, while ongoing monitoring should pause automated actions if predictions drift from reality. Results from actions taken should then feed back into the model, which is the current level of automation we are working towards, but at the moment most customers keep a person in the loop.

Sources indicate that what is the hardest unresolved research problem in causal AI today? What progress would most expand the range of business decisions these systems can reliably support?

Hidden variables are the biggest challenge. Most methods assume every relevant variable is in the data, but in business data that is never true. We can find hidden variables, but using them inside simulations, and mapping them back to things the business can measure, is unsolved. This is where much of our research team’s time goes.

Direction is another challenge. With time series data, time gives direction. Without it, direction is a guess, and a wrong direction breaks every simulation downstream. This is a major area of research amongst our PhD team, with RootCause able to right now tell you when relevant variables are missing. Our research breakthrough in this area allows us to significantly expand the cases, especially for many cases represented in real world scenarios, where we can detect these variables and model them accurately. We are also the only organization that we are aware of to have commercialized this capability, and combined it with an ontology system to try to “match” external data that we have curated to the patterns we established in customer data.

Thank you for the great interview, readers who wish to explore a causal AI platform for modeling their business and simulating decisions should visit RootCause.ai.

The new and planned connections expand the existing Gmail, Calendar and Photos sources. Sources indicate that google says Drive support will draw context from documents, spreadsheets and PDFs, with a personalized tax-season preparation initiative as one example. The forthcoming Gemini app connection will share context in both directions, allowing an idea explored in Gemini to provide the foundation for an AI Mode response and vice versa. Recent findings suggest that google began rolling out Wallet in the Gemini app on November 13, 2026 for all U.S. Gemini app consumers across web, Android and iOS. Connections sit under Connected Apps in Search Personalization. Owners decide whether to opt in and can turn individual connections on or off at any time. Google also plans a Personalization icon below tailored AI Mode responses that will show the context used; people can correct details directly in a thread or disable personalization through Search Settings.

Sources indicate that google’s March 17, 2026 expansion made Personal Intelligence available in AI Mode in the U.S. and started rolling it out to free-tier Gemini and Gemini in Chrome consumers. The connected experiences are limited to personal Google accounts rather than Workspace business, enterprise or education accounts, placing this expansion in Google’s consumer AI business.

In a recent development, on data use, Google notes Gemini and AI Mode do not train directly on a user’s Gmail inbox or Photos library. They do train on limited information, including specific prompts and model responses, to improve functionality over time. For those sources, the distinction is between referencing personal material to answer a request and training directly on the underlying inbox or photo collection.

Google’s January 14, 2026 beta introduction described remaining risks: testing had not eliminated inaccurate responses or over-personalization, including mistaken connections between unrelated topics. The model could also misread timing or relationship changes and infer interests without understanding the reason behind an activity.

The patch makes Search more continuous across financial planning, document-based projects and research, while giving those documented failure modes a wider set of personal inputs. That makes the planned context display and correction tools part of the core product: the value of each fresh connection depends on whether users can see what Search used and fix it when the inference is wrong.

I assume you know about the P vs. NP problem. But what is this wacky thing Anthropic just posted?

You learned how to take a determinant in your linear algebra class:.

Industry observers note that the naive way is fine for 3Ã3 matrices, but notice that you need to perform Î(n!) arithmetic operations here. Exercise for the reader is to find the exact number of operations (hint: start with a recurrence relation).

Recent findings suggest that luckily, if you paid attention, you will remember there are faster ways to do this for major nÃn matrices, like Gaussian elimination. If we stick only to adding and multiplying, we can still find a determinant in polynomial time (there are better ways, but this is an old, readable method).

A related problem to the determinant is finding the permanent. Itâs like a determinant without any subtraction:.

Industry observers note that unlike determinants, there is no known way to compute permanents in polynomial time. Since finding the permanent of a matrix of 0s and 1s is NP-hard (and in fact #P-complete), it would be pretty important if there were a way.

What the Anthropic proof that VPâ VNP means is that there is no way to do this if we are limited to arithmetic circuits of size polynomial in the input-size, which look like this:.

This means that for P to equal NP, there must be some trick to computing permanents using AND/OR/NOT on the bits of the input that is better than addition and multiplication. There are many problems where access to Boolean operators is helpful, but it isnât clear how they would help with the permanent. If you think of a way, go claim your $1 million.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • To that end, here are some of the significant improvements we've added to Gradio MCP servers as of version 5.38.0.
  • If you've tried to use a remote Gradio MCP server that takes a file as input (image, video, audio), you've probably encountered this error:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, gradio is an open-source Python package for creating AI-powered web applications. Gradio is compliant with the MCP server protocol and powers thousands of MCP servers hosted on Hugging Face Spaces. The Gradio team is betting significant on Gradio and Spaces being the best way to build and host AI-powered MCP servers.

To that end, here are some of the significant improvements we've added to Gradio MCP servers as of version 5.38.0.

If you've tried to use a remote Gradio MCP server that takes a file as input (image, video, audio), you've probably encountered this error:.

This happens because the Gradio server is hosted on a different machine, meaning any input files must be accessible via a public URL so they can be downloaded remotely.

In a recent development, while many ways exist to host files online, they all add a manual step to your workflow. In the age of LLM agents, shouldn't we expect them to handle this for you?

Gradio now includes a "File Upload" MCP server that agents can use to upload files directly to your Gradio application. If any tools in your Gradio MCP server require file inputs, the connection documentation will now show you how to start the "File Upload" MCP server:.

Learn more about using this server (and notable security considerations) in the Gradio Guides.

Depending on the AI task, getting results can take some time. Now, Gradio streams progress notifications to your MCP client, allowing you to monitor the status in real-time!

As an MCP developer, it's highly recommended to implement your MCP tools to emit these progress statuses. Our guide shows you how.

Industry observers note that if you want to integrate an existing backend API into an LLM, you have to manually map API endpoints to MCP tools. This can be a time-consuming and error prone chore. With this release, Gradio can automate the entire process for you! With a single line of code, you can integrate your business backend into any MCP-compatible LLM.

In a recent development, openAPI is a widely adopted standard for describing RESTful APIs in a machine-readable format, typically as a JSON file. Gradio now features the gr.load_openapi function, which creates a Gradio application directly from an OpenAPI schema. You can then launch the app with mcp_server=True to automatically create an MCP server for your API!

Find more details in the Gradio Guides.

A common pattern in MCP server development is to use authentication headers to call services on behalf of your users. As an MCP server developer, you want to clearly communicate to your users which credentials they need to provide for proper server usage.

Industry observers note that to make this possible, you can now type your MCP server arguments as gr.Header. Gradio will automatically extract that header from the incoming request (if it exists) and pass it to your function. The benefit of using gr.Header is that the MCP connection docs will automatically display the headers you need to supply when connecting to the server!

In the example below, the X-API-Token header is extracted from the incoming request and passed in as the x_api_token argument to make_api_request_on_behalf_of_user.

You can read more about this in the Gradio Guides.

Gradio automatically generates tool descriptions from your function names and docstrings. Now you can customize the tool description even further with the api_description parameter. In this example, the tool description will read "Apply a sepia filter to any image.".

It has been revealed that want us to add a new MCP-related feature to Gradio? Let us know in the comments of the blog or on GitHub. Also if you've built a cool MCP server or Gradio app let us know in the comments and we'll amplify it!

Recent findings suggest that anthropic has added Code Mode to Claude Code, an experimental feature in which the model writes JavaScript to drive its tools instead of requesting each Bash, Read, or Edit call separately. Code Mode is off by default, requires Claude Code v2.1.323 or later, and is enabled with the CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_CODE_MODE=1 environment variable. Anthropic warns it may change or be removed in any release.

In a normal session, Claude asks for one tool call, reads the full result, and decides the next step. In Code Mode, one script can run commands in parallel, pass one result into the next call, and return only the output the model needs. The documentation's example finds a file with rg, raises a retry limit, runs the tests, and returns just the path and test output. The conversation still reveals each tool call and diff, while the generated code sits in the transcript viewer. Anthropic recommends it for edits repeated across many files, searches that need filtering, and independent commands. Code that Claude waits on stops after ten minutes; sessions started in auto or bypassPermissions mode can push it to the background for up to two hours while the conversation continues.

Industry observers note that the permission model is the part architects should read first. Each call inside a script still goes through deny and ask rules and PreToolUse hooks, but in auto mode the classifier reviews the script before it runs, not each call, and cannot see values computed at run time. A git push can now reach a hook as cd 'app' && git push, so hooks must check every part of a command; a hook matching the REPL tool can read the JavaScript from tool_input.code. Project settings cannot enable Code Mode, so a cloned repository cannot switch it on, and administrators can block it through managed settings.

Code Mode runs only in interactive terminal sessions of the native build, on Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5, or Fable 5.2, through a Claude subscription or Console account. It does not work with -p, the Agent SDK, the VS Code panel, the Desktop app, Amazon Bedrock, gateways, or zero-data-retention organizations. Agent teams need v2.1.326. Anthropic has published no token or latency figures for it.

George (@bolyki) compared Code Mode with normal mode across eight interactive Sonnet 5.5 runs and posted:.

Same results every time. Context 20-25% smaller. On the bigger task: 37% fewer tokens, 19% lower cost. But it is not faster, and on a tiny task it cost more.

Ravi Madabhushi, who builds agent auth infrastructure, pushed back on claims that the feature makes MCP obsolete:.

It doesn't materially change anything wrt authentication, authorization and audit policy layers; Your agent still makes those same MCP calls, with the same auth tokens and context and what materially changes is how much context gets into the model window and how much can be discarded.

It has been revealed that the idea, and the name, predate Anthropic's release. Cloudflare introduced Code Mode for MCP converting MCP tools into a TypeScript API that models code against inside sandboxed Workers, where bindings keep API keys away from generated code. Anthropic's own post on code execution with MCP described one workflow dropping from 150,000 to 2,000 tokens, and the Claude API offers programmatic tool calling in a remote code execution container. Code Mode instead runs the script in the developer's local session, against Claude Code's built-in tools and permission system.

Code Mode remains opt-in and experimental, and Anthropic collects feedback through /feedback. Setup steps and troubleshooting are in the Claude Code documentation.

Google DeepMind Agent Teams Discover Lean-Verified Quantum Algorithms

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1008 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google DeepMind presented research on November 23, 2026 showing that teams of Gemini 4 agents, checked by the Lean theorem prover, produced lower-cost quantum programs for five problems.
  • The work covered parallel Grover search, fixed-point arcsin arithmetic and three simulations: alpha-particle stopping power in fusion fuel, non-Born–Oppenheimer molecular dynamics and Cytochrome P450 energy estimation.
  • Recent findings suggest that quantum algorithm discovery has an evaluation problem: candidates spanning hundreds or thousands of qubits generally cannot be tested through classical simulation or on present quantum processors.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google DeepMind presented research on November 23, 2026 showing that teams of Gemini 4 agents, checked by the Lean theorem prover, produced lower-cost quantum programs for five problems. Its largest scientific gain was an 11.8-fold reduction in the estimated cost of a fusion simulation, in work with Google Quantum AI.

The work covered parallel Grover search, fixed-point arcsin arithmetic and three simulations: alpha-particle stopping power in fusion fuel, non-Born–Oppenheimer molecular dynamics and Cytochrome P450 energy estimation. For fault-tolerant circuits, researchers measured spacetime cost as peak logical qubits multiplied by T-gate count, combining memory demand with operations that are costly in error-corrected quantum computers.

Recent findings suggest that quantum algorithm discovery has an evaluation problem: candidates spanning hundreds or thousands of qubits generally cannot be tested through classical simulation or on present quantum processors. DeepMind’s system therefore treats a proposed circuit as a mathematical object. Researchers wrote frozen Lean specifications containing correctness and resource-cost theorems; agents supplied programs, cost bounds and proofs, using high-level optimization prompts rather than problem-specific starting ideas. The large autonomous runs used Gemini 4 Carbon models.

It has been revealed that the Lean 4 library is grounded in quantum Hoare logic, a logic for reasoning about preconditions and postconditions, and handles classical control flow alongside unitary operations, measurement and qubit reset. It can prove bounds on expected or worst-case resource costs. An external verifier replayed every submission in a clean sandbox against the frozen specification, checking dependent definitions, permitted axioms and claimed costs to prevent agents from weakening theorems or otherwise gaming local checks.

Independent teams shared their best verified solutions, reusable lemmas and reviewed dead-end notes through a wiki, while agents met every four hours in virtual conferences to critique proposals. Conference claims counted only after verification. The paper estimates that, averaged across the three scientific applications, 61% of the measured cost reduction originated within teams, 15% came through cross-team wiki material and 24% through conferences, while cautioning that credit is difficult to separate cleanly.

For fusion stopping power, the discovered circuit moves electron interactions onto a real-space grid and uses Pauli exclusion to simplify short-range interactions. The paper reports that this cut walk steps by a factor of 12.8; retaining total electron momentum in a 42-qubit register reduced T gates per step by another 10%. The resulting circuit needs 4,338 logical qubits, down from 5,650, but uses 1.42 times as many T gates per step, illustrating why the combined memory-and-operation metric matters.

In a recent development, for non-Born–Oppenheimer dynamics of C₂₃H₂₀N₃O, the paper reports an 8.22-fold cost reduction, from 4.98 × 10¹⁵ to 6.06 × 10¹⁴, through measurement-based cleanup of copied coordinates, a Bernstein-polynomial approximation that avoids the baseline’s multiplication step when evaluating 1/r and simpler handling of nuclear charges. For Cytochrome P450, cost fell by a factor of 2.49 while memory dropped from 481 to 333 logical qubits, principally by replacing bulky angle lookups with one-hot registers, which mark the chosen term on a dedicated qubit.

Sources indicate that the arithmetic result combined two forms of search. The paper reports that agents first tested circuits within a restricted, classically simulable gate set, then used Lean verification to optimize beyond it, reaching 3,698 T gates on 100 qubits and reducing spacetime cost by a factor greater than 290. For parallel Grover search, where the circuits had to succeed with certainty, expected oracle rounds fell by factors of up to 1.22 when finding any target and 2.57 when finding all targets in the tested multi-target regimes.

The November 23 post is the later official presentation of research already public elsewhere. The arXiv record for Discovering formally verified quantum programs with AI dates the first submission to November 6, 2026 and the third version to November 16, 2026; the manuscript is dated November 17, 2026. The official repository carries a November 17, 2026 publication commit.

It has been revealed that the repository separates the core QuantumComputation library from QuantumComputationSpecs, which holds specifications and benchmark challenges; discovered programs sit in its discoveries branch. It is under active development, with explicit models for costing classical computation and control flow listed as the next milestone.

DeepMind indicates the end-to-end simulations still demand far more resources than projected for the first fault-tolerant quantum computers and that further orders-of-magnitude reductions are needed. The results are also bounded by their specifications: the molecular-dynamics task requires correctness even on unphysical input states, while the Cytochrome P450 task fixes the tensor factorization and excludes possible representation improvements.

The immediate advance is a verified discovery process rather than a demonstration on quantum hardware: agents can propose and prove reductions beyond classical testing, while humans remain responsible for the physical model and cost conventions those proofs enforce. The practical question is how much of the reported gain remains as specifications grow to include error-correcting codes, qubit routing and physical layouts.

Their work explores how AI techniques are being applied to optimize qubit control, improve quantum error correction, and accelerate quantum algorithms—bridging the gap between abstract theory and experimental progress.

Recent findings suggest that with a theoretical and deeply intellectual perspective, Aster examines research emerging from quantum labs, academic institutions, and national research programs. They focus on how machine learning models assist in managing quantum noise, calibrating hardware, and navigating the immense complexity of quantum systems, while remaining clear about the limitations and uncertainties that still define the field.

#104083. Back to The Future: Evaluating AI Agents on Predicting Future Events

📅 17 Jul 2025 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1855 w)

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Back to The Future: Evaluating AI Agents on Predicting Future Events

📅 17 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1855 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Most current AI benchmarks focus on answering questions about the past, either by testing models on existing knowledge (in a static manner, such as HLE or GPQA, or augmented, like BrowseComp or GAIA) or previously solved problems (like PaperBench, DABStep, or most coding evaluations).
  • Forecasting future events is a complex and holistic task: it requires sophisticated reasoning, synthesis, weighing probabilities and genuine understanding, rather than pattern matching against or searching existing information.
  • It has been revealed that beyond its inherent importance, this forecasting-based approach also solves many methodological problems faced by current evaluations and benchmarks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Most current AI benchmarks focus on answering questions about the past, either by testing models on existing knowledge (in a static manner, such as HLE or GPQA, or augmented, like BrowseComp or GAIA) or previously solved problems (like PaperBench, DABStep, or most coding evaluations). However, we believe that more valuable AI, and ultimately AGI, will be distinguished by its ability to use this past to forecast interesting aspects of the future, rather than merely reciting old facts.

Forecasting future events is a complex and holistic task: it requires sophisticated reasoning, synthesis, weighing probabilities and genuine understanding, rather than pattern matching against or searching existing information. Evaluating models on their ability to predict future outcomes, whether in science, economics, geopolitics, or technology tests the kind of intelligence that creates real-world value.

It has been revealed that beyond its inherent importance, this forecasting-based approach also solves many methodological problems faced by current evaluations and benchmarks. Traditional benchmarks that measure accuracy on fixed test sets are inevitably affected by possible data contamination, and without access to the full reproducible training pipeline of a model, it's hard to trust the results. The most serious evaluation efforts now keep their test sets completely private, creating a frustrating arms race between evaluators and potential "gaming the leaderboard" mechanics (Singh et al., 2025).

In a recent development, forecasting makes contamination impossible by design, as you can't train on data that doesn't yet exist! This creates a level playing field where success depends on reasoning capability rather than memorization.

Perhaps most importantly, predictions about the future are inherently verifiable. We can wait and see who was right, creating an objective, time-stamped measure of model performance.

Sources indicate that we therefore propose evaluating agents on their ability to predict future events (Ye et al., 2024; Karger et al., 2025). FutureBench draws from real-world prediction markets and emerging news to create interesting prediction tasks grounded in actual future outcomes. We collect events from platforms and live news coverages and manifold markets, filtering them to focus on emerging events worth predicting. Using an agent-based approach, we curate scenarios that require genuine reasoning rather than simple pattern matching. Think geopolitical developments, market movements, or technology adoption trends - events where informed analysis actually matters.

This is the obvious question, and it's at the heart of what makes this benchmark interesting! We believe the answer cannot be a simple “yes” or a “no”, as it mostly depends on the actual questions; there are always notable caveats to consider. Humans constantly use their ability to weigh current information to predict future events. Aren't most career moves, relationship choices, or even business strategies essentially bets on future outcomes?

Some predictions involve irreducible uncertainty (Will it rain on December 17th, 2027 at noon?), but many don't. When a skilled analyst predicts a company's quarterly earnings or a policy expert forecasts election outcomes, they're using available information to make informed decisions. This is precisely what we're asking AI agents to do with FutureBench! The task isn't to get agents to fortune-tell, but rather to synthesize information and reason under stronger uncertainty than most other benchmarks.

The agent's prediction quality directly reflects its ability to search relevant information, synthesize complex data, and reason about cause-and-effect relationships. These are precisely the capabilities we want to measure in real-world applications.

Recent findings suggest that tools like DeepResearch are already used for market analysis and strategic planning. The quality of information collection strongly correlates with decision-making effectiveness. FutureBench is inspired by this evaluation process and tries to compute agents’ quality with objective, verifiable outcomes.

Building a benchmark that tests real prediction capabilities requires a steady stream of meaningful questions. We've developed two complementary approaches that capture different types of future events:.

According to recent reports, our first approach uses AI to mine current events for prediction opportunities. We deploy a smolagents-based agent to scrape a few major news websites, analyze front-page articles, and generate prediction questions about their likely outcomes. The agent reads through and identifies interesting articles and formulates specific, time-bound questions from their content, for example "Will the Federal Reserve cut interest rates by at least 0.25% by July 1st, 2025?".

We guide this process with carefully crafted prompts that specify what makes a good prediction question—events that are meaningful, verifiable, and uncertain extraction time.

In a recent development, the agent typically generates 5 questions per scraping session, with a time horizon of a single week, meaning that we assume we’ll know the answer to the question after seven days. This gives us a natural pipeline of fresh evaluation material tied to real-world events.

Sources indicate that our second source draws from Polymarket. These questions come from a prediction market platform where real participants make forecasts about future events. We currently ingest around 8 questions per week.

However, the raw data needs filtering. We apply strong filtering to remove general questions regarding temperature and some questions regarding the stock and crypto markets, which would otherwise be too numerous for practical use in our benchmark. In addition to this, polymarket questions have less constraints regarding the final “realization” time, the actual outcome of the event could be available only next month or by the end of the year. These are still very relevant questions, but the data collection of the outcome is more sparse.

Here's an example of what comes out of our question generation pipeline:.

The next question is, what does this type of benchmark allow us to measure? The framework operates on three distinct levels, allowing us to isolate exactly what we're measuring:.

In a recent development, level 1: Framework Comparison Keep the underlying LLMs and tools constant while varying frameworks. How does a LangChain-based agent compare to one built with CrewAI when both use GPT-4 and the same search tools? This isolates the impact of different agentic frameworks.

Level 2: Tool Performance Fix the LLM and framework while comparing different implementations. Which search tool (for example Tavily, Google, Bing) leads to better predictions than other search engines, holding everything else constant? This reveals which tools actually provide value. How much value do tools bring in general with respect to models without tools?

Level 3: Model Capabilities Hold the framework and tools constant while testing different LLMs. Given access to the same set of tools, does DeepSeek-V3 use them as effectively as GPT-4? This measures pure reasoning ability. This systematic approach lets us understand exactly where performance gains and losses occur in the agent pipeline.

The benchmark also serves as a robust test of instruction following. Agents must respect specific formatting requirements and generate actions that can be correctly parsed and executed. In practice, this often reveals where smaller language models struggle with complex multi-step reasoning.

🚀 Try it yourself! Explore the live leaderboard: FutureBench Interactive Leaderboard.

We use SmolAgents as a baseline agent framework for all the questions. We also compute performance on the base models. For the prediction task itself, the agents get access to a focused toolkit:.

This intentionally lean setup forces agents to be strategic about information gathering while still providing the tools needed for informed predictions.

Sources indicate that we compare different models using smolagents as a baseline (you can find the leaderboard on our HF Space). We also run the standard language models without internet access to estimate a general prior. As expected, we see agentic models performing better than simple language models; stronger models show more stable prediction quality. Overall we also find interesting patterns in how different models try to approach a question:.

Running this benchmark has revealed insights into how different models approach information gathering. One striking difference is with respect to scraping. GPT-4.1 appears to rely more on search results. Claude3.7 and 4 explore the web space in more detail and tend to use web scraping more frequently; this thorough approach also means collecting many more input tokens during the research process, thus increasing the cost.

Models show interesting approaches to making predictions, for example, to answer the question "Will annual inflation increase by 2.6 or more in June?":.

The DeepSeekV3 agent analyzed June 2025 inflation prospects by searching recent CPI data (finding current inflation at 2.4-2.8%), considered tariff impacts as upward pressure, and concluded inflation would exceed the 2.6% threshold.

Claude3.7 analyzed June 2025 inflation through comprehensive research (11 searches vs DeepSeekV3's 3), systematically gathering May 2025 CPI data (2.4% year-over-year), identifying decelerating monthly trends (0.2%→0.1%), weighing tariff pressures against Fed restrictive policy, calculating precise 0.2% gap needed, and concluded recent deceleration made reaching 2.6% threshold unlikely, answering "No.".

GPT4.1 analyzed June 2025 inflation through targeted searches for market consensus and forecasts, identified May 2025 CPI at 2.4% (below 2.5% expectations), noted weak 0.1% monthly increases, found no forecaster predictions of 2.6%+ for June, and concluded the jump from 2.4% to 2.6% was unlikely given recent below-expectation trends.

Interestingly, Claude was the only model that tried to access the Bureau of Labor Statistics website to scrape it directly, which failed because it is a .gov website and we do not allow this type of action.

The models exhibit distinct reasoning patterns in their outputs. GPT's analysis focused on consensus forecasts as the key signal for future events rather than extrapolating from current data, while Claude's approach exhibited rigorous analytical structure with its systematic pro/con framework and quantitative gap analysis, and DeepSeekV3's output displayed explicit acknowledgment of data limitations and systematic methodology adjustments when initial approaches encountered constraints.

It has been revealed that these behavioral differences reveal interesting patterns in how different models approach information gathering. The variations in web usage and token consumption suggest that models have distinct strategies for tackling prediction tasks, which FutureBench can help us measure and understand.

One challenge is that evaluation can be expensive due to the large number of input tokens. For example, Claude tends to visit web pages frequently, thus accumulating many input tokens. In a multi-turn loop, this can make the number of input tokens skyrocket very quickly. This increases the cost of any subsequent generation, even though most tokens are eventually cached.

Recent findings suggest that futureBench is an evolving benchmark, as we discover latest findings and better patterns, we’ll keep incorporating them. We would love feedback from the community to understand how to better source questions, which experiments to run and which data is the most interesting to analyze.

Tech Report: Ai2 Releases RoboTrack to Test and Train Robot Point Trackers

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1004 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Allen Institute for AI (Ai2) released RoboTrack on November 23, 2026, pairing a robotic point-tracking benchmark and training suite with two models.
  • Point tracking follows the same physical point through video, estimates when it is occluded and identifies it when it reappears.
  • RoboTrack-Bench contains 307 clips and 2,522 human-verified tracks drawn from DROID, Ego-Exo4D, MolmoAct 2 and EgoVerse.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Allen Institute for AI (Ai2) released RoboTrack on November 23, 2026, pairing a robotic point-tracking benchmark and training suite with two models. Ai2 reported that RoboTracker completed 17 of 20 wet-lab pipetting trials, compared with eight using object masks and five using optical flow.

Point tracking follows the same physical point through video, estimates when it is occluded and identifies it when it reappears. Those trajectories can help robots learn from demonstrations and guide manipulation, but grippers, hands, clutter and changing viewpoints can break that correspondence. RoboTrack addresses the problem with RoboTrack-Bench, a human-verified evaluation set, and RoboTrack-15M, synthetic training data generated from robot simulations. A technical report and model weights accompany the release.

RoboTrack-Bench contains 307 clips and 2,522 human-verified tracks drawn from DROID, Ego-Exo4D, MolmoAct 2 and EgoVerse. The clips cover four robot embodiments and human manipulation in cluttered scenes, filmed from first- and third-person views. Thirty-three synchronized two-camera pairs identify the same physical points across views.

Recent findings suggest that annotators prioritized moving or occluded points over static backgrounds, and a separate verification pass checked every track frame by frame. Fifty-seven percent of points are occluded at least once; each track provides position and visibility labels for every frame.

Recent findings suggest that average Jaccard (AJ), a higher-is-better measure combining tracking accuracy and visibility prediction, is the main metric. Ai2’s evaluation of the final CoTracker3, BootsTAPNext, AllTracker and CoWTracker models found scores 3.0 to 6.6 AJ lower on RoboTrack-Bench than on RoboTAP. CoWTracker, the strongest off-the-shelf baseline, fell from 70.5 AJ on RoboTAP to 63.9, indicating that controlled tabletop results did not transfer intact to the benchmark’s broader interactions and viewpoints.

Recent findings suggest that bootsTAPNext adds training on 15 million real videos to TAPNext. Ai2 reported that this raised its RoboTrack-Bench score from 55.1 to 60.2 AJ but lowered its synthetic RGB-Stacking result from 75.0 to 65.5, so the extra training helped on real manipulation while hurting on simulated block stacking.

Sources indicate that roboTrack-15M targets robot-object interaction rather than general scene motion. Its 3,000 videos capture 1,500 picking episodes across 300 procedurally generated homes, recorded by wrist and base-mounted cameras. A simulated Franka arm handles everyday objects, while MolmoSpaces and MuJoCo supply geometry, object poses, depth and camera information to calculate point positions and visibility without human annotation. Each video contains 5,000 tracks.

Point selection proved as important as dataset size. Ai2 reported that its first synthetic-data attempt produced no RoboTrack-Bench gain because many points lay on static backgrounds. Restricting supervision to the robot and movable objects, and excluding the robot’s fixed base, produced a 63.0 AJ ablation score, 1.5 points above the Kubric-only control. That ties the improvement to supervision resembling manipulation motion rather than to synthetic-data volume alone.

RoboTracker fine-tunes the 17-million-parameter AllTracker, while RoboTracker-Warp fine-tunes CoWTracker, which has about 1 billion parameters. Both use RoboTrack-15M alongside the original training data.

Ai2 reports that RoboTracker improved from 62.6 to 63.4 AJ on RoboTrack-Bench and RoboTracker-Warp from 63.9 to 66.0, with both models remaining close to their base models on general video. Warp had the highest AJ among the evaluated models on four of five benchmarks. Both checkpoints are listed in Ai2’s public artifact collection, but RoboTracker-Warp’s weights are restricted to noncommercial use.

The wet-lab system used one arm of a bimanual I2RT YAM robot to pick up an electronic pipette, draw liquid from one vial, dispense it into another and return the pipette to its holder. It learned the sequence from one teleoperated demonstration divided into steps. At each key frame, RoboTracker estimated the alignment between demonstration and live-camera points; the robot then replayed the demonstrated motion without further feedback, making alignment accuracy central to success.

The test split layouts evenly between clear views and partial occlusion. Ai2’s results show RoboTracker succeeding in all 10 clear-view trials and seven of 10 occluded trials. SAM3 mask-centroid alignment completed seven clear-view transfers but only one occluded transfer, while RAFT optical flow completed three and two, respectively.

Ai2 attributes optical-flow failures to large displacements and mask failures to similar-looking objects or occlusion. Point tracking instead carries the same vial’s correspondence through the video, although RoboTracker still failed under extended or complete occlusion. The experiment connects better point correspondence to physical execution in a task where the pipette tip must align with a vial opening within millimeters.

Those results do not resolve the trackers’ remaining weaknesses. Ai2 says they still struggle with long occlusions, re-identifying points after reappearance and small objects against busy backgrounds. The benchmark is modest in scale, deformable-object and tool-use tasks are underrepresented, and only two tracker families were fine-tuned. RoboTrack-15M separately omits human hands and industrial, outdoor and laboratory scenes, and its simulated rendering and motion differ from real video.

Ai2’s next step is to simulate precise actions such as pipette handling more closely and test whether their trajectories improve tracking during deployment. The open question is whether training data built around the exact manipulation a robot must perform can extend the gains beyond simulated object picking.

Consilium: When Multiple LLMs Collaborate

📅 17 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1208 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Picture this: four AI experts sitting around a poker table, debating your toughest decisions in real-time.
  • The platform works both as a visual Gradio interface and as an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server that integrates directly with applications like Cline (Claude Desktop had problems as the timeout could not be adjusted).
  • This wasn't my original hackathon idea.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Picture this: four AI experts sitting around a poker table, debating your toughest decisions in real-time. That's exactly what Consilium, the multi-LLM platform I built during the Gradio Agents & MCP Hackathon, does. It lets AI models discuss complex questions and reach consensus through structured debate.

The platform works both as a visual Gradio interface and as an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server that integrates directly with applications like Cline (Claude Desktop had problems as the timeout could not be adjusted). The core idea was always about LLMs reaching consensus through discussion; that's where the name Consilium came from. Later, other decision modes like majority voting and ranked choice were added to make the collaboration more sophisticated.

This wasn't my original hackathon idea. I initially wanted to build a simple MCP server to talk to my projects in RevenueCat. But I reconsidered when I realized a multi-LLM platform where these models discuss questions and return well-reasoned answers would be far more compelling.

The timing turned out to be perfect. Shortly after the hackathon, Microsoft published their AI Diagnostic Orchestrator (MAI-DxO), which is essentially an AI doctor panel with different roles like "Dr. Challenger Agent" that iteratively diagnose patients. In their setup with OpenAI o3, they correctly solved 85.5% of medical diagnosis benchmark cases, while practicing physicians achieved only 20% accuracy. This validates exactly what Consilium demonstrates: multiple AI perspectives collaborating can dramatically outperform individual analysis.

After settling on the concept, I needed something that worked as both an MCP server and an engaging Hugging Face space demo. Initially I considered using the standard Gradio Chat component, but I wanted my submission to stand out. The idea was to seat LLMs around a table in a boardroom with speech bubbles, which should capture the collaborative discussion while also making it visually engaging. As I did not manage to style a standard table nicely so it was actually recognized as a table, I went for a poker-style roundtable. This approach also let me submit to two hackathon tracks by building a custom Gradio component and MCP server.

According to recent reports, the custom Gradio component became the heart of the submission; the poker-style roundtable where participants sit and display speech bubbles showing their responses, thinking status, and research activities immediately caught the eye of anyone visiting the space. The component development was remarkably smooth thanks to Gradio's excellent developer experience, though I did encounter one documentation gap around PyPI publishing that led to my first contribution to the Gradio project.

The visual design proved robust throughout the hackathon; after the initial implementation, only features like user-defined avatars and center table text were added, while the core interaction model remained unchanged.

If you are interested in creating your own custom Gradio component you should take a look at Custom Components in 5 minutes and yes the title does not lie; it literally only takes 5 minutes for the basic setup.

In a recent development, the visual roundtable maintains state through a session-based dictionary system where each user gets isolated state storage via user_sessions[session_id]. The core state object tracks participants, messages, currentSpeaker, thinking, and showBubbles arrays that are updated through update_visual_state() callbacks. When models are thinking, speaking, or research is being executed, the engine pushes incremental state updates to the frontend by appending to the messages array and toggling speaker/thinking states, creating the real-time visual flow without complex state machines - just direct JSON state mutations synchronized between backend processing and frontend rendering.

While implementing, I realized there was no real discussion happening between the LLMs because they lacked clear roles. They received the full context of ongoing discussions but didn't know how to engage meaningfully. I introduced distinct roles to create productive debate dynamics, which, after a few tweaks, ended up being like this:.

It has been revealed that this solved the discussion problem but raised a new question: how to determine consensus or identify the strongest argument? I implemented a lead analyst system where users select one LLM to synthesize the final result and evaluate whether consensus was reached.

I also wanted people to control communication structure. Beyond the default full-context sharing, I added two alternative modes:.

It has been revealed that finally, discussions need endpoints. I implemented configurable rounds (1-5), with testing showing that more rounds increase the likelihood of reaching consensus (though at higher computational cost).

The current model selection includes Mistral Large, DeepSeek-R1, Meta-Llama-3.3-70B, and QwQ-32B. While notable models like Claude Sonnet and OpenAI's o3 are absent, this reflected hackathon credit availability and sponsor award considerations rather than technical limitations.

For models supporting function calling, I integrated a dedicated research agent that appears as another roundtable participant. Rather than giving models direct web access, this agent approach provides visual clarity about external resource availability and ensures consistent access across all function-calling models.

According to recent reports, the research agent accesses five sources: Web Search, Wikipedia, arXiv, GitHub, and SEC EDGAR. I built these tools on an extensible base class architecture for future expansion while focusing on freely embeddable resources.

Since research operations can be time-intensive, the speech bubbles display progress indicators and time estimates to maintain user engagement during longer research tasks.

After the hackathon, Deborah Dahl introduced me to the Open Floor Protocol, which aligns perfectly with the roundtable approach. This protocol provides standardized JSON message formatting for cross-platform agent communication. Its key differentiator from other agent-to-agent protocols is that all agents maintain constant conversation awareness exactly like sitting at the same table. Another feature I have not seen with other protocols is that the floor manager can dynamically invite and remove agents from the floor and agents.

The protocol's interaction patterns map directly to Consilium's architecture:.

I'm presently integrating Open Floor Protocol support to allow users to add any OFP-compliant agents to their roundtable discussions. You can follow this development at: https://huggingface.co/spaces/azettl/consilium_ofp.

In a recent development, the hackathon introduced me to multi-agent debate research I hadn't previously encountered, including foundational studies like Encouraging Divergent Thinking in Large Language Models through Multi-Agent Debate. The community experience was remarkable; all participants actively supported each other through Discord feedback and collaboration. Seeing my roundtable component integrated into another hackathon project was one of my highlights working on Consilium.

I will continue to work on Consilium and with expanded model selection, Open Floor Protocol integration, and configurable agent roles, the platform could support virtually any multi-agent debate scenario imaginable.

Building Consilium reinforced my conviction that AI's future lies not just in more powerful individual models but in systems enabling effective AI collaboration. As specialized smaller language models become more efficient and resource-friendly, I believe roundtables of task-specific SLMs with dedicated research agents may provide compelling alternatives to general-purpose large language models for many use cases.
