💡 Key Takeaways
  • Venture firm Team8 confirmed Infra Village on November 23 at the Newly introduced York Stock Exchange, expanding its work building and investing in AI and software infrastructure companies.
  • The exchange was the venue, not the product.
  • According to recent reports, the infrastructure needs change once a pilot goes live.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Venture firm Team8 confirmed Infra Village on November 23 at the Newly introduced York Stock Exchange, expanding its work building and investing in AI and software infrastructure companies. The initiative adds a community for the executives responsible for putting AI into production, including CIOs, CTOs and infrastructure leaders. Team8 says it manages more than $2 billion across its business, but the company’s announcement did not disclose a new fund, a dedicated investment budget or the first companies the initiative would create.

The exchange was the venue, not the product. The idea is to put the people buying and operating infrastructure in the same room as the founders building it. An executive can explain where a promising pilot broke down, what it cost to keep running, or why an existing tool could not fit the manufacturer’s approval process. Founders can use those examples to decide whether they are hearing about a problem specific to one customer or something many companies would pay to fix.

According to recent reports, the infrastructure needs change once a pilot goes live. A prototype can call one model and log a handful of requests. A production service has to deal with spikes in traffic, slow responses and failed calls. It needs to track which model or workflow produced an output and which team owns the cost. If a manufacturer routes a request to a less expensive model, it also needs to know whether the change hurts the outcome that matters, such as whether the system correctly resolves a customer’s glitch.

Team8 already has investments that illustrate those problems. Port develops an internal developer portal that gives teams a view of software they own and a way to request or launch approved workflows. In an AI rollout, that kind of catalog can help a team find out who owns a service before an incident lands in the wrong queue. Finout works on a different problem: attributing AI and cloud spending so that teams can see which workloads are driving costs. Neither example is a new release tied to Infra Village. They show the kinds of operational problems Team8 is already backing.

The distinction is useful when evaluating a new AI infrastructure tool. A developer portal can make it easier for a team to deploy a service, but that does not tell finance what the service costs to run. A cost dashboard can surface a spike, but it does not by itself explain which change caused it. Whether those functions should live in one platform or stay separate depends on how much companies already have invested in their monitoring, cloud and developer tools.

Team8 is borrowing from the way it built relationships between security executives and founders through its CISO Village. It also used the Newly introduced York event to announce its Next AI Leaders program. That recognition may help bring operators into the community, but the results of the investment initiative will be easier to judge by the companies it creates and the customers they win.

The practical test is whether teams in different businesses keep describing the same bottlenecks. If several operators cannot reliably trace a model-related failure back to the deployment that caused it, for example, a founder has more to work with than a broad prediction about the growth of enterprise AI. The launch gives Team8 another way to find those problems. It does not yet show how many will become standalone businesses.

Quality IMAP, Part 2: Mailbox Concurrency

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2596 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Deuxfleurs

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that in the past year, we have been significantly improving the reliability and correctness of Aerogramme's IMAP implementation.
  • Aerogramme is an experimental email server (& calendar, contacts), designed to be geo-distributed, hosted outside of datacenters, on refurbished hardware, and reliable even in presence of network problems and hardware failures.
  • Recent findings suggest that this is the second post in a series in which we argue that implementing an IMAP server is not easy, essentially due to two classes of features that are fundamentally challenging to implement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that in the past year, we have been significantly improving the reliability and correctness of Aerogramme's IMAP implementation. This is the second part in a series discussing why implementing IMAP correctly is not so easy, and presenting our work on making Aerogramme's IMAP code as high-quality as we can. Today we focus on challenges that arise when considering concurrent access to a mailbox.

Aerogramme is an experimental email server (& calendar, contacts), designed to be geo-distributed, hosted outside of datacenters, on refurbished hardware, and reliable even in presence of network problems and hardware failures. It is built on top of Garage and shares the same philosophy. Aerogramme is AI-free: we do not wish to use unethical technology and prefer to spend effort on careful craftmanship and community-building.

Recent findings suggest that this is the second post in a series in which we argue that implementing an IMAP server is not easy, essentially due to two classes of features that are fundamentally challenging to implement. In the previous post, we talked about the first class of features: fine-grained retrieval and querying of email contents. In this post, we talk about the second class of features that make implementing an IMAP server tricky: concurrent access to user mailboxes.

Industry observers note that concurrent and distributed software are famously hard to get right; concurrency bugs are known to be hard to find. In our recent work on refining Aerogramme we have tried to approach the problem from different angles. This is the topic of this post: the different ways in which we have improved the correctness of Aerogramme in concurrent settings.

This work was funded by NLNet under the "Aerogramme 1.0" grant, and could not have been possible without their support.

Feel free to join the Aerogramme matrix channel for updates or if you just want to chat!

A core feature of IMAP is that multiple email clients can simultaneously access the same mailbox. For example, we may want to access our emails both from our phone and our computer. Concurrent access to a mailbox can also happen when a single client is involved: some clients (including Thunderbird) open multiple concurrent connections to a same mailbox to speed up processing. In any case, clients accessing the same mailbox should be able to coordinate between themselves and avoid stepping on each other's toes.

In a recent development, why must clients be able to coordinate when accessing the same mailbox? Assume that we are an email client that sends two commands to read information from a mailbox. Since another client can modify the mailbox in between the two commands, the information we read may have been invalidated by the other client and is now inconsistent! Clients thus need to be able to detect concurrent changes made by other clients. Similarly, a client that reconnects to the server after being offline needs to fetch the changes that happened while it was disconnected. This is possible thanks to mechanisms defined by the IMAP specification and that specifically exist because concurrent access is allowed.

The overall consistency of the mailbox data must be taken seriously: an IMAP server exposing inconsistent views of a mailbox could result in a confused client deleting the wrong emails, for example.

To our best knowledge, concurrent mailbox behaviors are tackled in the following (parts of) specifications:.

The base IMAP4 specification has few explicit mentions of concurrent mailbox access, but does talk about re-synchronizing disconnected clients, which can be seen as a restricted form of concurrent access. It defines mechanisms for assigning IDs to emails (UIDNEXT/UIDVALIDITY) and associated properties which can be extrapolated to concurrent contexts. This is relevant when concurrently adding new emails to a mailbox. After an email has been added to a mailbox it cannot be modified, so there are no issues with reading emails concurrently.

The improvements that we will talk about in this post are related to these aspects of the base IMAP specification.

According to recent reports, as an additional complication, IMAP defines in fact two (!) email-numbering systems. One of these has the drawback that deleting an email can invalidate email IDs used in concurrent commands. This is purely a quirk of a numbering system that can nowadays be considered legacy, but must still be supported. This issue is not acknowledged in the base IMAP specification, leaving a class of problematic behaviors completely unspecified, but is later addressed in an informational RFC which specifies what to do in such cases.

Aerogramme's latest release includes changes and bugfixes to make sure that we follow the recommendations of this informational RFC, but we won't enter into the details of these legacy quirks in this post.

Recent findings suggest that email flags can be modified concurrently, but the base IMAP specification does not specify a mechanism for clients to coordinate around flag changes. This is done in the later CONDSTORE specification that extends IMAP with mechanisms to coordinate flag changes across concurrent connections. Aerogramme has preliminary support for CONDSTORE, but we disabled it in the last release, as we found out it needs a redesign to be nicer to email clients1.

Recent findings suggest that A later specification further extends IMAP and CONDSTORE by adding a more general mechanism (QRESYNC) for synchronizing all mailbox changes across concurrent sessions. Aerogramme does not supports QRESYNC at the moment2.

Sources indicate that on top of the complexity carried by the IMAP specification, Aerogramme's distributed infrastructure comes with its own challenges. Not only we need to think about concurrency at the IMAP protocol level, but also internally in Aerogramme: how do we handle concurrent changes to the server internal data storage? Can we simply take a lock or a transaction over mailbox data each time we need to enhancement it, serializing all concurrent updates? The answer is no: things are a bit more complicated...

Recall that Aerogramme is a distributed IMAP server. A typical Aerogramme deployment looks like this:.

In this schema, A nodes are Aerogramme instances running on separate servers. Running multiple Aerogramme nodes provides fault-tolerance: even if some of the nodes crash, the Aerogramme cluster stays operational as long as one node remains available. When an email client (a C node) connects to the "Aerogramme cluster" (the dashed potato), it can open a connection to any of the Aerogramme nodes, depending on what kind of load-balancing is implemented.

Aerogramme nodes do not talk to each other directly and do not store data themselves. Instead, they connect a shared Garage cluster (itself geo-distributed with fault-tolerance properties) which stores data for the whole Aerogramme cluster (emails, mailbox state, etc.).

This means that an Aerogramme node deals with concurrency at two levels. It must handle concurrent connections from email clients to a mailbox, as we explained before. But it must also handle concurrent changes made by other Aerogramme nodes to the data stored in Garage. These concurrent accesses must be coordinated properly so that the Aerogramme cluster exposes a consistent view of a mailbox (according to IMAP's consistency requirements), even when connecting concurrently to different nodes of the Aerogramme cluster.

In a recent development, A central challenge in Aerogramme's design is that Garage does not provide locks, transactions, or anything that would require distributed consensus between Garage nodes. This is by design, and it allows Garage and Aerogramme to perform well even with non-negligible latency between nodes. The consequence for Aerogramme is that its nodes cannot simply reason on their shared data as if it was updated sequentially. The approach used by Aerogramme insteadâa convergent operation logâis a central part of its design. We'll talk more below on how we adjusted the consistency properties provided by Garage when storing that operation log.

A basic IMAP mechanism is assigning IDs to emails when they are added into a mailbox. Adding emails concurrently can already make it tricky to assign these IDs. Our first step was to find a way of testing this case and to fix any bugs that we would find.

Industry observers note that for context, IMAP specifies that each email in a mailbox must be assigned a UID: a number that identifies it uniquely. UIDs are assigned in increasing order; this allows clients to check if new emails have been added by checking the value of the mailbox "next UID". On top of that, IMAP also allows the server to renumber the emails with different UIDs. When this happens, the IMAP server must increase the value of UIDVALIDITY, a global integer counter attached to the mailbox. Now, in Aerogramme, increasing UIDVALIDITY is done in some cases when emails are added concurrently in the mailbox in a way that would assign conflicting UIDs; an unavoidable consequence of its distributed architecture.

From an IMAP client's perspective UIDVALIDITY must always increase monotonically. We also assume that this property must hold across all concurrent connections; although the specification does not say so explicitly, it is the most prudent assumption since a single client may open multiple connections to the same mailbox.

The logical next step is to setup a test bench to ensure that it holds in practice for Aerogramme! We deployed an Aerogramme cluster with three nodes, running on a simulated network with added latency between nodes. Then:.

Sources indicate that running Aerogramme on this test bench found state synchronization bugs: bugs showing that Aerogrammeâs distributed state (stored in Garage) was not always properly synchronized between nodes and concurrent sessions. Amusingly, most of these bugs were not specific to the IMAP logic related to UIDVALIDITY...

Recent findings suggest that fixing these synchronization bugs motivated a redesign of the internal read/enhancement mailbox interface. In Aerogramme, the IMAP "business logic" accesses mailbox state stored in distributed storage using an abstract interface exposing a small number of operations. Before, these operations were the following (in pseudo-Rust):.

The synchronization bugs found during testing revealed that this interface is in fact error-prone and tricky to reason about:.

The solution was to redesign Aerogramme's mailbox state interface to provide more control over state synchronization: reading concurrent changes from storage becomes a separate operation, laying the following interface:.

This new interface separates local reasoning about mailbox contents from synchronization. This makes it easier to write the IMAP logic in a way that is "obviously correct". Plainly speaking, this interface provides "local" views of mailbox state, where a view (denoted as self above) is specific to a client connection. Then, get and push_op operate on the local view with sequential semantics and are both fast; and calls to sync mark explicitly the places in the code where we have to think about concurrent changes. (Note that push_op synchronously updates remote storage, so there is no risk of losing write by forgetting to run sync.).

In a recent development, notice that the design of this interface reflects the high-level distributed architecture that we described in the previous section. For instance, an implementation of the interface needs to "merge" the operations pushed concurrently with push_op when they are put together in distributed storage, in a way that is consistent with local views; this is backed by the "convergent operation log" mentioned earlier and domain-specific logic3. Note that this interface offers no transactional or lock-like operations; matching Garage's lack of consistency primitives.

Most of the changes described here were part of Aerogramme 0.4, with in particular #129 implementing the refactoring of the state synchronization interface.

Talking about consistency guarantees in Aerogramme raises the question: what are the consistency guarantees provided by Garage, its storage backend?

This question is most relevant for Garage K2V, a NoSQL-inspired key-value store, which is used to store mailbox state as an operation log. (Garage K2V is experimental and was added in Garage for the needs of Aerogramme.) Mailbox state describes (among other things) email numbering, and as we've seen before, we want this information to be properly synchronized between Aerogramme nodes.

Garage K2V provides read-after-write consistency4: this guarantees that as soon as a write is acknowledged by Garage, any subsequent read will see the update made by the write. In terms of Aerogramme's state synchronization interface, after running push_op(op);, this guarantees that sync(); get() returns a state that includes op on any Aerogramme node.

Industry observers note that however, it turns out that read-after-write consistency alone is not enough for Aerogramme. Let's think of the fact that UIDVALIDITY needs to increase monotonically according to the IMAP specification. This means that calling sync(); get() twice on any two Aerogramme nodes must return a state that is more recent the second time than the first. In other words, when making several reads to Garage K2V in sequence, we must not see time go backward. This means that, to ensure consistency of the UIDVALIDITY counter, Aerogramme needs Garage K2V to guarantee an additional consistency property called monotonic reads!

Recent findings suggest that as a result we have extended Garage K2V to provide monotonic reads consistency. Luckily, the design of Garage makes it possible to provide monotonic reads at only a small performance cost. For a reference, Martin Kleppmann's Designing data-intensive applications (in particular ChapterÂ 9, "Linearizability and quorums") helps understanding which scenarios lead to non-monotonic reads in a quorum-based architecture like Garage's, and what to implement to guarantee monotonic reads.

To experimentally validate our changes, we first built a test bench that triggers non-monotonic reads on stock K2V. Reproducing non-monotonic reads requires variable network delays, so we deployed a Garage cluster with 3 nodes, on a simulated network with delay between cluster nodes. This test setup allows observing non-monotonic reads, by running:.

We then modified Garage K2V to provide monotonic reads by default, by implementing "synchronous read repair". We validated that we cannot observe non-monotonic reads anymore on our test bench, while they could be observed before this change: a good sanity check.

It has been revealed that this change in Garage K2V ensures that there are no scenarios in which a precise combination of network delays in the cluster results in an IMAP client observing non-increasing values of UIDVALIDITY. One could argue that this is unlikely to happen in practice; and indeed, we could not reproduce it with our simple-minded test bench: while we could observe non-monotonic reads with Garage K2V alone, we could not observe non-monotonic UIDVALIDITY on a full Garage+Aerogramme deployment with the same testing methodology. Nevertheless, we want Aerogramme to rest on strong, correct foundations as much as possible; eliminating a rare but possible cause of bugs was fully worth the effort.

The work described here was made available as part of Garage 2.4.0; it required no specific change in Aerogramme itself.

We designed Aerogramme to be part of a low-tech computing stack meant to be robust and reliable when hosted outside of data-centers, and Aerogramme's geo-distributed design is part of the answer. In the future, we hope to expand on the values and high-level ideas behind Aerogramme; this will have to be for an other blogpost...

The current implementation (now gated by a feature flag disabled by default) tends to disconnect clients more often than reasonable. This is correct with respect to the specification, but likely leads to bad UX in clients. We are working on a better strategy that does not require disconnecting clients.

The first step would be to gather data on how many clients actually support QRESYNC today...

We have not shown this "domain specific" merge logic (here, mailbox-specific) because it is a whole different topic, but it needs to be provided when instantiating the generic interface shown before with concrete state and operations.

read-after-write consistency is also the key consistency guarantee provided by Garage S3.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Arc Institute recently unveiled the Virtual Cell Challenge.
  • Goal Train a model to predict the effect on a cell of silencing a gene using CRISPR.
  • Doing things in the world of atoms is expensive, laborious and error prone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Arc Institute recently unveiled the Virtual Cell Challenge. Participants are required to train a model capable of predicting the effect of silencing a gene in a (partially) unseen cell type, a task they term context generalization. For ML engineers with little to no biology background, the jargon and required context can seem quite daunting. To encourage participation, we recapitulate the challenge in a form better suited to engineers from other disciplines.

Goal Train a model to predict the effect on a cell of silencing a gene using CRISPR.

Doing things in the world of atoms is expensive, laborious and error prone. What if we could test thousands of drug candidates without ever touching a petri dish? This is the goal of the virtual cell challenge — a model (most likely a neural network) that can simulate exactly what happens to a cell when we change some parameter. Given that tightening your feedback loop is often the best way to speed up progress, a model capable of doing this accurately would have significant impact.

To train this neural network, we will need data. For the challenge, Arc has curated a dataset of ~300k single-cell RNA sequencing profiles. It may be worthwhile to revisit the Central Dogma before continuing. This essay will build off of this to provide the ~minimum biology knowledge you'll need for the challenge.

The training set consists of a sparse matrix and some associated metadata. More specifically, we have 220k cells, and for each cell we have a transcriptome. This transcriptome is a sparse row vector, where each entry is the raw count of RNA molecules (transcripts) that the corresponding gene (our column) encodes for. Of the 220k cells, ~38k are unperturbed, meaning no gene has been silenced using CRISPR. These control cells are crucial as we will see shortly.

To understand the dataset more concretely, let's select a gene, TMSB4X (the most frequently silenced gene in the dataset) and compare the number of RNA molecules detected for a control cell and a perturbed cell.

We can see that the cell with TMSB4X silenced has a greatly reduced number of transcripts compared with the control cells.

According to recent reports, the astute among you may be wondering why you don't just measure the count of the RNA molecules before and after silencing the gene — why do we need the control cells at all? Unfortunately, reading the transcriptome destroys the cell, which is a problem reminiscent of the observer effect.

This inability to measure the cell state before and after introduces many issues, as we are forced to use a population of basal (a.k.a control, unperturbed) cells as a reference point. The control cells and perturbed cells are not entirely homogeneous even prior to the perturbation. This means that we have to now separate out our true signal, the perturbation, from noise induced by the heterogeneity.

More formally, we can model observed gene expression in perturbed cells as:.

X^p∼T^p(Dbasal)+H(Dbasal)+ε,ε∼Pε \hat{X}_p \sim \hat{T}_p(\mathcal{D}_{\text{basal}}) + H(\mathcal{D}_{\text{basal}}) + \varepsilon, \quad \varepsilon \sim P_\varepsilon X^p​∼T^p​(Dbasal​)+H(Dbasal​)+ε,ε∼Pε​.

In a recent development, prior to the Virtual Cell Challenge, Arc released STATE, their own attempt to solve the challenge using a pair of transformer based models. This serves as a strong baseline for participants to start with, so we will explore it in detail.

Sources indicate that STATE consists of two models, the State Transition Model (ST) and the State Embedding Model (SE). SE is designed to produce rich semantic embeddings of cells in an effort to improve cross cell type generalization. ST is the "cell simulator", that takes in either a transcriptome of a control cell, or an embedding of a cell produced by SE, along with a one hot encoded vector representing the perturbation of interest, and outputs the perturbed transcriptome.

The State Transition Model is a relatively simple transformer with a Llama backbone that operates upon the following:.

Sources indicate that using a covariate matched set of control cells with paired target cells should assist the model in discerning the actual effect of our intended perturbation. Both the control set tensor and the perturbation tensor are fed through independent encoders, which are simply 4 layer MLPs with GELU activations. If working directly in gene expression space (i.e producing a full transcriptome), they pass the output through a learned decoder.

ST is trained using Maximum Mean Discrepancy. Put simply, the model learns to minimize the difference between the two probability distributions.

It has been revealed that the State Embedding Model is a BERT-like autoencoder. To understand this more deeply, first we have to take a little detour for some more biological grounding.

A gene consists of exons (protein coding sections) and introns (non-protein coding sections). DNA is first transcribed into pre-mRNA, as shown above. The cell then performs Alternative Splicing. This is basically "pick and choose exons", cut out all introns. You can think of the gene as an IKEA manual for making a table. One could also construct a 3 legged table, perhaps an odd bookshelf with some effort, by leaving out some parts. These different objects are analogous to protein isoforms, proteins coded for by the same gene.

With this basic understanding, we can move on to how the SE model works. Remember, our core goal for SE is to create meaningful cell embeddings. To do this, we must first create meaningful gene embeddings.

It has been revealed that to produce a single gene embedding, we first obtain the amino acid sequence (e.g SDKPDMAEI\texttt{SDKPDMAEI}SDKPDMAEI... for TMSB4X) of all the different protein isoforms encoded for by the gene in question. We then feed these sequences to ESM2, a 15B parameter Protein Language Model from FAIR. ESM produces an embedding per amino acid, and we mean pool them together to obtain a "transcript" (a.k.a protein isoform) embedding.

Industry observers note that now we have all of these protein isoform embeddings, we then just mean pool those to get the gene embedding. Next, we project these gene embeddings to our model dimension using a learned encoder as follows:.

g~j=SiLU(LayerNorm(gjWg+bg)) \tilde{g}_j = \text{SiLU}(\text{LayerNorm}(g_j \mathbf{W}_g + \mathbf{b}_g)) g~​j​=SiLU(LayerNorm(gj​Wg​+bg​)).

According to recent reports, we've now obtained a gene embedding, but what we really want is a cell embedding. To do this, Arc represents each cell as the top 2048 genes ranked by log fold expression level.

We then construct a "cell sentence" from our 2048 gene embeddings as follows: c~(i)=[zcls,g~1(i),g~2(i),…,g~L(i),zds]∈R(L+2)×h \tilde{\mathbf{c}}^{(i)} = \left[\mathbf{z}_{\text{cls}}, \tilde{\mathbf{g}}_1^{(i)}, \tilde{\mathbf{g}}_2^{(i)}, \ldots, \tilde{\mathbf{g}}_L^{(i)}, \mathbf{z}_{\text{ds}}\right] \in \mathbb{R}^{(L+2) \times h} c~(i)=[zcls​,g~​1(i)​,g~​2(i)​,…,g~​L(i)​,zds​]∈R(L+2)×h.

We add a [CLS]\texttt{[CLS]}[CLS] token and [DS]\texttt{[DS]}[DS] token to our sentence. The [CLS]\texttt{[CLS]}[CLS] token ends up being used as our "cell embedding" (very BERT-like) and the [DS]\texttt{[DS]}[DS] token is used to "disentangle dataset-specific effects". Although the genes are sorted by log fold expression level, Arc further enforces the magnitude of each genes expression by incorporating the transcriptome in a fashion analogous to positional embeddings. Through an odd "soft binning" algorithm and 2 MLPs, they create some "expression encodings" which they then add to each gene embedding. This should modulate the magnitude of each gene embedding by how intensely it is expressed in the transcriptome.

Sources indicate that to train the model, they mask 1280 genes per cell, and the model is tasked with predicting them. The 1280 genes are selected such that they have a wide range of expression intensities. For the graphically inclined, the below demonstrates the construction of the cell sentence.

Understanding how your submission will be evaluated is key to success. The 3 evaluation metrics chosen by Arc are Perturbation Discrimination, Differential Expression and Mean Average Error. Given that Mean Average Error is simple and exactly as it sounds, we will omit it from our analysis.

Perturbation Discrimination intends to evaluate how well your model can uncover relative differences between perturbations. To do this, we compute the Manhattan distances for all the measured perturbed transcriptomes in the test set (the ground truth we are trying to predict, yty_tyt​ and all other perturbed transcriptomes, ypny_p^nypn​) to our predicted transcriptome y^t\hat{y}_ty^​t​. We then rank where the ground truth lands with respect to all transcriptomes as follows:.

Sources indicate that rt=∑p≠t1{d(y^t,yp) After, we normalize by the total number of transcriptomes: PDisct=rtT \text{PDisc}_t = \frac{r_t}{T} PDisct​=Trt​​ Where 000 would be a perfect match. The overall score for your predictions is the mean of all $$\text{PDisc}_t$$. This is then normalized to: PDiscNorm=1−2PDisc \text{PDiscNorm} = 1 - 2\text{PDisc} PDiscNorm=1−2PDisc We multiply by 2 as for a random prediction, ~half of the results would be closer and half would be further away. Differential Expression intends to evaluate what fraction of the truly affected genes did you correctly identify as significantly affected. Firstly, for each gene compute a ppp-value using a Wilcoxon rank-sum test with tie correction. We do this for both our predicted perturbation distribution and the ground truth perturbation distribution. Next, we apply the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure, basically some stats to modulate the ppp-values, as with 20,00020,00020,000 genes and a ppp-value threshold of 0.050.050.05, you'd expect 1,0001,0001,000 false positives. We denote our set of predicted differentially expressed genes Gp,predG_{p,pred}Gp,pred​, and the ground truth set of differentially expressed genes Gp,trueG_{p,true}Gp,true​. If the size of our set is less than the ground truth set size, take the intersection of the sets, and divide by the true number of differentially expressed genes as follows: DEp=Gp,pred∩Gp,truenp,true DE_p = \frac{G_{p,pred} \cap G_{p,true}}{n_{p,true}} DEp​=np,true​Gp,pred​∩Gp,true​​ If the size of our set is greater than the ground truth set size, select the subset we predict are most differentially expressed (our "most confident" predictions, denoted G~p,pred\tilde{G}_{p,pred}G~p,pred​), take the intersection with the ground truth set, and then divide by the true number. DEp=G~p,pred∩Gp,truenp,true DE_p = \frac{\tilde{G}_{p,pred} \cap G_{p,true}}{n_{p,true}} DEp​=np,true​G~p,pred​∩Gp,true​​ Do this for all predicted perturbations and take the mean to obtain the final score. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Agoda Reduces API Code Review Time by 64% with Modular Architecture.

Nov 23, 2026 2 min read.

Sources indicate that agoda has introduced a modular monolith framework in its post-booking API to reduce code coupling and enforce domain boundaries without rewriting the existing service. The approach combines component-based code organization, automated architecture checks, and incremental migration. The team reported 64% shorter median code review time and 34% shorter time to initial substantive feedback for framework-backed changes compared with legacy code.

According to recent reports, the change addresses growing maintenance challenges in BAPI, which coordinates cancellations, booking amendments, refunds, and customer communications. Agoda extracted the API from its aging core monolith in 2019 through a largely line-by-line migration. As development increased, merge requests more than quadrupled between 2022 and 2025, while some files exceeded 4,000 lines.

The team characterized the migration as a tactical design trade-off, drawing on John K. Ousterhout's A Philosophy of Software Design,.

We had deliberately traded a strategic design approach for a tactical one to prioritize speed to market. This tactical mindset was exactly what the business needed at the time.

Rather than undertake a complete rewrite, the team introduced architectural boundaries incrementally.

Recent findings suggest that the framework, called Platform, organizes code around business domains such as cancellations, rebooking, and payments rather than technical layers. Each component encapsulates its business logic and data access behind defined interfaces, with application, service, repository, and model layers contained within the component. This package-by-component approach aims to localize changes and reduce dependencies between business domains.

Platform framework boundaries inside a domain module (Source: Agoda Blog Post).

Sources indicate that agoda uses the Data Mapper pattern to keep repository-specific models, including database entities and API payloads, out of business logic. Typed builders centralize object creation and transformations, making it easier for developers to find where domain objects and service inputs are constructed.

Recent findings suggest that the team also uses ArchUnit to encode architectural constraints as automated tests in continuous integration. For example, repository-specific models can only be accessed by their respective repositories. Violations fail the build rather than relying on code reviewers to identify unauthorized dependencies manually.

In a recent development, the team described these constraints as architectural fitness functions, a concept discussed by Neal Ford and Mark Richards in Software Architecture: The Hard Parts. One engineer explained:.

By codifying our layer boundaries into an ArchUnit test suite, our CI pipeline serves as an automated guardrail, catching structural drift on every pull request before a human reviewer ever sees it.

Platform is now the default for new modules, while existing functionality is migrated incrementally when feature development provides an opportunity.

Recent findings suggest that agoda compared framework-backed and legacy merge requests in Q2 2026. Median review completion time was 1.08 hours for framework-backed changes, compared with 3.02 hours for legacy changes. Time to first substantive feedback was 10.34 hours versus 15.77 hours. Between June and August, framework-backed changes also used 29% fewer AI prompts per 100 changed lines, although median prompts per merge request were similar (20 vs. 22). Agoda cautioned that the AI findings were directional due to the short observation period. A related approach is Spring Modulith, which provides module verification and dependency-cycle checks for Spring Boot applications.

Google Research Details DeepCrossAttention’s Dynamic Layer Routing

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that google Research published a technical overview of DeepCrossAttention on November 23, 2026, describing a transformer architecture that routes information from earlier layers separately for each token.
  • It has been revealed that A conventional residual connection adds a layer’s input directly to its output, preserving a path for information and gradients through deep networks.
  • The post was written by staff research scientist Kyriakos Axiotis and principal engineer Thomas Fu.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that google Research published a technical overview of DeepCrossAttention on November 23, 2026, describing a transformer architecture that routes information from earlier layers separately for each token. Google reports that it can achieve the same model quality up to three times faster.

It has been revealed that A conventional residual connection adds a layer’s input directly to its output, preserving a path for information and gradients through deep networks. Google’s overview argues that treating all previous representations equally can blur or distort detailed early features, leaving later layers to reconstruct them; DCA responds by letting each token select and route features from the history of preceding layers.

The post was written by staff research scientist Kyriakos Axiotis and principal engineer Thomas Fu. It explains research presented at ICML 2025, rather than announcing a new model. The underlying paper was first submitted to arXiv on February 10, 2025 and revised on July 23, 2025.

Sources indicate that for every token, DCA starts with a learned baseline set of mixing weights and adjusts it through a projection of the input. The resulting weights can move the effective processing arrangement between sequential and parallel behavior according to token context. A second mechanism, split-query/key/value cross-attention, works across network depth instead of across tokens, allowing each token to query a dynamically weighted mixture of embeddings from preceding layers.

Google claims the routing machinery adds less than 0.2% of total model parameters. The trade-off is greater memory-bandwidth demand, because representations from different layers remain intact rather than being blended together. At initialization, DCA can also reproduce the behavior of an ordinary residual network, so it can be retrofitted to a pretrained transformer without starting training from scratch.

Google reports improvements in convergence speed, training stability and final model quality across controlled synthetic settings, language-modeling benchmarks and image-classification tasks. On C4 and LM1B, DCA reached standard-transformer performance in up to five times fewer training steps. With equal training durations or step counts, it consistently produced lower perplexity, a measure of how well a model predicts a sample.

In a fixed-width LM1B comparison, Google reports that a standard transformer required 42 layers to reach perplexity below 14, while a 30-layer DCA model achieved lower perplexity, representing a 29% reduction in depth and parameter count. The result connects selective retrieval to a smaller architecture as well as a shorter optimization run.

Retrofitting produced a separate result for existing models. When DCA was added to a pretrained transformer and training briefly continued, Google reports that LM1B perplexity fell by 0.19, compared with 0.02 for continued standard training. That makes the initialization property practically important: it creates a way to improve an existing model without repeating the full pretraining process.

DCA is part of a broader effort to make information flow across depth adaptive. Moonshot AI’s Attention Residuals technical report uses softmax attention over preceding layer outputs and a layer-specific pseudo-query, while its Block AttnRes variant groups layers into blocks to reduce memory and communication overhead. Google’s post states Thinking Machines’ Inkling 2 combined Attention Residuals with DCA’s split-Q/K/V mechanism.

ByteDance’s Hyper-Connections paper takes a different approach, expanding the residual state into parallel hidden streams and mixing them with learnable depth and width matrices, including dynamic input-dependent weights. Google cautions that unconstrained mixing can break the identity-mapping property of residual connections and destabilize training at scale. The Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections paper proposes projecting the hyper-connection residual space onto a manifold to restore identity mapping while retaining the expanded residual stream.

According to recent reports, axiotis and Fu expect future architectures to route and weight earlier-layer representations according to the token being processed, effectively allowing layers to operate as specialized experts with greater information sharing. DCA makes the associated hardware trade-off clear: the reported training and model-size gains require earlier representations to remain available intact, increasing memory-bandwidth demand. Dynamic residual routing thus broadens transformer efficiency from parameter counts and training steps to the hardware needed to retain and move a model’s history.

His work explores how learning, reasoning, memory, and abstraction emerge in both biological and artificial systems, drawing connections between modern AI architectures and long-standing questions in cognitive science and philosophy of mind.

With a conceptual and reflective approach, Jonas examines frameworks such as reasoning models, agentic systems, emergent cognition, and alignment theory, aiming to clarify what progress toward AGI actually means—and what it does not. Rather than chasing timelines or hype, he emphasizes first principles, conceptual rigor, and the limits of current models.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, AI builders want a choice of the latest large language models (LLM) architectures and specialized variants for use in AI agents and other apps, but handling all the diversity can slow testing and deployment pipelines. In particular, managing and optimizing different inference software frameworks to achieve best performance across varied LLMs and serving requirements is a time-consuming bottleneck to getting performant AI apps in the hands of end-users.

NVIDIA AI customers and ecosystem partners leverage NVIDIA NIM inference microservices to streamline deployment of the latest AI models on NVIDIA accelerated infrastructure, including LLMs, multi-modal and domain-specific models from NVIDIA, Meta, Mistral AI, Google and hundreds more innovative model builders. We’ve seen customers and partners deliver more innovation, faster, with a simplified, reliable approach to model deployment, and today we’re excited to unlock over 100,000 LLMs on Hugging Face for rapid, reliable deployment with NIM.

NIM now provides a single docker container for deploying a broad range of LLMs supported by leading inference frameworks from NVIDIA and the community including NVIDIA TensorRT-LLM, vLLM and SGLang. When an LLM is provided to the NIM container, it performs several steps for deployment and performance optimization, without manual configuration:.

Table 1. NVIDIA NIM LLM adaptation phases and functionality.

The single NIM container supports common LLM weight formats, including:.

To use NIM, ensure your environment has NVIDIA GPUs with appropriate drivers (CUDA 12.1+), Docker installed, an NVIDIA NGC Account and API Key for NIM Docker images, and a Hugging Face account and API token for models requiring authentication. Learn more about environment prerequisites in the NIM documentation.

Environment setup involves setting environment variables and creating a persistent cache directory. Ensure the nim_cache directory has correct Unix permissions, ideally owned by the same Unix user launching the Docker container, to prevent permission issues. Commands use -u $(id -u) to manage this.

For ease of use, let’s store some of the frequently used information in environment variables.

Deploying an LLM from Hugging Face is demonstrated with Codestral-22B:.

For locally downloaded models, point NIM_MODEL_NAME to the path and mount the directory:.

It has been revealed that while deploying a model, feel free to inspect the output logs to get a sense of the choices NIM made during model deployment. Deployed models are available at http://localhost:8000, with API endpoints at http://localhost:8000/docs.

Additional arguments are available by the underlying engine. You can inspect the full list of such arguments by running nim-run --help in the container, as shown below.

To inspect compatible backends or choose a specific one, use list-model-profiles:.

This command demonstrates compatible profiles, including for LoRA adapters. To deploy with a specific backend like vLLM, use the NIM_MODEL_PROFILE environment variable, using the output supplied by list-model-profiles:.

NIM facilitates deploying quantized models. It automatically detects the quantization format (e.g., GGUF, AWQ) and selects the appropriate backend using standard deployment commands:.

For advanced customers, NIM offers customization through environment variables such as NIM_MAX_MODEL_LEN for context length. For large LLMs, NIM_TENSOR_PARALLEL_SIZE enables multi-GPU deployment. Ensure --shm-size= is passed to Docker for multi-GPU communication.

Industry observers note that the NIM container supports a broad range of LLMs supported by NVIDIA TensorRT-LLM, vLLM and SGLang, including popular LLMs and specialized variants on Hugging Face. For more details on supported LLMs, see the documentation.

According to recent reports, NIM is designed to simplify AI model deployment on NVIDIA accelerated infrastructure, speeding innovation and time to value for high performance AI builders and enterprise AI teams. We look forward to engagement and feedback from the Hugging Face Community.

Get started with a developer example in an NVIDIA-hosted computing environment at build.nvidia.com.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI agents will help Mercedes-Benz technicians diagnose and repair electrical and electronic (E/E) faults on production lines under a global agreement the automaker and Arena Physica declared on November 23, 2026.

Arena Physica reported that technicians using Atlas diagnosed and repaired problems 20–30% faster in initial testing, for both fresh and experienced technicians.

Recent findings suggest that deployment begins at the Tuscaloosa, Alabama, plant for the latest GLE and GLS models, with pilots planned at additional Mercedes-Benz plants. The initial plant has a global production role: Mercedes-Benz’s North America overview identifies the site as its assembly location for all large SUVs across global markets and says roughly 60% of the SUVs assembled there are exported.

It has been revealed that atlas fits into the current workflow as an add-on to Mercedes-Benz’s existing E/E rework assistance system. It draws on a digital model of the vehicle’s electrical architecture and relevant diagnostic and repair data to give technicians diagnostic guidance and a repair plan.

It has been revealed that new measurements can prompt Atlas to revise its repair initiative, while the eventual cause and repair outcome are added to its knowledge base. The aim of this closed-loop design is to keep technicians directed toward the most likely root cause as the diagnosis develops.

It has been revealed that arena Physica notes Atlas combines deterministic and probabilistic reasoning to approximate an experienced engineer’s understanding of hardware. Its underlying Metagraph represents pins, connectors and wires digitally, linking their physical locations to their functional importance. Fresh data can enrich that representation, which is also designed to extend to other systems and applications.

Industry observers note that the companies expect Atlas to raise first-time-fix rates, reduce rework and disassembly costs, accelerate technician onboarding, detect root causes sooner and prevent repeat E/E issues. Those objectives connect the speed of one repair with wider production quality: the system is intended to address the immediate fault while retaining information that can support later diagnostic work.

Mercedes-Benz North America CEO Jason Hoff said increasingly sophisticated vehicles demand more expertise from line technicians, presenting Atlas as extra diagnostic support for skilled teams within a global AI strategy intended to empower employees and benefit customers.

Recent findings suggest that arena Physica co-founder and CEO Pratap Ranade described the knowledge challenge: “One of the challenges in advanced manufacturing is encoding decades of engineering expertise and scaling it across the organization to support all team members. Atlas helps to capture the deep diagnostic knowledge that takes engineers years of experience to build and to make that expertise available to every technician on the line.”.

The agreement puts that knowledge-sharing approach directly into the production workflow, connecting faster repairs with retained diagnostic outcomes and technician onboarding. The planned pilots beyond Tuscaloosa will test how consistently the approach works across Mercedes-Benz’s wider manufacturing operation.

He is particularly interested in how AI enables faster iteration, reduces waste, and unlocks new material capabilities that were previously impractical or impossible to manufacture.

Fast LoRA inference for Flux with Diffusers and PEFT

📅 23 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1393 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • LoRA adapters provide a great deal of customization for models of all shapes and sizes.
  • In a recent development, in this post, we take the Flux.1-Dev model for text-to-image generation because of its widespread popularity and adoption, and how to optimize its inference speed when using LoRAs (~2.3x).
  • Note that even though we demonstrate speedups with Flux, our belief is that our recipe is generic enough to be applied to other models as well.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

LoRA adapters provide a great deal of customization for models of all shapes and sizes. When it comes to image generation, they can empower the models with different styles, different characters, and much more. Sometimes, they can also be leveraged to reduce inference latency. Hence, their importance is paramount, particularly when it comes to customizing and fine-tuning models.

In a recent development, in this post, we take the Flux.1-Dev model for text-to-image generation because of its widespread popularity and adoption, and how to optimize its inference speed when using LoRAs (~2.3x). It has over 30k adapters trained with it (as reported on the Hugging Face Hub platform). Therefore, its importance to the community is significant.

Note that even though we demonstrate speedups with Flux, our belief is that our recipe is generic enough to be applied to other models as well.

If you cannot wait to get started with the code, please check out the accompanying code repository.

According to recent reports, when serving LoRAs, it is common to hotswap (swap in and swap out different LoRAs) them. A LoRA changes the base model architecture. Additionally, LoRAs can be different from one another – each one of them could have varying ranks and different layers they target for adaptation. To account for these dynamic properties of LoRAs, we must take necessary steps to ensure the optimizations we apply are robust.

Sources indicate that for example, we can apply torch.compile on a model loaded with a particular LoRA to obtain speedups on inference latency. However, the moment we swap out the LoRA with a different one (with a potentially different configuration), we will run into recompilation challenges, causing slowdowns in inference.

In a recent development, one can also fuse the LoRA parameters into the base model parameters, run compilation, and unfuse the LoRA parameters when loading latest ones. However, this approach will again encounter the problem of recompilation whenever inference is run, due to potential architecture-level changes.

Our optimization recipe takes into account the above-mentioned situations to be as realistic as possible. Below are the key components of our optimization recipe:.

In a recent development, note that amongst the above-mentioned, FP8 quantization is lossy but often provides the most formidable speed-memory trade-off. Even though we tested the recipe primarily using NVIDIA GPUs, it should work on AMD GPUs, too.

In our previous blog posts (post 1 and post 2), we have already discussed the benefits of using the first three components of our optimization recipe. Applying them one by one is just a few lines of code:.

The FA3 processor comes from here.

The problems start surfacing when we try to swap in and swap out LoRAs into a compiled diffusion transformer (pipe.transformer) without triggering recompilation.

Normally, loading and unloading LoRAs will require recompilation, which defeats any speed advantage gained from compilation. Thankfully, there is a way to avoid the need for recompilation. By passing hotswap=True, diffusers will leave the model architecture unchanged and only exchange the weights of the LoRA adapter itself, which does not necessitate recompilation.

It has been revealed that (As a reminder, the first call to pipe will be slow as torch.compile is a just-in-time compiler. However, the subsequent calls should be significantly faster.).

This generally allows for swapping LoRAs without recompilation, but there are limitations:.

For more information on hotswapping in Diffusers and its limitations, visit the hotswapping section of the documentation.

The benefits of this workflow become evident when we look at the inference latency without using compilation with hotswapping.

The optimization recipe we have discussed so far assumes access to a powerful GPU like H100. However, what can we do when we’re limited to using consumer GPUs such as RTX 4090? Let’s find out.

In a recent development, flux.1-Dev (without any LoRA), using the Bfloat16 data-type, takes ~33GB of memory to run. Depending on the size of the LoRA module, and without using any optimization, this memory footprint can increase even further. Many consumer GPUs like the RTX 4090 only have 24GB. Throughout the rest of this section, we will consider an RTX 4090 machine as our testbed.

In a recent development, first, to enable end-to-end execution of Flux.1-Dev, we can apply CPU offloading wherein components that are not needed to execute the current computation are offloaded to the CPU to free more accelerator memory. Doing so allows us to run the entire pipeline in ~22GB in 35.403 seconds on an RTX 4090. Enabling compilation can reduce the latency down to 31.205 seconds (1.12x speedup). In terms of code, it’s just a few lines:.

According to recent reports, notice that we didn’t apply the FP8 quantization here because it’s not supported with CPU offloading and compilation (supporting issue thread). Therefore, just applying FP8 quantization to the Flux Transformer isn’t enough to mitigate the memory exhaustion problem, either. In this instance, we decided to remove it.

According to recent reports, therefore, to take advantage of the FP8 quantization scheme, we need to find a way to do it without CPU offloading. For Flux.1-Dev, if we additionally apply quantization to the T5 text encoder, we should be able to load and run the complete pipeline in 24GB. Below is a comparison of the results with and without the T5 text encoder being quantized (NF4 quantization from bitsandbytes).

According to recent reports, as we can notice in the figure above, quantizing the T5 text encoder doesn’t incur too much of a quality loss. Combining the quantized T5 text encoder and FP8-quantized Flux Transformer with torch.compile gives us somewhat reasonable results – 9.668 seconds from 32.27 seconds (a massive ~3.3x speedup) without a noticeable quality drop.

It is possible to generate images with 24 GB of VRAM even without quantizing the T5 text encoder, but that would have made our generation pipeline slightly more complicated.

We now have a way to run the entire Flux.1-Dev pipeline with FP8 quantization on an RTX 4090. We can apply the previously established optimization recipe for optimizing LoRA inference on the same hardware. Since FA3 isn’t supported on RTX 4090, we will stick to the following optimization recipe with T5 quantization newly added to the mix:.

In the table below, we show the inference latency numbers with different combinations of the above components applied.

To enable hotswapping without triggering recompilation, two hurdles have to be overcome. First, the LoRA scaling factor has to be converted into torch tensors from floats, which is achieved fairly easily. Second, the shape of the LoRA weights needs to padded to the largest required shape. That way, the data in the weights can be replaced without the need to reassign the whole attribute. This is why the max_rank argument discussed above is crucial. As we pad the values with zeros, the results remain unchanged, although the computation is slowed down a bit depending on how large the padding is.

It has been revealed that since no fresh LoRA attributes are added, this also requires that each LoRA after the first one can only target the same layers, or a subset of layers, that the first one targets. Thus, choose the order of loading wisely. If LoRAs target disjoint layers, there is the possibility to create a dummy LoRA that targets the union of all target layers.

To see the nitty-gritty of this implementation, visit the hotswap.py file in PEFT.

This post outlined an optimization recipe for fast LoRA inference with Flux, demonstrating significant speedups. Our approach combines Flash Attention 3, torch.compile, and FP8 quantization while ensuring hotswapping capabilities without recompilation issues. On high-end GPUs like the H100, this optimized setup provides a 2.23x speedup over the baseline.

Industry observers note that for consumer GPUs, specifically the RTX 4090, we tackled memory limitations by introducing T5 text encoder quantization (NF4) and leveraging regional compilation. This comprehensive recipe achieved a substantial 2.04x speedup, making LoRA inference on Flux viable and performant even with limited VRAM. The key insight is that by carefully managing compilation and quantization, the benefits of LoRA can be fully realized across different hardware configurations.

Hopefully, the recipes from this post will inspire you to optimize your LoRA-based use cases, benefitting from speedy inference.

Anthropic Rolls out Zero-Retention Enterprise Frontier Safeguards Beta

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Anthropic on November 23, 2026 opened Enterprise Frontier Safeguards in public beta after developing it with more than 100 customers.
  • Sources indicate that bridgewater, Salesforce and Stripe evaluated EFS in private beta.
  • It has been revealed that the beta is available through Claude Platform, Claude Platform on AWS, Amazon Bedrock and Claude on Google Cloud.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anthropic on November 23, 2026 opened Enterprise Frontier Safeguards in public beta after developing it with more than 100 customers. The system pairs zero data retention with automated monitoring for misuse patterns across multiple requests while keeping sealed safety data in customer-owned cloud storage.

Sources indicate that bridgewater, Salesforce and Stripe evaluated EFS in private beta. Anthropic said the development group included a quarter of the Fortune 100 and companies in healthcare, financial services and law.

It has been revealed that the beta is available through Claude Platform, Claude Platform on AWS, Amazon Bedrock and Claude on Google Cloud. Microsoft Foundry support is listed as coming soon, and eligible customers will receive setup instructions.

Wells Fargo chief information security officer Munish Kumar Sharma described the division of responsibilities: “We keep custody of our data while Anthropic operates the detection.”.

Anthropic first revealed EFS on September 1, 2026, planning a phased rollout and temporary zero data retention on Fable 5 and Fable 5.1 for eligible customers. The earlier announcement remarked Anthropic had introduced 30-day retention starting with Fable 5 because effective detection can require correlating activity across sessions and accounts, while many regulated enterprises found it difficult to use models with data retention.

Legacy zero data retention relies on real-time classifiers that screen individual requests. EFS adds automated safety monitoring across many requests, addressing the possibility that each query can appear benign in isolation while forming part of a broader attack.

The EFS documentation defines Sealed Safety Data as prompts, responses and model reasoning encrypted in Anthropic’s format; even the customer’s team cannot read it. A Transcript is the readable copy of a prompt and response used for investigation. Storage can use Amazon S3 or Google Cloud Storage, depending on the Claude platform.

Anthropic states that inputs and outputs are deleted promptly after being written to customer-controlled storage, and that neither its personnel nor cloud-provider personnel access them. Only automated safety monitoring accesses that content, which is not used for model or classifier training. Customers configure access policies and audit logging and can encrypt safety data with their own keys.

A Safety Case identifies its policy category and related messages and points to their Transcripts, without including inputs and outputs. Anthropic staff handling the case see limited details and cannot read those Transcripts. The customer’s team investigates using its own logs and responds whether it found a violation, without having to provide names, evidence or Transcripts. A valid response closes the case.

Recent findings suggest that the review documentation gives customers seven calendar days to respond and states an unanswered case may lead to suspended access. There are no automatic notifications or webhooks, so teams must monitor their storage or, on Claude Platform, poll the beta Safety Cases API. Anthropic can also suspend access in rare cases of clear, intentional harm while the customer investigates.

Access is restricted to eligible organizations’ internal use, and organizations with HIPAA readiness enabled cannot obtain EFS. The setup guide requires an Organization Admin and customer-owned cloud storage; a customer-managed encryption key is optional.

On Claude Platform, the product overview claims EFS covers every Messages API request in an enabled workspace regardless of model. It does not cover data stored by code execution containers, Files API uploads, Batch API results or Claude Managed Agents sessions. Separate workspaces are required to apply EFS to only selected traffic.

Anthropic does not charge for EFS, and the service does not change model behavior, API pricing or rate limits. The cloud provider bills for storage, reads, writes, key operations and applicable network transfer.

According to recent reports, the beta makes the customer’s security team part of the safeguard itself: data custody and human review sit with the enterprise, while automated detection and potential enforcement remain with Anthropic. Its usefulness for sensitive workloads will therefore depend on how well customers absorb those review duties within the product’s coverage limits.

  • For PDFs, documents and presentations, the document-processing controls accept inclusive start and end pages, a choice of extracted page text, rendered page images or both, and low, medium or high resolution for rendering.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google on November 23, 2026, launched native file-slicing controls in the Gemini API, together with native upload support for Microsoft Office and OpenDocument files. Developers can request selected pages, spreadsheet ranges and media segments, with tokens billed only for the content Gemini inspects.

Recent findings suggest that the patch is aimed at agents that need a chart in a long report, one worksheet in a workbook or a short passage in a recording. Instead of converting and loading an entire file in the client, developers can send a Files API URI and have Google slice, render and tokenize it server-side, reducing prompt-token use and the local processing needed around the model.

For PDFs, documents and presentations, the document-processing controls accept inclusive start and end pages, a choice of extracted page text, rendered page images or both, and low, medium or high resolution for rendering. Spreadsheet requests can select a worksheet by tab position and an A1-style visible_cells range, then choose evaluated data, raw formulas or a rendered visual for charts and layout.

The video-processing and audio-clipping references extend the same approach to recordings. Static video mode, which samples frames at a fixed rate, supports start and end offsets, custom sampling up to 24 frames per second, and transcript, frames or audio layers. Billing covers only the clipped interval and selected layers. Audio accepts offsets in seconds, with an omitted start defaulting to zero and an omitted end to the file’s end; only the selected duration is billed.

According to recent reports, A file can be uploaded once and its URI reused across turns and tool calls. Tools can return sliced pages, spreadsheet ranges or media clips inside function_result, the response a tool sends back to the model. The function-calling reference says the model automatically receives page counts and worksheet names so it can request narrower ranges later. That enables a cheap text or transcript skim before a high-resolution inspection of a relevant page or clip.

Industry observers note that gemini counts and bills tokens only for the sliced output sent to the model. For Gemini 3 and Gemini 4 page images, Google estimates approximately 280 tokens per page at low resolution, 560 at medium and 1,120 at high. Resolution therefore becomes a cost control as well as a detail setting: a team can use text for discovery and reserve rendered images for charts or dense layouts.

For supported Office and OpenDocument files, omitted processing options leave Gemini 4 and later models with medium-resolution page or slide images for documents and presentations, and all sheets with values, formulas and sheet names for spreadsheets.

For documents, slicing does not relax the original upload limits: 50 MB per file, 1,000 pages per PDF, 2,000 pages or slides per Office or OpenDocument file, and 50,000 cells per spreadsheet sheet. Files API uploads are stored for 48 hours, and the Files API is available at no cost in regions where the Gemini API is available.

Vercel reported that, in its production test, extracting text to skim a document page used 14 times fewer tokens than rendering the whole PDF.

Sources indicate that liteLLM reported that slicing cut prompt tokens by 67% for a PDF and 33% for a workbook in its testing. The feature works through LiteLLM’s Gemini routes without additional setup.

Recent findings suggest that native slicing, content-layer controls and the expanded file support are available through the API in Google AI Studio and Gemini for business. Google says native slicing works across all Gemini 4 models, and the document, presentation and spreadsheet controls also support Gemini 3.

For agent builders, the trade-off is explicit: text and transcripts provide a low-cost way to locate material, while page, frame and resolution choices control the cost of closer inspection. The quality of that first-pass search is therefore central to whether the partner-reported savings carry over to other document and media workflows.

TimeScope: How Long Can Your Video Large Multimodal Model Go?

📅 23 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1003 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • TimeScope is an open-source benchmark designed to measure how well vision-language models understand long videos.
  • Recent advances in multimodal AI have produced models claiming to understand hour-long videos.
  • Sources indicate that text benchmarks such as HELM and RULER have exposed the fragility of long-context claims, showing that models often struggle when tasks demand more than simple retrieval, like reasoning or aggregation at long context lengths.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TimeScope is an open-source benchmark designed to measure how well vision-language models understand long videos. By adding short “needle” clips into videos ranging from 1 minute to 8 hours, it evaluates three skills:.

Recent advances in multimodal AI have produced models claiming to understand hour-long videos. This trend mirrors progress in long-context language models, which excel at reasoning over lengthy text. Following this, vision-language systems now advertise context windows that can handle thousands of frames. But these claims require a closer look: do these models truly demonstrate understanding of the sequence of events? Are they limited to surface-level retrieval \ recognition? It's crucial to ask if their capabilities are being overstated.

Sources indicate that text benchmarks such as HELM and RULER have exposed the fragility of long-context claims, showing that models often struggle when tasks demand more than simple retrieval, like reasoning or aggregation at long context lengths. In the video domain, however, we're still playing catch-up. The most common test, Video Needle in a Haystack (VideoNIAH), injects static images as "needles" into videos, effectively measuring visual search rather than true temporal dynamics. As a result, even top-tier models advertising massive frame capacities are rarely trained beyond ~256 frames and see sharp drops on benchmarks like Video-MME when pushed further.

This measurement gap leaves us wondering: What does it really mean for a model to "understand" long videos? To address this, we're excited to introduce TimeScope, a new open-source benchmark hosted on Hugging Face. TimeScope probes the limits of long-video capabilities by inserting several short (~5-10 second) video clips—our "needles"—into base videos ranging from 1 minute to 8 hours. With three distinct task types, it evaluates not just retrieval but synthesis, localization, and fine-grained motion analysis, providing a more holistic view of temporal comprehension.

The promise of long-video AI is transformative — enabling agents to summarize hours of footage, detect subtle anomalies, and answer complex questions about extended narratives. Integrated into robotics, these models could analyze prolonged operations, adapt in real time, and push autonomous decision-making. Just as powerful is the vision of a personal assistant that understands daily life and offers continuous, actionable feedback.

In practice, this leads to overstated capabilities. Models might claim to process 10,000+ frames, but training data often caps at 256 frames per clip, leading to degraded performance on longer inputs. We've seen this in evaluations where increasing frame sampling rates tanks accuracy on tasks requiring temporal insight.

TimeScope flips the script by emphasizing three pillars of long-video understanding:.

TimeScope’s key idea is using short video clips as “needles,” and instead of just spotting the needle, it pushes models to deeply understand the whole video. We start with a long base video (e.g., a documentary, lecture, or ambient footage) and insert one or more hand-curated short video needles (5-10 seconds each) at random positions. These needles contain the key information needed to solve the task, forcing models to process the entire input without shortcuts like sparse sampling.

Figure 1: Overview of TimeScope's needle insertion process. A long base video (1 min to 8 hours) serves as the haystack, into which we splice short video needles (~5-10 seconds). Tasks require detecting, synthesizing, or analyzing content from these needles, embedded at varying depths.

We evaluate across three needle types, each targeting a different aspect of long-video comprehension:.

This tests basic retrieval and understanding of a localized event. Questions are put so that sampling a relevant frame from the needle should suffice—like asking about a shorter part in a longer video.

Example:What mode of transportation is shown in the video?

According to recent reports, here, we embed multiple text-based needles (e.g., 2-4 short clips displaying "secret words" via on-screen text) at different points in the video. The model must identify all words and report them in chronological order, simulating tasks like extracting timestamps or key facts from dispersed scenes. This requires scanning the full timeline and understanding relative positioning.

For questions focusing on motion or sequences within a short clip, single-frame sampling won't cut it—the model needs to perceive dynamics across frames. This probes whether long-context handling preserves temporal fidelity.

Industry observers note that example:How many times did the man swing his axe? (a) one (b) two (c) three (d) four (e) five (f) six.

With different video lengths and varying needle placements, TimeScope measures how much video a model can really handle—and highlights that performance drops as the video gets longer.

Recent findings suggest that to kick things off, we ran TimeScope on a suite of leading vision-language models, from open-source favorites to the juggernauts like Gemini 2.5-Pro. The results underscore the benchmark’s value: even models that claim to handle long videos well still struggle with real long-video tasks. These findings reveal clear patterns—performance cliffs around certain durations, strengths in static retrieval versus weaknesses in motion analysis—and pave the way for targeted improvements in model training. For detailed results and visualizations, check out our Hugging Face Space embedded above.

Model size isn’t everything. Qwen 2.5-VL 3B and 7B, as well as InternVL 2.5 models at 2B, 4B, and 8B parameters, exhibit nearly indistinguishable long-video curves to their smaller counterparts. All of them plateau at roughly the same context length, showing that simply scaling parameters does not automatically grant a longer temporal horizon.

According to recent reports, gemini 2.5-Pro is in a league of its own. It is the only model that maintains strong accuracy on videos longer than one hour.

Trade-offs across tasks matter. Qwen 2.5-VL shines in the Information-Synthesis (OCR) task—identifying and ordering dispersed text snippets—yet it falls behind on Fine-Grained Temporal Perception, where precise motion counting is required.

TimeScope demonstrates that “hour-long video understanding” is still more slogan than reality. By revealing where even state-of-the-art models stumble on temporal reasoning, information synthesis, and motion perception, the benchmark invites us to rethink how we train and evaluate multimodal systems.

We hope this benchmark helps the community make steady, measurable progress toward models that better understand video over time.

We are open-sourcing all components of TimeScope:.
