  • At QCon San Francisco 2026, Mark Khuzam, senior software engineer at Netflix, described how the tech giant's Commerce team retrofitted its software development lifecycle so that AI coding agents and engineers could ship together safely.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Netflix at QConSF 2026: Retrofitting the SDLC for AI Coding Agents.

Nov 23, 2026 3 min read.

At QCon San Francisco 2026, Mark Khuzam, senior software engineer at Netflix, described how the tech giant's Commerce team retrofitted its software development lifecycle so that AI coding agents and engineers could ship together safely.

Khuzam argued that most of the work was not about agents at all, but about documentation, consistency and review.

Much of Commerce runs as server-driven UI, an approach Netflix has discussed at QCon before. A single screen-composition service behind the API gateway builds screens for iOS, Android, web and TV.

Sources indicate that khuzam opened with a mock company email announcing that every engineer now had Claude Code and asking how much faster everyone was shipping. The problem the team ran into next was summed up in one line.

The team's first attempt was having an agent migrate tests, and it took four tries. The team started with "migrate this file," then added instructions, then the APIs to use, then how to mock data.

In a recent development, the docs were also hard to find, since the agent's context window ran out before it found the right page. And they were inconsistent, because tests were not written the same way across the codebase.

Developers rated the internal framework at a Net Promoter Score of -3. Moving from one test to a whole feature, from screen to data to route to test, meant teaching the agent how the team builds.

Khuzam described the fix as context engineering, "getting what engineers know into what agents see." The team wrote 45 architecture decision records, each "written for people and for agents.".

Industry observers note that each record covers the context, the decision, a pattern and an anti-pattern, and AI usage notes on what an agent should do. It also links to related docs and code, and the records now ship inside almost every repository.

Industry observers note that to keep those records and more than 300 other documents findable, the team borrowed from how search engines read a site. An AGENTS.md file, the project instructions file that coding agents read before anything else, plays the part of robots.txt.

The second half of the talk followed code after an agent writes it. Khuzam noted that the CI pipeline is still deterministic, running builds, tests, screenshot diffing, merge queues and canaries.

Industry observers note that what changed is how agents plug into each phase. A review agent pre-reviews each pull request against the docs and ADRs, flags anti-patterns and looks at what depends on the change.

Its first version left 23 comments on a single PR, starting with "Overall this PR looks great!" It now posts only verified blockers, each with evidence, a fix and the ADR rule it breaks. Engineers can add a revise label to have an agent read the review and push a fix to the same PR. Changes aren't yet auto-merged, and engineers own the code.

Recent findings suggest that khuzam reported no Sev 1 incidents in 2026 on a core service and 32% more pull requests year over year. Developer NPS rose from -3 to +25 over three quarters.

Ahead of the session, Khuzam framed the stakes on LinkedIn: "Agents can write code, but what gives us the confidence to ship Tier 0 services to 300M+ members without everything falling apart?".

It has been revealed that work that crosses services raised a harder question. A product engineer building one feature touches the payment API, billing, the gateway and every client, so the team had to decide who owns the context and how it follows the work.

Khuzam listed approaches that did not hold up. Loading every repository did not fit, Git submodules were brittle, a Git MCP server "sees one file, not the system," and shared copies went stale.

Recent findings suggest that the team needed context that was accurate, portable across agents, owned per domain and kept fresh. It settled on GraphRAG per domain, taking structure from the code and meaning from the docs and ADRs.

In a recent development, each graph is pinned to specific commits and served through a single Model Context Protocol tool. Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, a Slack bot and CI review all query the same graph, and every answer cites a file and a line.

Recent findings suggest that khuzam closed with three rules: decide what agents should do and tell them, make it easy to find how to do it, and remember that human judgement still matters. "None of this is upcoming. It's good engineering, built for a new reader.".

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Decider handles repeated choices without generating prose.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Amazon Web Services released five open-weight Strands Decider v2 models on November 23, 2026, and added native Claude Code, Codex, and Kiro CLI support to its open-source Strands Box sandbox, targeting the inference cost of routine agent decisions and the security of unattended coding sessions.

Decider handles repeated choices without generating prose. Box wraps installed coding agents in operating-system isolation and external policy checks, addressing the choice between approving every action and giving an agent broad access to files, commands, networks, and credentials.

According to recent reports, decider is a system-one model for fixed choices: one forward pass scores the supplied options and returns their probabilities without producing a text response. The same mechanism can select a tool, route a request, or judge whether an answer is sufficient.

The models use Gemma 4 bases, are licensed under Apache-2.0, and span E2B, E4B, 12B, 26B-A4B, and 31B sizes. Weights are available on Hugging Face, with v2 support in the open-source Decider repository.

AWS’s reported six-benchmark text average rises from 70.0 for v1 26B-A4B to 82.1 for v2 31B. At the smaller end, v2 E4B reaches 74.4, versus 62.7 for its v1 counterpart; the 31B version also scores 90.1 on image tasks and 70.2 on video tasks.

In a recent development, the gap between predicted confidence and observed accuracy also narrowed: AWS puts expected calibration error at 0.027 for v2 31B, versus 0.062 for v1 26B-A4B across the six text tests. Expected calibration error measures how closely predicted probabilities match actual correctness. Lower values make confidence scores more useful for deciding whether an agent should act, call a larger model, or ask a human.

V2’s training set contains 17.48 million decision examples, and its readout directly scores option tokens instead of using v1’s pointer head. Prefix-bidirectional attention processes shared state once in both directions; each subsequent question reads that encoded state and adds computation only for its own tokens.

Recent findings suggest that deployment options include local CUDA, Mac, or CPU serving, a real-time Amazon SageMaker AI endpoint, and AWS Lambda. The Lambda stack runs a quantized model on Arm64 CPUs with nothing running between requests.

Recent findings suggest that the production cost evidence comes from v1, not the latest models. In a November 9, 2026 account, AWS stated engineers on one of Amazon’s largest internal ticketing systems replaced Claude Sonnet 4.6 with Decider E4B to assign tickets to one of 20 categories. Average call time fell from 4,215 milliseconds with Sonnet to 897 milliseconds with Decider, while estimated cost dropped from about $22,200 to $500 per million tickets under AWS’s stated usage and list-price assumptions.

According to recent reports, the engineers limited that conclusion to high-volume tasks with a fixed set of answers. Workloads that require written explanations, revise their label catalog often, or depend on context beyond the model window may still require an LLM.

AWS reports that v2, without fine-tuning, routed customer-service and app-automation requests between Claude Haiku 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5. The routed setup retained 94% of Sonnet’s task-completion level while spending 44% as much. Here, calibrated confidence becomes an infrastructure control: it determines when a workload can avoid the more expensive model.

It has been revealed that the Box patch follows the original October 7, 2026 developer preview, which combined operating-system containment with fine-grained Dogwood policies. Developers can now start an installed agent with a command such as box run claude; Claude Code, Codex, and Kiro CLI retain their usual interfaces while Box enforces the selected profile’s boundaries.

It has been revealed that enforcement happens outside the model: shell activity, filesystem operations, outbound requests, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) calls are evaluated against the profile’s Dogwood rules. Those rules can identify individual files, commands, hosts, or tools and can depend on earlier session activity. An AWS example rejects the 61st AWS MCP call within an hour. Since policy decisions sit outside the model, content the agent reads cannot revise the answer, and the agent cannot alter its own rules.

Recent findings suggest that profiles combine packs, policies, and settings into task-specific personas, while packs configure agents, model providers, and tools. Separate profiles keep sessions and memory apart, and policy edits can be applied without restarting a session.

Sources indicate that routed secrets never enter the agent’s environment in usable form. It handles a placeholder; after policy permits an outbound request, Box’s egress gateway substitutes the actual credential. Keys stored where the agent can already read them, including project files and MCP configuration, receive no such protection and should be moved into routes.

Box CLI remains in preview and runs on Apple silicon Macs with macOS 15 or later and on Linux ARM64 and x86-64.

Sources indicate that the releases divide agent overhead into two control points: Decider can reduce how often expensive inference is needed for fixed choices, while Box limits the systems and secrets an unattended agent can reach. The open question for both is broader work: whether v2 can reproduce v1’s production economics outside a closed-choice workload, and whether Box’s policies can contain less predictable sessions without restoring manual approvals.

UQ researchers send an unblockable message using gravity

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Professor Matthew Davis, Dr Charles Woffinden and Professor Andrew White inside the elevator they used to send a message.
  • Sources indicate that (Photo credit: The University of Queensland.
  • University of Queensland researchers have used gravity to transmit a message through a brick wall using an elevator and a sensitive gravimeter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Professor Matthew Davis, Dr Charles Woffinden and Professor Andrew White inside the elevator they used to send a message.

Sources indicate that (Photo credit: The University of Queensland. ).

University of Queensland researchers have used gravity to transmit a message through a brick wall using an elevator and a sensitive gravimeter.

The unusual experiment took place in UQ’s Parnell Building, where the team of physicists sent the elevator back and forth between 2 levels, moving its 1.8-tonne counterweight between positions representing binary 0 and 1.

A gravimeter in an adjacent bathroom detected the changes in the gravitational field and translated the message into a single word, ‘Gravity’.

Dr Charles Woffinden from the School of Mathematics and Physics said gravitational communication had an intriguing advantage.

“Unlike the electromagnetic signals used in modern wireless communication, a gravitational signal cannot simply be screened out by placing ordinary material in its path,” Dr Woffinden mentioned.

“Anyone who has lost phone reception in a tunnel or struggled with Wi-Fi through a solid wall will understand the appeal.

“While the present system is far from practical, it demonstrates the possibility of communicating using a method that ordinary physical barriers cannot block.”.

Dr Andrew Groszek noted the idea came from a project to develop a contactless weighbridge.

“We were aiming to determine the mass of trucks and other large vehicles by measuring their tiny gravitational pull,” Dr Groszek noted.

“Once we had shown that the idea worked, we realised the same physics could be used to encode and transmit information.”.

Professor Andrew White mentioned the biggest limitation to future gravity-based communication was its slow speed.

“Our lift was snail-paced – it’s from the 1950s – so our experiment transmitted just 1 bit per minute, meaning it took an hour to send a single word,” Professor White said.

“The speed of gravity communication would come down to how major the mass is, how fast you can move it and the sensitivity of the detector.

“It took more than 100 years to go from the first telegraph system to the mobile phone, so while gravity communication is not practical today, it could be in the future.”.

A gravimeter in an adjacent bathroom detected the changes in the gravitational field from the elevator's movement and translated the message.

(Photo credit: The University of Queensland.).

Professor Matthew Davis stated the UQ team had established an important underlying principle.

“It’s not often that you get to demonstrate an entirely latest way of communicating,” Professor Davis stated.

“We have shown experimentally that information can be encoded in the gravitational field and recovered at the other end.

“Our experiment used a classical gravity sensor, but our modelling indicates that quantum sensors could, with rather ambitious assumptions, support ranges of up to about 500 metres and data rates of around 15 bits per minute.”.

Such sensors could eventually support communication in environments where radio waves, light and other conventional signals cannot penetrate.

Read the research published in Science Advances.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Reduce Parquet file upload and download times on Hugging Face Hub by leveraging the newly introduced Xet storage layer and Apache Arrow’s Parquet Content-Defined Chunking (CDC) feature enabling more efficient and scalable data workflows.

Sources indicate that TL;DR: Parquet Content-Defined Chunking (CDC) is now available in PyArrow and Pandas, enabling efficient deduplication of Parquet files on content-addressable storage systems like Hugging Face's Xet storage layer. CDC dramatically reduces data transfer and storage costs by uploading or downloading only the changed data chunks. Enable CDC by passing the use_content_defined_chunking argument:.

Apache Parquet is a columnar storage format that is widely used in the data engineering community.

According to recent reports, as of today, Hugging Face hosts nearly 21 PB of datasets, with Parquet files alone accounting for over 4 PB of that storage. Optimizing Parquet storage is therefore a high priority. Hugging Face has introduced a newly introduced storage layer called Xet that leverages content-defined chunking to efficiently deduplicate chunks of data reducing storage costs and improving download/upload speeds.

In a recent development, while Xet is format agnostic, Parquet's layout and column-chunk (data page) based compression can produce entirely different byte-level representations for data with minor changes, leading to suboptimal deduplication performance. To address this, the Parquet files should be written in a way that minimizes the byte-level differences between similar data, which is where content-defined chunking (CDC) comes into play.

Let's explore the performance benefits of the newly introduced Parquet CDC feature used alongside Hugging Face's Xet storage layer.

For demonstration purposes, we will use a manageable sized subset of OpenOrca dataset.

Since pyarrow>=21.0.0 we can use Hugging Face URIs in the pyarrow functions to directly read and write parquet (and other file formats) files to the Hub using the hf:// URI scheme.

We can see that the table has been uploaded entirely (total bytes == total transfer) as fresh data because it is not known to the Xet storage layer yet. Now read it back as a pyarrow table:.

Note that all pyarrow functions that accept a file path also accept a Hugging Face URI, like pyarrow datasets, CSV functions, incremental Parquet writer or reading only the parquet metadata:.

To demonstrate the effectiveness of the content-defined chunking feature, we will try out how it performs in case of:.

While this use case sounds trivial, traditional file systems do not deduplicate files resulting in full re-upload and re-download of the data. In contrast, a system utilizing content-defined chunking can recognize that the file content is identical and avoid unnecessary data transfer.

We can see that no fresh data has been uploaded, and the operation was instantaneous. Now let's see what happens if we upload the same file again but to a different repository:.

Recent findings suggest that the upload was instantaneous again since deduplication works across repositories as well. This is a key feature of the Xet storage layer, allowing efficient data sharing and collaboration. You can read more about the details and scaling challenges in the From Chunks to Blocks: Accelerating Uploads and Downloads on the Hub blog post.

First write out the original and changed tables to local parquet files to see their sizes:.

Now upload them to Hugging Face to see how much data is actually transferred:.

Recent findings suggest that we can see that only the latest columns and the new parquet metadata placed in the file's footer were uploaded, while the original data was not transferred again. This is a huge benefit of the Xet storage layer, as it allows us to efficiently add new columns without transferring the entire dataset again.

Same applies to removing columns, as we can see below:.

To have a better understanding of what has been uploaded, we can visualize the differences between the two parquet files using the deduplication estimation tool:.

Sources indicate that adding two new columns mean that we have unseen data pages which must be transferred (highlighted in red), but the rest of the data remains unchanged (highlighted in green), so it is not transferred again. Note the small red area in the footer metadata which almost always changes as we modify the parquet file. The dedup stats show / = where smaller ratios mean higher deduplication performance.

Also visualize the difference after removing a column:.

Since we are removing entire columns we can only see changes in the footer metadata, all the other columns remain unchanged and already existing in the storage layer, so they are not transferred again.

Sources indicate that another common use case is changing the column types in the table e.g. to reduce the storage size or to optimize the data for specific queries. Let's change the question_length column from int64 data type to int32 and see how much data is transferred:.

Again, we can see that only the new column and the updated parquet metadata were uploaded. Now visualize the deduplication heatmap:.

In a recent development, the first red region indicates the upcoming column that was added, while the second red region indicates the updated metadata in the footer. The rest of the data remains unchanged and is not transferred again.

We are going to append newly introduced rows by concatenating another slice of the original dataset to the table.

Now check that only the fresh rows are being uploaded since the original data is already known to the Xet storage layer:.

According to recent reports, since each column gets latest data, we can see multiple red regions. This is due to the actual parquet file specification where whole columns are laid out after each other (within each row group).

According to recent reports, here comes the difficult part as insertions and deletions are shifting the existing rows which lead to different columns chunks or data pages in the parquet nomenclature. Since each data page is compressed separately, even a single row insertion or deletion can lead to a completely different byte-level representation starting from the edited row(s) to the end of the parquet file.

This parquet specific problem cannot be solved by the Xet storage layer alone, the parquet file itself needs to be written in a way that minimizes the data page differences even if there are inserted or deleted rows.

Let's try to use the existing mechanism and see how it performs.

Also visualize both cases to see the differences:.

We can see that the deduplication performance has dropped significantly (higher ratio), and the deduplication heatmaps show that the compressed parquet files are quite different from each other. This is due to the fact that the inserted and deleted rows have shifted the existing rows, leading to different data pages starting from the edited row(s) to the end of the parquet file.

Sources indicate that we can solve this problem by writing parquet files with a latest pyarrow feature called content-defined chunking (CDC). This feature ensures that the columns are consistently getting chunked into data pages based on their content, similarly how the Xet storage layer deduplicates data but applied to the logical values of the columns before any serialization or compression happens.

The feature can be enabled by passing use_content_defined_chunking=True to the write_parquet function:.

Pandas also supports the new feature:.

Let's visualize the deduplication difference before and after using the Parquet CDC feature:.

Looks much better! Since the proof of the pudding is in the eating, let's actually upload the tables using the content-defined chunking parquet feature and see how much data is transferred.

Note that we need to upload the original table first with content-defined chunking enabled:.

The uploaded data is significantly smaller than before, showing much better deduplication performance as highlighted in the heatmaps above.

Notable to note that the same performance benefits apply to downloads using the huggingface_hub.hf_hub_download() and datasets.load_dataset() functions.

There are cases depending on the reader/writer constraints where larger or smaller row-group sizes might be beneficial. The parquet writer implementations use fixed-sized row-groups by default, in the case of pyarrow the default is 1Mi rows. Dataset writers may change to reduce the row-group size in order to improve random access performance or to reduce the memory footprint of the reader application.

Sources indicate that changing the row-group size will shift rows between row-groups, shifting values between data pages, so we have a similar problem as with inserting or deleting rows. Let's compare the deduplication performance between different row-group sizes using the parquet CDC feature:.

Sources indicate that datasets are often split into multiple files to improve parallelism and random access. Parquet CDC combined with the Xet storage layer can efficiently deduplicate data across multiple files even if the data is split at different boundaries.

Let's write out the dataset with three different file-level splitting then compare the deduplication performance:.

Even though we uploaded the dataset with three different sharding configurations, the overall upload size would be barely larger than the original dataset size.

So far we've used PyArrow, let’s explore using the same CDC feature with Pandas by downloading, filtering then uploading the dataset with the content-defined chunking feature enabled:.

According to recent reports, since Parquet CDC is applied at the parquet data page level (column chunk level), the deduplication performance depends on the filter's selectivity, or rather the distribution of the changes across the dataset. If most of the data pages are affected, then the deduplication ratio will drop significantly.

More details about the feature can be found at:.

Recent findings suggest that we explored the performance benefits of the upcoming Parquet content-defined chunking feature used alongside Hugging Face's Xet storage layer. We demonstrated how it can efficiently deduplicate data in various scenarios making parquet operations faster and more storage-efficient. Comparing to traditional cloud storage solutions, the Xet storage layer with Parquet CDC can significantly reduce data transfer times and costs.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that P3 State, an Australian foundational AI startup, unveiled an A$9.5 million (US$6.5 million) raise led by Main Sequence, with participation from US deep-tech investor DCVC. The manufacturer’s news index dates the post November 23, 2026, while the release itself is datelined November 24, 2026, in Australia.

According to recent reports, the funding will expand P3 State’s research and engineering team in Australia and advance its core technology toward a public release. The startup, a spin-off of the Australian Institute for Machine Learning (AIML) at Adelaide University, is working to lower the cost of developing and operating AI without reducing performance.

P3 State’s central argument is that adding capacity has become an increasingly expensive way to improve AI. The dominant approach applies more compute and data to ever-larger models, requiring substantial energy and capital for training and operation. Those requirements restrict frontier development to a small group of organizations, while data-center projects face growing resistance.

Industry observers note that existing efficiency techniques also tend to involve a compromise: faster or cheaper operation often comes at the expense of accuracy or capability. P3 State intends to remove that trade-off by rethinking how AI models work at a foundational level.

Chief executive and co-founder Simon Lucey explained why that requires more than refining existing systems: “You can engineer a system to be ten times better, but if you want it to be dramatically more efficient than that, you have to go back to the foundations.”.

Industry observers note that the founding team combines academic research with large-scale deployment experience. Lucey is an Adelaide University professor and former AIML director who has held faculty roles at Carnegie Mellon University. Chief technology officer and co-founder Arpit Garg has trained and deployed AI models at AIML and TikTok. Chief scientist and co-founder Hemanth Saratchandran researches efficient, reliable AI systems and holds a pure mathematics PhD from the University of Oxford.

According to recent reports, P3 State’s leadership biography describes chief operating officer Iain McCowan as a two-time deep-tech founder with experience in speech and language AI research and commercial AI product teams. That background spans theory, model deployment and company building, connecting the startup’s academic origins to the practical work of preparing a public release.

Main Sequence investment manager Danielle Haj-Moussa said the firm sees P3 State as Australian AI research becoming a commercial venture, with the founders’ first-principles approach offering the potential for a “step change rather than a marginal gain.” Main Sequence also identifies compute as one of six systems the world depends on, making its efficiency important to every industry that uses it.

In a recent development, the announcement did not include performance benchmarks or a release date, and P3 State said further details would follow. The central question for that release is whether the tech giant can demonstrate lower development and operating costs without sacrificing accuracy or capability, the compromise its efficiency thesis is intended to avoid.

We are glad to announce a long-awaited quality-of-life improvement: the Hugging Face CLI has been officially renamed from huggingface-cli to hf!

Typing huggingface-cli constantly gets old fast. More importantly, the CLI’s command structure became messy as new features were added over time (upload, download, cache management, repo management, etc.). Renaming the CLI is a chance to reorganize commands into a clearer, more consistent format.

According to recent reports, we decided not to reinvent the wheel and instead follow a well-known CLI pattern: hf . This predictable grammar makes the Hugging Face CLI more ergonomic and discoverable, while also setting the stage for upcoming features.

To start playing with the new CLI, you’ll need to install the latest huggingface_hub version:.

and reload your terminal session. To test the install completed successfully, run hf version:.

Next, let’s explore the new syntax with hf --help:.

In a recent development, as we can see, commands are grouped by "resource" (hf auth, hf cache, hf repo, etc.). We also surface hf upload and hf downloadat the root level since they’re expected to be the most-used commands.

To dive deeper into any command group, simply append --help:.

Industry observers note that if you are used to huggingface-cli, most commands will look familiar. The biggest change affects authentication:.

All auth commands have been grouped together with the existing hf auth switch (to switch between different local profiles) and hf auth list (to list local profiles).

The legacy huggingface-cli remains active and fully-functional. We’re keeping it around to ease the transition. If you use any command from the legacy CLI, you’ll see a warning that points you to the fresh CLI equivalent:.

We couldn’t resist shipping our first dedicated command: hf jobs.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Embo announced on November 23, 2026 that it had raised a $110 million seed round led by Andreessen Horowitz to build AI models for intelligent robots, using internet video and simulated practice to develop skills that hold up in unfamiliar situations.

According to recent reports, khosla Ventures, DST Global, NVIDIA’s venture arm NVentures and other strategic investors also participated. Embo is developing models that combine an understanding of physical reality with fine-grained motor skills, intended to serve as the control system for robots. Its stated objective is machines that work out of the box in unfamiliar scenarios, rather than depending on preparation for every object or task.

In a recent development, the problem Embo is targeting is the fragility of demonstration-trained robots. A machine can learn repetitive behaviors from demonstrations yet struggle when it encounters a fresh object, altered lighting or an unfamiliar situation. In its investment announcement, Andreessen Horowitz described the required capabilities as generalization and resilience: a robot trained in one kitchen should work in another, and recover when an object slips or a drawer sticks.

Recent findings suggest that embo’s approach starts with a world model, a system that learns how objects, physical interactions and tasks unfold by predicting internet video. Pretraining on a large volume of video is intended to supply broader physical knowledge than could be collected through demonstrations on its own robots. The model then provides imagined scenarios in which an agent can practice motor skills and improve through reinforcement learning, including how to recover from mistakes.

Andreessen Horowitz describes this as a path for robot learning to scale with compute. Agents can train on more experience than is practical to collect on physical hardware, including failures and unexpected events that demonstrations rarely capture, while practicing recovery as well as success.

It has been revealed that embo’s training strategy starts with a unified model built from scratch on internet-scale data. The same system will then be fine-tuned on experience from the company’s humanoid fleet before a final reinforcement-learning stage. Embo indicates the design can process dense video streams alongside rapid motor-control signals, a combination beyond the capabilities of language models. That places infrastructure and algorithm development at the center of the robotics effort.

Recent findings suggest that danijar Hafner and Wilson Yan are part of a team whose research includes Dreamer, VideoGPT and Diffusion Forcing. Its members bring experience from Google DeepMind, Meta Superintelligence Labs, NVIDIA Cosmos, UC Berkeley and MIT. Embo notes they have also built infrastructure for training multimodal models across 70,000 GPUs, experience relevant to its plan to pretrain a unified model at internet scale.

Sources indicate that A Dreamer 4 preprint, submitted by Hafner, Yan and Timothy Lillicrap on September 29, 2025, highlights how that research translates into agent training. The authors report that Dreamer 4 was the first agent to obtain diamonds in Minecraft purely from offline data, without environment interaction, by learning behaviors inside a world model. The task required choosing sequences of more than 20,000 mouse and keyboard actions from raw pixels.

In a recent development, the paper presents that challenge as relevant to robotics, where learning through environment interaction can be slow or unsafe. It supplies a concrete research example of Embo’s underlying idea: learn broad knowledge from video, then turn it into behavior through practice inside a model rather than relying exclusively on physical trial and error.

Industry observers note that andreessen Horowitz sees potential applications in manufacturing, product movement and service delivery. Embo now has to show that video-derived physical knowledge and imagined practice can produce reliable skills on physical humanoids outside controlled demonstrations; that transfer is the central test of both its technical approach and the seed investment.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, NOTICE: Sneakernet is a work in progress. The documentation makes some promises that are not reflected in the current state of affairs. Links to to-be-written parts of the documentation are indicated in red.

Sneakernet is a system for securely1 sending digital messages to other people without using the Internet. Instead, messages are automatically passed on to other Sneakernet users on your local network – at your hackerspace, an event or conference, your local cafe, etc — and then physically carried to their destination on your “sneakers”, where they will be automatically delivered to any recipients on the same network (or handed over to be carried further on by someone else).

Sneakernet encourages slow, thoughtful participation in community and face-to-face meetings with the users who will carry your messages onwards to their destination, and entrust their own messages to you.

⇒ Head to Getting started to set up Sneakernet on your device.

Sources indicate that many applications can be built on top of sneakernet’s general-purpose messaging system, provided that they are tolerant of high latency and out-of-order messages. Some examples include:.

Building your own sneakernet applications is easy, too, in any programming language – see Building applications for more details.

Industry observers note that all messages are authenticated and all private messages are also encrypted. People who carry your messages along cannot tamper with them and cannot read your private messages. See Security for more details.

InfoQ Homepage News Java News Roundup: Java4Shell, Oracle CSPUs, OpenJDK, Azul Payara, BellSoft, Helidon, LangChain4j.

Nov 23, 2026 7 min read.

This week's Java roundup for November 16th, 2026, features news highlighting: the Java4Shell RCE vulnerability; Oracle CSPUs; Lazy Constants targeted for JDK 28; the November 2026 edition of Azul Payara; point releases of Java Operator SDK, LangChain4j and Micrometer; maintenance releases of Liberica JDK and Helidon; and second release candidates of Hibernate Reactive.

Oracle has released versions 27.0.1.0.3, 25.0.5.0.3, 21.0.13.0.3, 17.0.21.0.3, 11.0.33.0.3 and 8u511b3 of the JDK as part of their quarterly Critical Security Patch Update Advisory for November 2026. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes for version 27.0.1.0.3, version 25.0.5.0.3, version 21.0.13.0.3, version 17.0.21.0.3, version 11.0.33.0.3 and version 8u511 b33.

JEP 547, Lazy Constants (Fourth Preview), has been elevated from Proposed to Target to Targeted for JDK 28. This JEP proposes a fourth preview, with no changes, after three rounds of preview delivered in the upcoming release of JDK 27 and JDK 26 through JDK 25. Formerly known as Stable Values and Computed Constants, this feature introduces the concept of computed constants, defined as immutable value holders that are initialized at most once. This offers the performance and safety benefits of final fields, while offering greater flexibility as to the timing of initialization. The name change from Stable Values to Lazy Constants with the release of JDK 26, better captures the intent of a high-level use case.

In a recent development, JEP 548, Vector API (Thirteenth Incubator), has been elevated from its JEP Draft 8397768 to Candidate status. This JEP proposes a thirteenth incubation with one notable change, after twelve rounds of incubation delivered in JDK 16 through JDK 27. This feature introduces an API to "express vector computations that reliably compile at runtime to optimal vector instructions on supported CPU architectures, thus achieving performance superior to equivalent scalar computations." This JEP adds support for Vector vectors, whose lanes hold 16-bit floating-point numbers in the IEEE 754 binary16 format. The Vector API will continue to incubate until the necessary features of Project Valhalla become available as preview features. At that time, the Vector API team will adapt the Vector API and its implementation to use them, and will promote the Vector API from Incubation to Preview.

Build 25 of the JDK 28 early-access builds was made available this past week featuring updates from Build 24 that include fixes for various challenges. More details on this release may be found in the release notes.

For JDK 28, developers are encouraged to report bugs via the Java Bug Database.

It has been revealed that A new Remote Code Execution (RCE) vulnerability, known as Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), affects versions 27.0.1.0.3, 25.0.5.0.3, 21.0.13.0.3, 17.0.21.0.3 and 8u511b33-perf of Oracle Java SE, versions 21.0.13.0.3 and 17.0.21.0.3 of Oracle GraalVM for JDK, and Oracle GraalVM Enterprise Edition: 21.3.20.0.3. As described in the CVE documentation:.

[This] difficult to exploit vulnerability allows [an] unauthenticated attacker with network access via multiple protocols to compromise Oracle Java SE, Oracle GraalVM for JDK, Oracle GraalVM Enterprise Edition. Successful attacks of this vulnerability can result in takeover of Oracle Java SE, Oracle GraalVM for JDK, Oracle GraalVM Enterprise Edition. Note: This vulnerability can only be exploited by supplying data to APIs in the specified Component without using Untrusted Java Web Start applications or Untrusted Java applets, such as through a web service.

Industry observers note that organizations and projects that have addressed this CVE include: BellSoft, Azul, JetBrains, GraalVM, Quarkus and WildFly. InfoQ will follow up with a more detailed news story.

It was a busy week over at Spring as the various teams have delivered GA releases that include: Spring Boot, Spring Framework, Spring Security, Spring Session, Spring Integration, Spring HATEOAS, Spring Modulith, Spring AI, Spring AMQP, Spring for Apache Kafka and Spring LDAP.

The Spring team has also resolved a total of 90 CVEs spanning multiple projects. InfoQ will follow up with a more detailed news story.

The release of Azul Payara 7.6.0, the November 2026 edition, includes Community Edition 7.2026.11, Enterprise Edition 6.44.0 and Enterprise Edition 5.93.0. Along with bug fixes and component upgrades, all three editions deliver resolutions to five CVEs, two of which are related to Azul Payara:.

Further details on this release may be found in the release notes and the Azul Payara security advisories page.

The second release candidates of Hibernate Reactive 5.1.0 and 5.0.0 ship with one single bug fix from the first release candidates, in which use of the Jakarta Persistence @TableGenerator annotation could cause a deadlock when a session holding the lock on the row of the generator table needed a fresh block of IDs.

Version 5.0.0.CR2 will be the last release candidate. With the GA release of version 5.0.0.Final, it will be declared as end-of-life and focus will be on version 5.1.0.

More details on these releases may be found in the release notes for version 5.1.0.CR2 and version 5.0.0.CR2.

Industry observers note that the release of Java Operator SDK 5.7.0 provides bug fixes, dependency upgrades and upcoming features such as: the ability to enable virtual threads via construction in the Operator class or the josdk.use-virtual-threads property; and a new keepAlive() method, defined in the Operator class that starts a non-daemon thread to keep the JVM running until the operator is shut down. Version 5.7 is now built on Fabric8 Kubernetes Client 8.0. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes.

Concurrent with Oracle's Critical Security Patch Enhancement (CSPU) for November 2026, BellSoft has released CSPU patches for versions 27.0.1.1 25.0.5.1, 21.0.13.1, 17.0.21.1, 11.0.33.1, 8u514 7u523 and 6u523 of Liberica JDK, their downstream distribution of OpenJDK, to address this list of CVEs. This release also includes a patch for the aforementioned Java4Shell Remote Code Execution vulnerability.

With an overall total of 111 fixes and backports, BellSoft states they have participated in eliminating 21 issues in all releases.

Sources indicate that the release of Helidon 27.0.2 delivers bug fixes and one notable change in which the default limit of decoded-input (strings, byte arrays, JSON, forms, and buffered multipart parts) for in-memory entity conversations has been increased to 1 mebibyte (MiB). More details on this release may be found in the release notes.

This release also aligns with the Oracle Critical Patch Updates for November 2026 and includes the Helidon 4.x and 3.x release trains as described in this blog post.

The formal release (along with the thirty-fourth beta release) of LangChain4j 1.24.0 ships with bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and new features such as: new DecisionSchedulerPlanner and DecisionModels classes to serve as a decision model-based agentic pattern; and support for resuming suspended agentic systems in the AgentMonitor class. Further details on this release, including breaking changes, may be found in the release notes.

According to recent reports, after two milestones and two releases candidates, the GA release of Micrometer Metrics 1.18.0 provides bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and latest features such as: an optimization of the PrometheusMeterRegistry and MicrometerCollector classes for collecting data snapshots; and a new RowState inner class, defined in the MultiGauge class, that eliminates the need to remove and re-register an instance of the existing Row inner class. More details on this release, including deprecations, may be found in the release notes.

In a recent development, similarly, the GA release of Micrometer Tracing 1.8.0 delivers bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and fresh features such as: a simplification of baggage handles and lookups by directly storing the name of the handle and its metadata by eliminating use of the CompositeBaggage and Java AtomicReference classes; and a refactor of the BaggageTextMapPropagator class for improved baggage propagation. Further details on this release, including deprecations, may be found in the release notes.

TL;DR: Trackio is a new, open-source, and free experiment tracking Python library that provides a local dashboard and seamless integration with Hugging Face Spaces for easy sharing and collaboration. Since trackio is a drop-in replacement for wandb, you can get started with the syntax you already know!

If you have trained your own machine learning model, you know how important it is to be able to track metrics, parameters, and hyperparameters during training and visualize them afterwards to better understand your training run.

Most machine learning researchers use specific experiment tracking libraries to do this. However, these libraries can be paid, require complex setup, or lack the flexibility needed for rapid experimentation and sharing.

At Hugging Face, our science team has started using Trackio for our research projects, and we've found several key advantages over other tracking solutions:.

It has been revealed that easy Sharing and Embedding: Trackio makes it incredibly simple to share training progress with colleagues or embed plots directly in blog posts and documentation using iframes. This is especially valuable when you want to showcase specific training curves or metrics without requiring others to set up accounts or navigate complex dashboards.

Recent findings suggest that standardization and Transparency: Metrics like GPU energy usage are key to track and share with the community so we can have a better idea of the energy demands and environmental impacts of model training. Using Trackio, which directly gets information from the nvidia-smi command, makes it easy to quantify and compare energy usage and to add it to model cards.

Data Accessibility: Unlike some tracking tools that lock your data behind proprietary APIs, Trackio makes it straightforward to extract and analyze the data being recorded. This is crucial for researchers who need to perform custom analysis or integrate training metrics into their research workflows.

In a recent development, flexibility for Experimentation: Trackio's lightweight design allows us to easily experiment with latest tracking features during training runs. For instance, we can decide when to move tensors from GPU to CPU when logging tensors while training, which significantly improves training throughput when you need to track model/intermediate states without impacting performance.

Ok then, so what is Trackio and how do you use it? Trackio is an open-source Python library that lets you track any metrics and visualize them using a local Gradio dashboard. You can also sync this dashboard to Hugging Face Spaces, which means you can then share the dashboard with other customers simply by sharing a URL. Since Spaces can be private or public, this means you can share a dashboard publicly or just within members of your Hugging Face organization.

You can install trackio using pip:.

Sources indicate that trackio is designed to be a drop-in replacement for experiment tracking libraries like wandb. The API is compatible with wandb.init, wandb.log, and wandb.finish, so you can simply import trackio as wandb in your code.

It has been revealed that after logging your experiments, you can launch the dashboard to visualize your results. Run the following command in your terminal:.

You can also specify a project name:.

To sync your local dashboard to Hugging Face Spaces, simply pass a space_id to init:.

If you are hosting your dashboard on Spaces, you can simply share the URL or embed it anywhere using an iframe:.

Since Spaces can be private or public, this means you can share a dashboard publicly or just within members of your Hugging Face organization — all for free!

When you sync your Trackio dashboard to Hugging Face Spaces, the data is logged to an ephemeral Sqlite database on Spaces. Because this database is reset if your Space restarts, Trackio also converts the Sqlite database to a Parquet dataset and backs it up to a Hugging Face Dataset every 5 minutes. This means you can visualize your logged metrics in a Hugging Face dataset at any time easily:.

Tip: you can set the name of this dataset by passing in a dataset_id to trackio.init().

Trackio integrates natively with Hugging Face libraries like transformers and accelerate, so you can log metrics with minimal setup.

No extra setup needed—just plug it in and start tracking.

It has been revealed that trackio is intentionally lightweight and is right now in beta. Some features found in other tracking tools, such as artifact management, or complex visualizations, are not available yet. If you'd like to have these features, please create issues here: https://github.com/gradio-app/trackio/issues.

Given Trackio's lightweight and open-source nature, we'd love to work with the machine learning community to design an experiment tracking product that works for all of us!

Please let us know any features you'd like to see in Trackio here: https://github.com/gradio-app/trackio/problems.

Many existing solutions are powerful, but they often come with setup overhead or limitations that can slow down rapid experimentation. A lightweight approach from Hugging Face feels like the right balance between functionality and ease of use... 👏.

Being able to promptly log results, compare runs, and visualize training progress can make a huge difference when iterating on models and testing new ideas. Simplicity is often underrated, especially when experimentation speed matters... ⚡🔬.

  • This is related to zizmor#1116, which has been bugging me for a year and a half.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TL;DR: GitHub Actions accepts several invalid YAML productions, making it difficult (read: impossible) to parse some real-world action and workflow definitions with a properly conforming YAML parser.

This is related to zizmor#1116, which has been bugging me for a year and a half.

Last April, a user reported that zizmor was rejecting a workflow containing a step that looks like this:.

Apart from the use of a multi-line flow-style string for the json: key, nothing particularly stands out about this step.

Except: it isn't valid YAML! YAML states this about flow-style nodes that are nested inside of a block-style parent collection (read: map or array):.

Flow nodes must be indented by at least one more space than the parent block collection. Note that flow nodes may begin on a following line.

That means the correct syntax is instead:.

The difference is barely visible:.

YAML is a massive and complicated spec, so it didn't even occur to me that this was invalid. Instead, I opened tree-sitter-yaml#36 to "fix" it. I've now opened tree-sitter-yaml#51 to revert that misbegotten fix.

According to recent reports, on GitHub's side, I'm not sure if they have a clean path towards spec conformance here. Much of the code behind Actions is proprietary, but it seems likely that the underlying parser on their end is YamlDotNet.

Industry observers note that actions appears to use YamlDotNet 5.3.0, which was released in 2018. However, even upgrading to the newest version (18.1.0 as of writing) wouldn't fix this particular bug, since it's still present on that version (note the !isSingleQuoted guard).

My best guess is that a 2020 patch (YamlDotNet#467) only fixed the double-quoted form because YAML's official test suite only tests rule 8.2.3 with a double-quoted string, despite it applying to both forms.

📚 3LM: A Benchmark for Arabic LLMs in STEM and Code

📅 01 Aug 2025 | ⏱️ 4 min read (844 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 📄 Paper on arXiv | 📦 Datasets on HuggingFace | 🔧 Code on GitHub.
  • Arabic Large Language Models (LLMs) have seen notable progress in recent years, yet existing benchmarks fall short when it comes to evaluating performance in high-value technical domains.
  • To address this gap, we introduce 3LM (علم), a multi-component benchmark tailored to evaluate Arabic LLMs on STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics) subjects and code generation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

📄 Paper on arXiv | 📦 Datasets on HuggingFace | 🔧 Code on GitHub.

Arabic Large Language Models (LLMs) have seen notable progress in recent years, yet existing benchmarks fall short when it comes to evaluating performance in high-value technical domains. Most evaluations to date have focused on general-purpose tasks like summarization, sentiment analysis, or generic question answering. However, scientific reasoning and programming are essential for a broad range of real-world applications, from education to technical problem-solving.

To address this gap, we introduce 3LM (علم), a multi-component benchmark tailored to evaluate Arabic LLMs on STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics) subjects and code generation. 3LM is the first benchmark of its kind, designed specifically to test Arabic models in structured reasoning and formal logic which are domains traditionally underrepresented in Arabic NLP.

3LM is made up of three datasets, each targeting a specific evaluation axis: real-world multiple-choice STEM questions (MCQs), synthetic high-difficulty STEM questions, and translated code generation tasks.

According to recent reports, the Native STEM benchmark consists of 865 MCQs extracted from authentic Arabic educational content, including textbooks, worksheets, and exam banks for grades 8 through 12. Questions span five core subjects: Physics, Chemistry, Biology, Mathematics, and Geography.

Each question is annotated with metadata including domain and difficulty (on a 1–10 scale). The data was sourced using a pipeline that combined OCR (including LaTeX math parsing via Pix2Tex), LLM-assisted question-answer extraction, and manual review. This dataset provides a realistic testbed for evaluating factual and conceptual understanding in Arabic models using real educational materials.

To introduce greater challenge and diversity, we created a synthetic subset of 1,744 MCQs using the YourBench pipeline. This component draws from Arabic textbook text, which is chunked, summarized, and used as input to an LLM-driven question generation system. The result is a curated set of questions focused on mid-to-high difficulty reasoning, including conceptual, analytical, and application-based problems.

It has been revealed that synthetic STEM provides an crucial counterbalance to native MCQs by probing deeper reasoning skills and minimizing answer bias. All generated questions underwent filtering based on clarity, structure, and content validity, followed by quality assurance via manual review.

The third component of 3LM targets code generation which is a growing area of LLM evaluation. We translated and adapted the widely-used HumanEval+ and MBPP+ benchmarks into Arabic, creating the first code datasets that test Arabic LLMs on natural language prompts for programming.

We used GPT-4o for prompt translation and validated the results with a backtranslation pipeline, rejecting low-quality samples based on ROUGE-L F1 thresholds (< 0.8). Additional human filtering ensured prompt clarity and correctness. The code and test suites remain unchanged to preserve scoring fidelity. Evaluations use the EvalPlus framework for pass@1 and pass@1+ metrics.

Each dataset in 3LM went through a multi-stage development process to ensure data quality, fairness, and representativeness.

For Native STEM, we collected Arabic PDF sources and applied a dual OCR approach to recover both plain text and math formulas. Questions were extracted using LLM-based chunking and pattern recognition, followed by classification into MCQ format with randomized answer order. Final samples were reviewed by native Arabic speakers with STEM expertise to confirm answer validity and readability.

Sources indicate that for Synthetic STEM, the YourBench pipeline was adapted for Arabic input. Source documents after ingestion were first summarized, chunked and then fed to a code-controlled generator for MCQ creation. We filtered out image-dependent or ambiguous content, and only retained questions within target difficulty ranges. The result is a set of clean, high-quality synthetic Arabic MCQs for STEM.

Industry observers note that for the Code Benchmarks, our goal was to isolate language understanding while preserving code logic. Prompt translation was handled by GPT-4o with verification via reverse translation. Code and tests were untouched to allow evaluation parity with English versions. The result is a benchmark where Arabic prompts can be evaluated directly with the EvalPlus toolchain.

We evaluated over 40 LLMs, including Arabic-first, multilingual, and general-purpose base and instruction-tuned models. Evaluation was performed using both multiple-choice accuracy and generative completion metrics.

Recent findings suggest that in the MCQ setting, Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct achieved top performance across both native (71.8%) and synthetic (67.0%) STEM subsets. For completion tasks, Gemma-3-27B indicated the strongest results with 43.2% accuracy on STEM answers.

In a recent development, in code generation, GPT-4o demonstrated best-in-class performance on both HumanEval-ar (83.5% pass@1+) and MBPP-ar (63.6% pass@1+). These results highlight strong correlation (~0.97) between Arabic and English pass@1 scores, suggesting language-specific prompt quality has a major influence on model outcomes.

Sources indicate that we also examined robustness under distractor perturbation, revealing that instruction-tuned models are significantly more stable than their base counterparts. Prompt engineering and zero-shot design were also shown to meaningfully affect Arabic STEM performance.

We built the benchmark to be easily reproducible using standard tools:.

All scripts, configs, and evaluation pipelines are available in our GitHub repository, and can be adapted to evaluate any model compatible with HuggingFace Transformers or OpenAI APIs.

All three datasets are open-source and hosted on HuggingFace Datasets:.

If you use 3LM in your research, please cite us:.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that indiana University revealed on November 23 that it will receive $25 million from Lilly Endowment Inc. to bring AI into undergraduate education and student support across its nine campuses. The university aims to use the funding through 2030 to teach AI skills within degree programs, help faculty redesign assessments and expand the capacity of staff who advise and support students.

The award is part of a $291.71 million round of implementation grants for 35 Indiana colleges and universities. Those awards range from $2.5 million to $25 million. The endowment has allocated up to $500 million for the broader initiative, which also covers planning and collaborative projects. Lilly Endowment is a private foundation separate from the pharmaceutical manufacturer Eli Lilly and Company.

It has been revealed that IU calls its program the Human + AI Learning Ecosystem, or HALE. The implementation grant follows a $300,000 planning grant that funded a university-wide effort to identify where AI could help and where it could undermine learning. IU indicates more than 120 faculty members, staff and students participated in four planning groups. The two investigators leading the implementation grant are Rahul Shrivastav, vice president for student success, and Anne Leftwich, chief academic and AI innovation officer.

The program aims to teach AI literacy in the context of each discipline. That distinction matters: checking an AI-generated cost projection calls for different evidence than checking an AI-generated interpretation of a historical document. Faculty also have to decide where students can use AI and where assignments should demonstrate what they can do independently. IU has a faculty group on student learning in the age of AI to bring perspectives from different campuses and disciplines into that work.

IU also plans to use AI to help staff spot barriers to student success earlier and spend more time directly supporting students. The announcement names academic advising, financial aid, career exploration and student communications as possible areas for improved workflows. IU says it wants to improve retention and graduation. It did not report measured gains from HALE or specify which systems would flag cases and how staff would review them.

Sources indicate that the university already operates several AI services, and its data-management guidance shows why the choice of tool matters. An institution-managed chatbot workspace, a cloud service for application developers and models hosted in the IU data center have different approved uses and data restrictions. IU separately warns that public AI services are not approved for institutional data, even when that data has been anonymized. An advising workflow that uses student records has to meet a different standard from a classroom exercise that uses public material. Availability of a tool alone does not determine what information it can process or who should act on the result.

The grant gives IU several years to test whether its approach works across programs with different student populations and staffing needs. Useful measures would include whether students can identify errors in AI output, whether redesigned assessments still test the skills a degree is supposed to certify and whether earlier outreach gets students to the support they need. Usage statistics can show how widely a tool was adopted, but they cannot answer those questions on their own.

The wider Lilly Endowment initiative will give other Indiana institutions room to try different approaches. For IU, the test through 2030 is whether AI can improve access to support and prepare students for the workplace while preserving the independent judgment the university wants graduates to develop.

In a recent development, NVIDIA’s AI-Q Blueprint—the leading portable, open deep research agent—recently climbed to the top of the Hugging Face “LLM with Search” leaderboard on DeepResearch Bench. This is a significant step forward for the open-source AI stack, proving that developer-accessible models can power advanced agentic workflows that rival or surpass closed alternatives.

In a recent development, what sets AI-Q apart? It fuses two high-performance open LLMs—Llama 3.3-70B Instruct and Llama-3.3-Nemotron-Super-49B-v1.5—to orchestrate long-context retrieval, agentic reasoning, and robust synthesis.

The AI-Q reference example also includes:.

The architecture supports parallel, low-latency search over local and web data, making it ideal for use cases that demand privacy, compliance, or on-premise deployment for reduced latency.

NVIDIA Llama Nemotron Super isn’t just a fine-tuned instruct model—it’s post-trained for explicit agentic reasoning and supports reasoning ON/OFF toggles via system prompts. You can use it in standard chat LLM mode or switch to deep, chain-of-thought reasoning for agent pipelines—enabling dynamic, context-sensitive workflows.

In a recent development, one of the core strengths of AI-Q is transparency—not just in outputs, but in reasoning traces and intermediate steps. During development, the NVIDIA team leveraged both standard and new metrics, such as:.

The architecture lends itself perfectly to granular, stepwise evaluation and debugging—one of the biggest pain points in agentic pipeline development.

DeepResearch Bench evaluates agent stacks using a set of 100+ long-context, real-world research tasks (across science, finance, art, history, software, and more). Unlike traditional QA, tasks require report-length synthesis and complex multi-hop reasoning:.

The open-source ecosystem is rapidly closing the gap—and, in some areas, leading—on real-world agent tasks that matter. AI-Q, built on Llama Nemotron, demonstrates that you don’t need to compromise on transparency or control to achieve state-of-the-art results.

Try the stack or adapt it to your own research agent projects from Hugging Face or build.nvidia.com.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Reviving wiki.alpinelinux.org during PHP2Shell · November 21, 2026.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Reviving wiki.alpinelinux.org during PHP2Shell · November 21, 2026.

It feels like this month (and last month..) has been nonstop chaos. PHP2Shell threw a nice little grenade into an already busy month, and while that was happening a GitLab RCE took down Alpine's GitLab instance. It was a whole thing, and as frustrating as it was, I'm kind of proud to say that I got to help respond to the event and write the incident announcement. Ikke did all of the real heavy lifting, but it takes a community to keep a distribution together. Everything, and I mean everything, is kept together by volunteers lending their time and talent with no expectation that there will be a reward for the effort.

It has been revealed that we do it because we care for the work being done. Whether it's a critical service enabling a community of tens of thousands to distribute hundreds of petabytes of data that we call "Alpine", or simply enabling a small piece of software to work for personal desires. All of it happens because someone cares enough to do the work. I love this so much, frankly. It's absolutely flabbergasting what we as a community can do with our spare time.

Sources indicate that I enjoy giving my time to Alpine Linux, because there's a community, and because we can have an outsized impact on the world by collaborating together. It's not perfect, but it's rewarding. I think I owe my career to it in a sense. I've learned so much by simply raising my hand and being willing to give my time and learn a few latest things. But there's a limit to how far you get on donated time, both personally, and as a project.

It has been revealed that not in the sense that it wasn't used; it gets tons of traffic and contains a treasure trove of useful information that people depend on and are excited to contribute to. But between keeping the infrastructure afloat, migrating off of Equinix to new sponsored compute, and mitigating the constant wave of problems, from scale to RCE, that plague a small engineering team trying to serve a massive consumer base, well, it's no wonder that once alice was no longer contributing, the infrastructure languished a bit. This wasn't intentional, nor was it bad. There simply wasn't spare time to contribute to it.

So in November of last year ikke asked if anyone was interested in lending a bit of spare time to fixing that problem. Naturally, I raised my hand, happy to have an opportunity to do so.

This was essentially the sum of information I got about the wiki; it was all that was really documented. And despite my eagerness to jump in immediately and lift it up from whatever state it happened to be in, it took time to get access. We had a release to get out. We were fighting to get 3.23 finished and didn't even get it wrapped up until 12/3/25! So it's no wonder that it took until 1/16/26 before I got access to the server itself to start poking around and even begin to understand how the deployment was handled.

And as you can guess by the fact that I'm writing this post in October of 2026, I did not get in there and immediately upgrade it and move on.

In a recent development, and I think that's important. Even if I'm only giving away a limited amount of time, I hate to rush through things without fully understanding them. There's just no way I can improve something if I don't have a solid grounding. More importantly, I actually really love spelunking inside of old systems other sysadmins have set up. Everyone has a unique flair to how they deploy something. Enterprise admins end up deploying things in a real textbook manner, and when you deal with small businesses it's usually a hodgepodge of "just get it done". I haven't had a ton of opportunities to spelunk FOSS infrastructure though! What I found was interesting in its own right, mostly because I don't think I'd have deployed the service this way.

According to recent reports, what ikke told me was spot on: MediaWiki was a git checkout with extensions and skins vendored as submodules inside the repo. You could slot in new modules using composer, and as long as you had an appropriate underlying PHP version to work with, you were golden. But that was then mixed with actual wiki data, like images, all of it lumped together in /var/www. Very simple, but not obvious if you'd not dealt with it before.

Sources indicate that when I got into the server, MediaWiki 1.40.0 was running on PHP 8.2 on top of Alpine 3.20, but the LocalSettings.php that controlled the wiki was generated under 1.25.3. Just to give you a sense, 1.40.0 is from July 2023, and 1.25.3 is from October of 2015! It's really neat to get a sense for how long something was tended for. Of course, our friends at the Internet Archive have been archiving the Alpine Wiki since April of 2010, and based on the main page I can tell you we've been using MediaWiki for a solid 16 years now, if not longer. I'm positive it's not the same exact server, but probably the same-ish data. I made notes about all the little important bits I found, everything from extension inventories to known issues and interesting shell snippets I found in the server's history file. Anything can be, and is, helpful when you're spelunking. Truthfully, given the age of the deployment, the public facing nature of the server, and my relative newness to administering MediaWiki servers, I was approaching the problem with the utmost caution.

Industry observers note that by the end of February I had MediaWiki figured out, but it wasn't committed until March. And not to bury the lede, but I mean that in the most me way possible. I went through the process of setting up a clone of the staging server in my homelab. From there I worked out how to package MediaWiki itself, and then break out all of the various extensions that comprise the core system into a proper APKBUILD. After packaging it, I was no longer surprised it hadn't been done before. The core extension list alone is absurdly long, and all told we use 36 different extensions for our wiki, so this isn't even a complete list.

Recent findings suggest that and given the complexity, and that this was all production infrastructure, I tried to get it merged into the community repositories before making any sort of change to the production infrastructure. Anything less wasn't really right in my mind.

Recent findings suggest that but it sat, not because it wasn't appreciated, but because we are woefully close to the absolute maximum storage we can host through our CDN. Not that we weren't working on that either; I started looking into our space limitations in earnest in March, when it was a potential blocker to our ability to release 3.24 in June. I knew the package was too substantial to go into community, but I also didn't think leaving it in testing made sense for production infrastructure. So I turned my focus to the clearer, bigger problem and started working with ikke and clandmeter to figure out a path to archive our older distributions.

By May that problem had turned into discussions with Jason at the Internet Archive, which, as this little aside suggests, was the least stressful component of any of this. Jason is an amazing archivist, and the work the Internet Archive is doing is a massive boon to FOSS projects.

And of course, dear reader, I bet you can guess what happened next. I packaged the ia tool, built a prototype to validate we could actually migrate things, and when a prototype wasn't enough, turned it into its own tool, arkivi, which can do partial migrations and reclaim space while it migrates data. None of that merged quickly either, because, well, we were out of space and had a release to cut. But once again, I had time to donate, and I wasn't going to provide half a solution to a problem I could solve.

According to recent reports, this might seem like a bit of a detour, but I swear it's not! We are in fact still talking about upgrading the wiki! I couldn't get the core MediaWiki package merged into a stable repo, let alone any of the extensions, which means it can't be released on a stable branch. As much as I personally trust Alpine and think we do a good job keeping edge decently stable, the reality is that it's a testing area sometimes, and it makes very little sense to run production infrastructure off of it. Or if you are going to do that, you need to ensure you have the time to keep up with the constant churn. You can probably guess my concern here: I might not have that time to give.

There are so many disparate but interconnected problems going on in the background of most FOSS distributions that you just can't fathom until you live with them. And the wild part? Nothing I've described is unique. I work within a community of clever and dedicated people who turn this type of work around on the regular. But as you can imagine, I lost my momentum on actually reviving the wiki too. I got blocked by infrastructure constraints and couldn't complete the task in what I felt was a professional and sustainable manner, so I simply waited. My small problem didn't outweigh the needs of the distribution, and there were bigger problems to solve elsewhere. The wiki was stable, it was fine.
