I'll get testing done tonight. Heading home from work now and should have time shortly after.

PHP2Shell isn't the kind of thing you leave running on a public server, and the wiki was sitting on PHP 8.2 on a branch that was already out of support. So the wiki went dark. We were forced to throw up a maintenance page and block people's access to the wiki. And of course people asked why, and when to expect it back. Like I noted earlier, a lot of people depend on this resource to use our distro!

Industry observers note that which of course kicked off a fever pitch of building, testing, and migrating. I wasn't ready for this! I was missing extensions, I hadn't fully tested the database upgrade process, it wasn't automated, and my packages weren't in a stable repo!

But I wasn't starting from zero either. The core package had been sitting in testing since March. I had a clone of stage in my homelab, and a README full of notes about every odd corner of the old install. The better part of a year that looked like stalling had at least given me some sense of how to proceed.

It would have been nice to take the easy out at this point, but it would have been the most temporary of bandaids:.

Industry observers note that so it was four upgrades at once: Alpine 3.20 to 3.24 (we're still working on 3.25 at the moment), PHP 8.2 to 8.3, MediaWiki 1.40 to 1.46.2, and the git submodule install to apk packages. Well, there really was no quick fix. Somewhere in that stack something would break, and it would keep creating problems down the line unless the work was done in a way that made it all easier to maintain long term.

Even if I wanted to take the quick path and just get the job done, that's the sort of logic that results in the same sort of languishing. Just run the old stuff, just upgrade the existing thing, keep it all similar, move onto the next thing. Sideload 1.46 the old way, get it up tonight, clean it up "later". I have so little time to give, and so many other crucial changes that need to be made. For anyone paying attention, that's only getting worse with the literal waterfall of RCEs being unveiled day after day after day, and we're expected to just keep up with it all. It's a lot, but it will only be worse if we cut corners and stop caring about doing it right. "Later" is exactly how the wiki got here in the first place.

Plus, that's not who I am. No, I'd rather dogfood a latest tool I've been working on, finish the packaging work, and prove out that everything can and will work on a v3.24 mock and provide a good stable experience. Anything less would be unprofessional, an affront to the craft, or at the very least to my sense of pride.

Sources indicate that which leaves just one awkward bit. Despite all of my effort, the mediawiki packages are still making their way through testing. The work is never truly finished, there's always one more thing that needs to be done. But I'm confident once everything catches up the path forward is that much easier. Every mediawiki component and extension packaged provides a simpler maintenance path going forward. Nobody needs to remember anything I've described thus far. And anyone who wants to suggest an extension to make the wiki better can actively contribute to that process by packaging and testing it.

Sources indicate that it turns out that emergencies are great times to stress test the library coverage of a configuration management tool, especially when you need to spin up a box, test a migration, and repeat it over and over. I could have done all of this with some shell scripts or with Salt, but it's a lot more fun to use scio and figure out how well the little Lua DSL I've put together maps onto things I'd either do by hand or know well enough another way. The reps are the point. Every time something broke, I fixed it in the state, threw the box away, and ran it again from nothing, until a fresh Alpine 3.24 container could become a working wiki without me touching it. If you're curious what that looks like, the full scio state is here.

Sources indicate that if I as a contributor only have so much time to give, and my standard is that it's done well and to the best of my abilities, well, then I'll combine pleasure and work and solve two problems in one go. Servers get upgraded, I get a production grade test case for my configuration management system, and the entire thing is held together by spare time and tenacity!

I'll write more about scio in the near future. There's a lot to say, but now's not the time.

Did I mention I try to be meticulous? All of the preflight work isn't nearly enough when working with production infrastructure; I wanted to know exactly what I was touching. So naturally, I wrote a quick diff script to compare stage and prod, and the answer I got in the process was very reassuring. The two servers were nearly identical. The only real difference was prod's exposure layer, with go-away out front and nginx listening behind it. Then I wrote a backup script, because the existing backups weren't something I was willing to bet on. My process was obvious afterward: a throwaway incus container restored from a prod dump first, then stage, and only then prod.

It has been revealed that good thing, too. I could see every place I might trip, and I still managed to stumble.

According to recent reports, first up was LocalSettings.php. Remember that file generated back in 2015 under 1.25.3? It had been carried forward through every upgrade since, collecting settings MediaWiki removed years ago ($wgScriptExtension, $wgDBmysql5, $wgUseTeX, $wgShowIPinHeader, $wgSquidServers) and path overrides pointing into a git tree that was about to stop existing. It fell over one dead path at a time. Fix a line, run the patch, watch it die on the next one. Eventually I stopped playing whack-a-mole and just started over from scratch. A decade of "it still works, don't touch it", gone. I'll try my best to remember to leave a note for the next sysadmin who comes after me.

Even then, once I could actually open a page on the wiki, every image on it came back with "Error creating thumbnail: File missing." The old backups had never included uploads. The database was covered, but as far as the backups were concerned, every image anyone had ever uploaded to the wiki existed in exactly one place. Nobody was careless here. In the old install the uploads sat right alongside everything else in /var/www, and I hadn't understood where things lived well enough to notice they were missing from the backups. My mock tests never checked for them either. What an obvious and embarrassing look it would have been if I hadn't caught it on staging first!

Industry observers note that but then I fucked up. On stage, I ran php maintenance/run.php install instead of patch. It was late, it must have been nearing 1am or 2am at this point, and I wasn't fully paying attention. I should have stopped and rested, it could have waited another day, but I had committed to fixing this. If it's not obvious, install is for empty databases. Pointed at a real one, it overwrites an existing db with a fresh schema and admin account right on top of everything that's already there. Thank goodness I had a backup. I was able to easily restore the dump, put things back the way they were, start the whole thing over.

It has been revealed that the rest were the kind of thing that just ate time, and they make for a pretty dull story. $wgMainCacheType = CACHE_ACCEL needs php83-pecl-apcu, and opcache doesn't count. The 3.24 mariadb client refuses non-TLS connections by default, so everything needed --skip-ssl initially. The packaged php-fpm listens on a unix socket rather than 127.0.0.1:9000, which I learned by way of 502s. Restored pages rendered stale, because their old page_touched values were older than the freshly built parser cache, which $wgCacheEpoch fixed. And AbuseFilter's grants were redacted in the capture I was working from, so I recovered them from the backup.

When it finally came together, the schema revision on stage took 28 seconds. After all of that effort, 28 seconds.

According to recent reports, 2026-10-22 06:41:46 durrendal ikke: I was able to get stage updated to v3.24, Mediawiki to 1.46.2 on php83. 2026-10-22 06:42:32 durrendal it was more time intensive than I had hoped so I didn't get to the prod server yet, but should be able to get to it tomorrow. about 3a here so I'm off to bed 2026-10-22 06:42:48 @ikke Alright, thanks so far! 2026-10-22 06:43:45 durrendal no problem :) I think prod will take less time now that I've worked out the kinks on staging. 2026-10-22 06:46:22 ncopa durrendal: thanks alot!

2026-10-23 10:00:21 ncopa durrendal: are you still working on wiki.a.o? 2026-10-23 11:34:07 durrendal ncopa: yeah sorry for the radio silence, also scrambling at work over this. I should be able to finish it today though, I'll keep you posted. 2026-10-23 11:34:19 ncopa thank you!

That radio silence was the day job. PHP2Shell didn't just land on Alpine, it landed on everyone, and I spent my days scrambling over the same bug I was fixing for the wiki in the evenings.

By the time I sat down with prod, the hard part was over. It had become routine and easy because I put the learning up front where it belonged. Prod got a maintenance mode, a flag file that nginx checks on every request. Touch it and the world sees a maintenance notice, while requests from the box itself still reach the wiki, so I could test everything from localhost before anyone else could see it. Then the same migrations I'd already run on stage, with no surprises this time. Rsync the uploads into /var/lib/mediawiki/images. Carry over the parts of prod that make it prod: minor tweaks to php-fpm for performance, go-away, the easy stuff.

2026-10-24 02:40:57 durrendal ikke ncopa the production wiki is fully upgraded and back online! 2026-10-24 02:41:12 durrendal https://wiki.alpinelinux.org/wiki/Special:Version 2026-10-24 02:48:22 lotheac nice! 2026-10-24 02:57:20 durrendal thanks :) and it's using packages instead of the old git submodule install too so hopefully this shouldn't languish ever again 2026-10-24 02:57:57 durrendal I just need to open a few MRs now.

Sources indicate that the wiki is on Alpine 3.24, MediaWiki 1.46.2, and PHP 8.3, and every piece of it comes from apk. Which means the next time a PHP2Shell comes along, the fix is apk upgrade, run.php enhancement, and a php-fpm restart. No submodules or composer, nobody needs to remember something special, all that's needed is a bit of Alpine specific systems administration knowledge and we're golden. This will get better as I finish documenting the new installation, so that when I inevitably run out of spare time, the next person to raise their hand can stand on my shoulders and reach a little higher.

Recent findings suggest that look, at the start of this I said there's a limit to how far you can get on donated time. I meant that, but not to signal some kind of fundamental flaw in the system. Alice tended to this before me, ikke kept it running alongside everything else, and when it needed someone, someone raised their hand. This time it was me. There are many, many people like me, what I've described is not unique. But look what it took, eleven months from "anyone want to help maintain the wiki?" to an actual upgrade, most of it spent trying to solve other problems around the one that was volunteered for. When the emergency came, it got fixed because someone was willing to pay down the technical debt all at once.

Recent findings suggest that that's what spare time can carry, and it's a lot. It's also why it matters that Alpine is choosing to fund dedicated infrastructure engineering. Not because volunteers can't do the work, but because the work shouldn't depend on whether someone happens to have a free evening when the next CVE drops. Spare time built this wiki, and spare time will keep tending it. It just shouldn't have to hold it together alone.

As for me, I got what I always hope to get from raising my hand, an opportunity to learn. I walked in knowing very little about Mediawiki administration, and while I wouldn't call myself an expert from one small engagement, I'm happy to have come away with a few more packages, more confidence in scio, and a once more working wiki for Alpine. And a great reminder that part of giving your spare time is knowing when to stop, nobody will ever be mad that you ran out of spare time.

JEP 545 Moves ZGC Memory Preparation off the Startup Path in JDK 28

💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News JEP 545 Moves ZGC Memory Preparation off the Startup Path in JDK 28.
  • Nov 23, 2026 4 min read.
  • According to recent reports, JEP 545, Faster Startup and Warmup with ZGC, has been integrated into JDK 28, moving the work of acquiring and preparing heap memory off the startup path and onto dedicated concurrent worker threads.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News JEP 545 Moves ZGC Memory Preparation off the Startup Path in JDK 28.

Nov 23, 2026 4 min read.

According to recent reports, JEP 545, Faster Startup and Warmup with ZGC, has been integrated into JDK 28, moving the work of acquiring and preparing heap memory off the startup path and onto dedicated concurrent worker threads. On Linux 6.1 and later it also upgrades 4 KB pages to 2 MB pages while the application runs. The 2 MB initial heap behind the JEP's headline numbers comes from elsewhere: adaptive heap sizing, in the companion JEP 546, which still defaults to off.

It has been revealed that deploying ZGC has until now meant choosing which half of a trade-off to pay for. The collector's pause times do not grow with the heap, but its collection frequency does, so a small heap brings on early and frequent cycles. The JEP describes the older ergonomic behavior of committing one sixty-fourth of physical memory for the initial heap.

Recent findings suggest that A team chasing fast startup set a tiny -Xms and accepted a long warmup, because the collector then had to acquire and prepare memory in increments while the application was already allocating. A team chasing fast warmup set a large -Xms, usually with -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch, and paid the whole bill before the first request landed. The JEP puts the spread at roughly a tenth of a second to start with a 2 MB heap against more than ten seconds with a 32 GB one on current hardware.

It has been revealed that that work now happens in a fresh thread, ZMemoryWorker, one per heap partition. It commits and uncommits memory concurrently as capacity changes. It also heats memory before application threads reach it, which means pre-touching page by page and collapsing small pages into large ones.

Recent findings suggest that the budget is fixed rather than adaptive. ZConcurrentWorkersCPUShare in zGlobals.hpp is 0.25, so preparation takes at most a quarter of the available CPU. ZGC's director caps young-generation worker counts when adaptive sizing is on, which keeps collection inside its CPU target while expansion continues and the collector deliberately runs above its heuristic heap size target.

Recent findings suggest that large pages on Linux no longer require an administrator to reserve them up front. ZGC probes for MADV_COLLAPSE, the madvise mode added in Linux 6.1, by mapping a 4 MB region, pre-touching a single page and collapsing an aligned 2 MB range. When the probe succeeds and memory heating is enabled, the collector enters a new Collapse state and upgrades pages in the background. The call races the kernel's khugepaged, so the implementation retries on EAGAIN.

It has been revealed that the change indicates up in what a deployer no longer has to decide. Where JDK 25 forced a choice between two tunings, JDK 28 offers a third option:.

Industry observers note that the third command produces the JEP's case study figures, a 38% drop in startup time and a fall in warmup from 80 seconds to 10 for Spring PetClinic on a 32 GB machine. -XX:+ZAdaptiveHeapSizing takes the minimum and initial heap down to 2 MB and raises the MaxHeapSize ceiling to 100% of physical memory. Without it, ZGC falls back to the shared heap sizing path and a 25% ceiling. Concurrent preparation still runs, but not the aggressive expansion the measurements depend on.

Using identical memory techniques on every operating system is an explicit non-goal, so large pages may be the default on Linux and not on Windows. The JEP also cautions that applications tuned around a larger initial heap may warm up more slowly and need re-tuning.

According to recent reports, two further edges live in the implementation rather than the text. Pairing -XX:+UseLargePages with adaptive sizing and no -Xmx logs a warning and disables explicit large pages for the heap. The retry loop around MADV_COLLAPSE can also spin indefinitely when EAGAIN persists, a case the code attributes to pinning through mlock or long-term DMA and treats as user error.

Teams can see the heap sizing difference for themselves on the JDK 28 early-access builds by comparing the resolved flags:.

The second run drops the minimum and initial sizes to the 2 MB floor and lifts the maximum from a quarter of physical memory to all of it. Adding -Xlog:gc+init reports Memory Heating: Enabled and, once the collapse path is active, Large Page Support: Enabled (Transparent, JVM enforced).

According to recent reports, services already running a modest heap on Linux 6.1 or later pick up concurrent pre-touch and background large pages without touching a flag, because memory heating is on by default. Services carrying a large pre-touched heap purely to buy warmup have something to delete, though only after enabling adaptive sizing. That 100% ceiling reads worse than it behaves. The policy tracks machine-wide memory and holds a reserve, preferring to leave a fifth of the machine free, fighting for a tenth and enforcing a twentieth, with those margins widening when usage is unstable or compressed.

JDK 28 reaches Rampdown Phase One on December 3, 2026, with general availability scheduled for March 9, 2027. The JEP's own future work points at better CPU sharing between concurrent collection and concurrent commit, and at ahead-of-time compilation from JEP 544, already Completed for JDK 28, which frees JIT cycles the memory workers could spend instead.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that anthropic released Claude Ship on November 23, 2026, making the beta product available to Claude Team and Enterprise organizations for GitHub repositories.
  • In a recent development, together, they address the handoffs after code is written.
  • Sources indicate that review depth is configurable.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that anthropic released Claude Ship on November 23, 2026, making the beta product available to Claude Team and Enterprise organizations for GitHub repositories. It pairs the generally available Code Review with two new public-beta agents, PR Steward and Claude Approvals, to carry pull requests through review, fixes and an approval decision.

In a recent development, together, they address the handoffs after code is written. Code Review reads a change alongside the surrounding codebase, gathers and adversarially verifies findings, and posts severity-ranked inline comments on the affected lines. PR Steward can push commits containing fixes, while Claude Approvals checks the pull request against a policy written by the team.

Sources indicate that review depth is configurable. Administrators can select Quick, Standard or Deep review levels for each repository and choose when reviews run, allowing different repositories to use different levels of scrutiny and automation.

PR Steward responds to failing continuous-integration checks, merge conflicts and feedback from Code Review, other review tools or team members. After every push, it comments on what changed and how to undo the work. Developers can steer the agent with an @claude instruction or tell it to step back with @claude stop.

PR Steward is designed not to approve or merge pull requests. Repository settings and GitHub branch rules determine what can merge, keeping the authority to complete a pull request separate from the agent’s ability to commit fixes.

Claude Approvals uses a policy file that the team writes in the repository. The policy can set how many people must approve changes to a path and where Claude may post an approving review. Routine changes can receive Claude’s approval when permitted, while designated scenarios require deeper human sign-off. Decision signals can include Code Review findings and the team’s own classifiers written in natural language.

Industry observers note that anthropic recommends that most customers begin in observe-only mode, where the check reports what the policy would decide and normally does not block merging. Enforcement requires the organization to make Claude Approvals a required GitHub check.

The technical documentation warns both that GitHub auto-merge or a merge queue can merge a change without anyone acting if the policy does not require a person’s approval, and that Claude Ship may miss bugs, security vulnerabilities or other issues.

Developers can start the process on their own changes with /ship, which began rolling out in Claude Code and the desktop app alongside the launch. The command pushes the change, opens a pull request, reviews it and works on feedback and failing checks, subject to the developer’s permissions and repository branch rules. Organizations can instead enable Claude Ship repository by repository so its agents start across team pull requests without a manual /ship invocation.

Anthropic runs Claude Ship on many of its own pull requests. On the Claude Code team, where Claude’s review is one layer of a broader process, the company reports that merged pull requests more than doubled from June to September 2026 while the share reverted fell by more than 40%.

Claude Ship usage is billed by tokens separately from a strategy’s included usage. Costs depend on the number and size of pull requests, review level and frequency, and the amount of PR Steward work. Administrators can set spend limits for Code Review and PR Steward. Claude Approvals has no base charge, but classifier runs consume billed tokens and a policy-requested Claude review triggers a billed Code Review even in observe mode. Running /ship counts as regular Claude Code usage.

In a recent development, eligible Claude Enterprise organizations can claim at least $10,000 in Claude Ship credits by January 15, 2027, for use within 30 days of claiming. The agents are unavailable to organizations using Zero Data Retention, the HIPAA configuration or customer-managed encryption keys.

It has been revealed that claude Ship moves Anthropic’s agents beyond producing code and into coordinating the work that surrounds a pull request. Its practical role is defined by those repository controls: policy, required checks and branch rules determine whether it assists human reviewers or allows changes to merge without human involvement.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

GPT OSS is a hugely anticipated open-weights release by OpenAI, designed for powerful reasoning, agentic tasks, and versatile developer use cases. It comprises two models: a significant one with 117B parameters (gpt-oss-120b), and a smaller one with 21B parameters (gpt-oss-20b). Both are mixture-of-experts (MoEs) and use a 4-bit quantization scheme (MXFP4), enabling fast inference (thanks to fewer active parameters, see details below) while keeping resource usage low. The large model fits on a single H100 GPU, while the small one runs within 16GB of memory and is perfect for consumer hardware and on-device applications.

To make it even better and more impactful for the community, the models are licensed under the Apache 2.0 license, along with a minimal usage policy:.

It has been revealed that we aim for our tools to be used safely, responsibly, and democratically, while maximizing your control over how you use them. By using gpt-oss, you agree to comply with all applicable law.

Industry observers note that according to OpenAI, this release is a meaningful step in their commitment to the open-source ecosystem, in line with their stated mission to make the benefits of AI broadly accessible. Many use cases rely on private and/or local deployments, and we at Hugging Face are super excited to welcome OpenAI to the community. We believe these will be long-lived, inspiring and impactful models.

Recent findings suggest that openAI GPT OSS models are accessible through Hugging Face’s Inference Providers service, allowing you to send requests to any supported provider using the same JavaScript or Python code. This is the same infrastructure that powers OpenAI’s official demo on gpt-oss.com, and you can use it for your own projects.

Below is an example that uses Python and the super-fast Cerebras provider. For more info and additional snippets, check the inference providers section in the model cards and the dedicated guide we crafted for these models.

Inference Providers also implements an OpenAI-compatible Responses API, the most advanced OpenAI interface for chat models, designed for more flexible and intuitive interactions.Below is an example using the Responses API with the Fireworks AI provider. For more details, check out the open-source responses.js project.

You need to install the latest transformers release (v4.55.1 or later), as well as accelerate and kernels. We also recommend installing triton 3.4 or better, as it unblocks support for mxfp4 quantization on CUDA hardware:.

It has been revealed that the model weights are quantized in mxfp4 format, which was originally available on GPUs of the Hopper or Blackwell families, but now works on previous CUDA architectures (including Ada, Ampere, and Tesla). Installing triton 3.4, together with the kernels library, makes it possible to download optimized mxfp4 kernels on first use, achieving large memory savings. With these components in place, you can run the 20B model on GPUs with 16 GB of RAM. This includes many consumer cards (3090, 4090, 5080) as well as Colab and Kaggle!

If the previous libraries are not installed (or you don’t have a compatible GPU), loading the model will fall back to bfloat16, unpacked from the quantized weights.

The following snippet reveals simple inference with the 20B model. As explained, it runs on 16 GB GPUs when using mxfp4, or ~48 GB in bfloat16.

In a recent development, the models use attention sinks, a technique the vLLM team made compatible with Flash Attention 3. We have packaged and integrated their optimized kernel in kernels-community/vllm-flash-attn3. At the time of writing, this super-fast kernel has been tested on Hopper cards with PyTorch 2.7 and 2.8. We expect increased coverage in the coming days. If you run the models on Hopper cards (for example, H100 or H200), you need to pip install --upgrade kernels and add the following line to your snippet:.

In a recent development, GPT OSS models are reasoning models: they therefore require a very large generation size (maximum number of upcoming tokens) for evaluations, as their generation will first contain reasoning, then the actual answer. Using too small a generation size risks interrupting the prediction in the middle of reasoning, which will cause false negatives. The reasoning trace should then be removed from the model answer before computing metrics, to avoid parsing errors, especially with math or instruct evaluations.

Here’s an example on how to evaluate the models with lighteval (you need to install from source).

For the 20B model, this should give you 69.5 (+/-1.9) for IFEval (strict prompt), and 63.3 (+/-8.9) for AIME25 (in pass@1), scores within expected range for a reasoning model of this size.

If you want to do your custom evaluation script, note that to filter out the reasoning tags properly, you will need to use skip_special_tokens=False in the tokenizer, in order to get the full trace in the model output (to filter reasoning using the same string pairs as in the example above) - you can discover why below.

Sources indicate that openAI GPT OSS uses the concept of “channels” in its outputs. Most of the time, you will see an “analysis” channel that contains things that are not intended to be sent to the end-user, like chains of thought, and a “final” channel containing messages that are actually intended to be displayed to the user.

Assuming no tools are being used, the structure of the model output looks like this:.

Industry observers note that most of the time, you should ignore everything except the text after <|channel|>final<|message|>. Only this text should be appended to the chat as the assistant message, or displayed to the user. There are two exceptions to this rule, though: You may need to include analysis messages in the history during training or if the model is calling external tools.

It has been revealed that when training: If you’re formatting examples for training, you generally want to include the chain of thought in the final message. The right place to do this is in the thinking key.

According to recent reports, you can feel free to include thinking keys in previous turns, or when you’re doing inference rather than training, but they will generally be ignored. The chat template will only ever include the most recent chain of thought, and only in training (when add_generation_prompt=False and the final turn is an assistant turn).

The reason why we do it this way is subtle: The OpenAI gpt-oss models were trained on multi-turn data where all but the final chain of thought was dropped. This means that when you want to fine-tune an OpenAI gpt-oss model, you should do the same.

In a recent development, openAI GPT OSS is unusual because it distinguishes between a “system” message and a “developer” message at the start of the chat, but most other models only use “system”. In GPT OSS, the system message follows a strict format and contains information like the current date, the model identity and the level of reasoning effort to use, and the “developer” message is more freeform, which makes it (very confusingly) similar to the “system” messages of most other models.

To make GPT OSS easier to use with the standard API, the chat template will treat a message with “system” or “developer” role as the developer message. If you want to modify the actual system message, you can pass the specific arguments model_identity or reasoning_effort to the chat template:.

It has been revealed that GPT OSS supports two kinds of tools: The “builtin” tools browser and python, and custom tools supplied by the user. To enable builtin tools, pass their names in a list to the builtin_tools argument of the chat template, as shown below. To pass custom tools, you can pass them either as JSON schema or as Python functions with type hints and docstrings using the tools argument. See the chat template tools documentation for more details, or you can just modify the example below:.

If the model chooses to call a tool (indicated by a message ending in <|call|>), then you should add the tool call to the chat, call the tool, then add the tool result to the chat and generate again:.

This is a genuinely impressive and consequential release. Open-weight models at this scale, with Apache 2.0 licensing and serious attention to inference efficiency, feel like a real inflection point rather than a symbolic gesture. The combination of MoE architecture, MXFP4 quantization, and practical ecosystem support (Transformers, vLLM, llama.cpp, and ROCm) makes this usable today, not just theoretically interesting.

What stands out most is the emphasis on deployment reality: single-H100 feasibility for 120B, 16GB consumer GPUs for 20B, and first-class support for multiple inference backends. That’s exactly what developers and researchers need if these models are going to be experimented with, fine-tuned, and embedded into real products rather than living only in benchmarks.

It’s also refreshing to see clear guidance around reasoning traces, chat templates, and evaluation pitfalls. Too many “reasoning models” gloss over those operational details, which matter a lot once you leave the demo stage.

As someone working across text, vision, and creative tooling, I also appreciate how releases like this pair well with the broader AI stack. Strong open reasoning models combined with next-gen creative tools—like Experience the future of AI image editing—open up some very compelling hybrid workflows for agents, content pipelines, and local-first applications.

Overall, this feels like a long-lived contribution to the open ecosystem, not a short-term headline. Kudos to OpenAI and Hugging Face for shipping something that’s both ambitious and genuinely usable.

Signal is Serious About Protecting Your Privacy

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1436 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Signal

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Privacy is our mission; it’s why we exist, and we do everything we can to protect it.
  • This means that we are restricting the latest AI agents built into mobile operating systems from potentially capturing and storing your Signal data.
  • Industry observers note that we’ve already had to do this once with Windows.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Meredith Whittaker on 20 Nov 2026.

Privacy is our mission; it’s why we exist, and we do everything we can to protect it.

This means that we are restricting the latest AI agents built into mobile operating systems from potentially capturing and storing your Signal data.

Industry observers note that we’ve already had to do this once with Windows. Last year, we used screenshot blocking to prevent Microsoft’s Recall AI from taking and storing screenshots of your Signal messages on Windows 11 operating systems by default.1 We will now be taking similar measures to restrict agentic systems built into iOS 27 and on Android versions where we can detect an AI assistant attempting to read your Signal screen.2.

The problem is similar to Microsoft Recall on Windows: Google and Apple are integrating agentic capabilities like Gemini Intelligence with Google Gemini and Onscreen Awareness with Siri AI deep into their operating systems. This is a significant move. Google (Android), Apple (iOS/macOS), and Microsoft (Windows) produce the three major consumer operating systems (OS), which comprise the environment that third-party developers – like Signal – build their apps to function and operate within. To put it differently, these three operating systems are the oceans in which Signal, and other applications, must swim; they dictate the conditions of life for the application ecosystem. Right now, these agentic AI integrations are changing this environment in a way that’s making it increasingly hostile to privacy. This is an existential threat to Signal, and our ability to responsibly uphold our mission.

In order to gain access to information about you, these OS AI agents “scan” the information that’s on your screen. In doing so, your Signal data is captured, then made available to these agentic systems in order to allow them to answer your questions and do your bidding.

The net result is that these AI capabilities in the operating system are undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy. For over a decade, this guarantee has been backed by our tried and trusted open source code base and our formally verified encryption protocol. These have been scrutinized by some of the best security experts and hackers across the world, and shown to be robust. Now, in service of AI agentic capabilities, your sensitive data is being captured, stored, and made accessible to whatever local database or remote server an OS-level AI agent is using at that moment. All of this is outside of Signal’s control once the data has been captured, and imperils the privacy of all the participants in a conversation.

So, we are blocking such capture by preventing screenshots in the app on iOS 27 and when AI assistants attempt to capture screen data on Android.2.

Recent findings suggest that people who want the ability to take screenshots can disable this protection within the Signal app’s settings. However, doing so will potentially expose your (and your contacts’) Signal content to these AI agents, and break our privacy guarantees. Our remedy is also incomplete – while we are doing everything we can, restricting screenshots does not address other more sneaky ways AI agents could potentially access application data, such as retrieving content already present on a user’s device via the filesystem.

We want to be very clear: it is a serious problem that Signal – and application developers beyond – lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from undermining application-level privacy. Even where we are able to detect and block AI data access, Google, Apple, Microsoft, and others do not provide ways for developers to easily restrict such AI data access without making drastic compromises to the core user experience. This is also the reason we are currently unable to implement these protections on macOS.3.

According to recent reports, we are also struggling with a significant lack of documentation about how these AI agents actually work. Over the past few months, we’ve spent considerable developer time and energy doing forensic investigations across Android and iOS in an attempt to learn what is actually happening when these AI systems access application data. Without better documentation and clear technical specifications, it will be increasingly difficult for Signal to provide robust privacy and security to the many millions of people who rely on us.

Recent findings suggest that we continue to call on the major consumer operating system companies – Apple, Google, and Microsoft – to provide simple technical tools and accurate documentation that give developers like Signal ways to prevent AI agents from accessing sensitive application data. In particular, we are calling on these companies to provide two common-sense remedies that can protect the privacy so many millions of people rely on:.

According to recent reports, we also see a growing need for tools that can prevent third-party agents, like Meta’s Muse, from accessing application data using the deep permissions that consumers are encouraged to grant them during setup. In many cases these agents are leveraging accessibility settings that were meant to empower actual people to get the most out of their apps and services, not to act as a skeleton key that provides access to AI agents.

According to recent reports, in addition to taking these technical measures to block capture, we are engaging in conversations across the ecosystem to make the stakes clear. There is a lot of work to be done in the industry to improve the ways that AI agents operate in the operating system, and how and whether they capture and process private data. We are cautiously optimistic that some major OS providers, like Google and Apple, are engaging with us on how these systems should better interface with privacy-sensitive apps like Signal. We hope to have more to share on this topic soon, and that these companies recognize the danger to the ecosystem and work with us and others to create standardized approaches that meaningfully protect privacy across the industry.

Finally, we want to acknowledge that we are not the only ones recognizing these perils, and we are grateful to our allies for pushing for similar changes. We all need to recognize that the current integration of AI agents into the operating system, without these common-sense remedies, represents an existential threat to privacy at the application layer, and the ability of independent developers like Signal to protect your sensitive data. Signal is the canary in the coal mine, but this affects the entire ecosystem and should galvanize anyone who cares about these fundamental rights.

Signal Technology Foundation is the nonprofit home of the Signal app, which is trusted by millions around the world. We protect free expression and enable secure global communication through open source privacy technology. Signal Technology Foundation is a US 501(c)(3) tax-exempt organization.

In a recent development, microsoft Recall captures your screen every few seconds, extracts text from screenshots via optical character recognition, then populates a searchable on-device database with this personal data in order to allow the AI system to query it – potentially exposing and retaining your Signal data indefinitely, including disappearing messages. ↩.

There are multiple versions of Android beyond the Google-provided distributions on Pixel devices. For many vendors, we don’t have a reliable way to detect when a screenshot was attempted if screenshots are already disabled. Rather than choose a poor user experience (where screenshots simply stop working, confusing consumers), we decided to instead focus on detecting when an AI assistant attempts to access the screen. We automatically enable the “Screen security” setting in Signal Android when this type of access is detected. ↩ ↩2.

It has been revealed that careful readers will note that in addition to not being able to cover all Android devices, we are also not blocking Siri AI on macOS. This is because we cannot reliably block screenshots on macOS. Faced with a lack of clearly documented APIs that allow us to implement screenshot protection, we do not have the tools available that let us do the job. While protections against continuous screen capture exist on macOS, we cannot apply them to screenshots (which is how most agentic systems access data from applications like Signal). Trying to implement screenshot blocking on macOS has revealed to us a minefield of bewildering decisions that place user privacy at risk, including APIs that have been deprecated in favor of screen-protection solutions that only work for streaming media and other DRM-protected content. This is something we hope Apple remedies urgently. For now, the only recommendation we have for macOS 27 users is to add Signal to the Excluded Apps section in System Settings > Siri to protect message content from proactive access by Siri AI. ↩.

Breaking: OpenAI Debuts Shirudo to Protect Running Linux Systems

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (936 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, openAI and Cisco rolled out the open-source Shirudo project on November 23, 2026, giving operators a runtime for applying temporary protections to Linux systems while permanent fixes are developed and rolled out.
  • The project targets the gap between finding a vulnerability and completing a patch rollout.
  • At the operating-system level, eBPF gives Shirudo a Linux mechanism for running small programs at designated points to observe activity and apply targeted protections.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, openAI and Cisco rolled out the open-source Shirudo project on November 23, 2026, giving operators a runtime for applying temporary protections to Linux systems while permanent fixes are developed and rolled out. The pre-release project combines eBPF controls with an agent-oriented design for developing targeted safeguards called shields.

The project targets the gap between finding a vulnerability and completing a patch rollout. The companies say that process can take days or weeks, and indiscriminately blocking the relevant Linux operation may take a service offline when malicious and legitimate requests depend on it. Shirudo lets teams evaluate a candidate shield against both exploit behavior and normal workloads before enforcement. Deployment still requires operator approval, and the service can remain online while the safeguard takes effect.

At the operating-system level, eBPF gives Shirudo a Linux mechanism for running small programs at designated points to observe activity and apply targeted protections. Its shields can block vulnerable code paths without restarting the system. The companies are also designing programmable controls that let agents investigate vulnerabilities, develop shields and validate them against exploits and real workloads, while security teams retain control over what is deployed.

Cisco’s technical account describes Shirudo as an agent-oriented rewrite of Tetragon, the eBPF security platform Isovalent open-sourced in 2022. The design lets agents generate code directly rather than work only through human-oriented consoles, configuration files or policy languages. Depending on the vulnerability, a mitigation can block the path an exploit needs, replace vulnerable code or add detection visibility. Application or user-space bytecode modification extends that approach to vulnerabilities for which eBPF is not suited.

Industry observers note that for deployment, the operator system builds eBPF or application-bytecode shields as signed .bee packages delivered through an OCI registry. Targets pull and validate the packages, and the architecture uses a one-shot command-line interface rather than a permanently running daemon on target or operator machines. Shields are verified before loading, Linux’s eBPF verifier applies its safety rules, and a Trusted Platform Module (TPM) supports a verifiable record of protections being loaded or removed.

In a recent development, in Cisco’s controlled-test account, OpenAI’s Codex produced a shield for Java’s Base64 decoder and attached the latest input-validation code to a live Elasticsearch process. The test used Elasticsearch 9.5.5; the shield rejected malicious input and blocked a Java4Shell exploit attempt while the service continued running without a restart. The bytecode is intended for Java applications on OpenJDK during the interval before OpenJDK itself receives a permanent patch.

The demonstrated agent workflow starts with vulnerability discovery or an external disclosure, then reproduces the exploit, selects a mitigation point and iterates until a mitigation works. The shield is signed and rolled out with application-health monitoring, while deployed shields record exploitation attempts for investigation. The result is one vendor-run controlled example, not a demonstration that every vulnerability can be mitigated automatically.

The public repository labels Shirudo pre-release. Production targets require a Linux kernel with the signed-loader application binary interface and Shirudo’s kernel patches, plus TPM 2.0. Continuous integration runs all test tiers on x86-64 and host tests on arm64; the test VM also boots locally on arm64, while target validation for riscv64 remains pending. The project uses BSD 2-Clause licensing, with BPF programs dual-licensed under BSD and GPL.

Industry observers note that the project documentation describes a pull-based delivery model: targets retrieve signed micropatches, called upatches, from OCI registries and push telemetry to configured OpenTelemetry collectors, leaving no target component listening for connections. The security boundary is equally explicit: an attacker who gains kernel code execution or arbitrary kernel writes could potentially bypass Shirudo’s in-kernel checks. Upatches can remove attack surface and block a known vulnerable path until a fixed kernel is deployed, but they do not replace kernel hardening or permanent fixes.

OpenAI and Cisco aim eventually to make tested shields available alongside vulnerability disclosures, giving operators temporary protections to evaluate while permanent patches are prepared. The broader goal is infrastructure that identifies affected systems, validates protections, contains compromises, limits attackers’ movement between systems and restores services to a verified known-good state. Kernel and core-service hardening, workload permission limits, hardware-backed attestation and independent network controls support that objective.

In a recent development, those ambitions extend well beyond the current pre-release code. The Java4Shell demonstration shows a specific agent-generated protection working under controlled conditions; whether the same validation, signing and verification model can handle diverse vulnerabilities across production fleets is the practical question raised by the launch.

According to recent reports, vision Language Models (VLMs) are getting stronger, but aligning them to human preferences still matters. In TRL, we already highlighted how to post-train VLMs with Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). This time, we’re going further.

tl;dr Here’s what’s new in TRL:.

These go beyond pairwise DPO, extracting richer signals from preference data and scaling better with modern VLMs.

We’ve also extended existing methods to support VLMs:.

This enables more efficient and scalable multimodal alignment.

Traditionally, you would take a base model, apply SFT to follow instructions, and then apply DPO to align it to preferential data. Previously, we adapted this approach to Vision Language Models (VLMs) and validated it on IDEFICS2, showing improvement in model responses.

DPO works by optimizing preferences between pairs of model responses using a contrastive loss: you have a chosen and a rejected answer and you optimize your preferences based on what you want and don’t want.

But in the last year, new multimodal alignment methods have gained popularity, GRPO and MPO, that can push VLM performance even further. At the end of the blog post you can find a table that showcases the differences between model responses.

Sources indicate that aligning multimodal models with SFT to do reasoning tasks falls short due to distribution shift. Meanwhile, models aligned with DPO fail to generate coherent rationales and might generate repetitive responses. To address this, there’s a new technique called Mixed Preference Optimization (MPO) specifically made for multimodal models. This method is essentially an extension of DPO with multiple losses: preference loss from DPO (sigmoid), quality loss from Binary Classifier Optimization (BCO), and generation loss from SFT. According to the paper, simply switching to this combined loss results in 6.2 pts improvement in MathVista!

Since this is only modifying the loss, we added combined loss support to TRL's DPOTrainer class. To use it, you can initialize the DPOConfig as follows:.

Sources indicate that group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) is a cutting-edge alignment method initially introduced in DeepSeek Math paper and later integrated to DeepSeek R1, the groundbreaking LLM. It’s an addition to PPO where the policy updates are done over groups (batches of trajectories that represent how a dialogue rolls out). This feature makes it more robust to reward noise, as the noise averages out within groups. Since the model learns broader sense of a good response rather than singular high reward samples, this method also makes the model highly performant.

In TRL, we now introduce GRPO support for vision language models. We will not provide a full training script example, as you can find it in the notebook. Instead, we'll focus on highlighting the key component and concepts.

In order to really see improvements in the latter reward, you would need a rather maximalist setup, where you have relatively larger models, a lot of generations, and a high-quality, diverse dataset.

Group Sequence Policy Optimization (GSPO) is a RL alignment algorithm recently released by Qwen that overcomes some limitations of GRPO. It achieves a more stable training computing importance sampling weights at the sequence level instead of per-token. Its benefits are more relevant in MoE style models.

How LinkedIn Built a View-Agnostic Analytics System for Modern iOS UI Architectures

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (588 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Infoq

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News How LinkedIn Built a View-Agnostic Analytics System for Modern iOS UI Architectures.
  • Nov 23, 2026 2 min read.
  • To address the challenge posed by modern iOS UI systems where the logical UI structure may not mirror the native UIKit hierarchy, LinkedIn engineers developed a view-agnostic analytics system build around a shared MeasurableNode contract.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News How LinkedIn Built a View-Agnostic Analytics System for Modern iOS UI Architectures.

Nov 23, 2026 2 min read.

To address the challenge posed by modern iOS UI systems where the logical UI structure may not mirror the native UIKit hierarchy, LinkedIn engineers developed a view-agnostic analytics system build around a shared MeasurableNode contract.

As LinkedIn senior software engineer Keerthana Reddy Ragi explains, while traditional iOS analytics relies on UIView instances as the unit of measurement, modern UI architectures increasingly use flattened layouts and custom rendering systems where UI elements such as cards, sections, and containers are represented by virtual nodes that never materialize as UIViews. Consequently, analytics systems built solely around UIKit may fail to capture impressions for virtual nodes, lose logical hierarchy and contextual information, miscalculate visibility and impression duration, and attribute user actions to the wrong elements.

Recent findings suggest that linkedIn's solution introduces a shared MeasurableNode contract relaxing the requirement for every measurable element to be a UIView. A MeasurableNode exposes four properties: identity, geometry, hierarchy, and lifecycle.

As MeasurableNode is a shared contract, both traditional UIViews and virtual nodes can participate in the same analytics system. Indeed, while existing UIKit views continue using native UIKit properties and lifecycle hooks, virtual nodes explicitly provide the corresponding information to the same analytics layer.

Recent findings suggest that the attach and detach methods are central to this approach, because they enable the layout or rendering system to notify the analytics system "when a node attaches, when its frame changes, and when it detaches". Unlike virtual nodes, UIKit already sends automatic lifecycle notifications to UIViews. Similarly, as virtual nodes are not directly recognized by UIKit as gesture-recognizer targets, the rendering framework must traverse the hybrid UIKit/virtual-node parent hierarchy to attribute user actions to the appropriate logical virtual node.

Ragi emphasizes that this design enables gradual adoption without requiring existing view-based analytics to be rewritten.

Industry observers note that teams can modernize one part of the UI without rewriting everything around it. Existing view-based analytics can keep working while newer virtual nodes use the new contract.

LinkedIn engineers encountered three main challenges developing this approach to analytics. First, the widespread assumption that everything is a UIView is embedded in existing codebases. For example, "helper code that walked superviews, visibility checks that read frames directly from views, cleanup logic tied to view removal". All these cases had to be found and updated. Second, they had to strike the right balance between short-term compatibility and long-term correctness. Third, they needed to enforce the attach/detach discipline at the framework level.

Commenting on Ragi's article on LinkedIn, senior AI prompt engineer Artien Nadal observed:.

Sources indicate that I think there's a bigger opportunity here than just making analytics independent of the UI. What if teams could automatically detect when a UI change breaks event tracking or changes what an event actually means?

As a final note, although LinkedIn's implementation focused on UIKit, the underlying approach is far from being limited to it. With many apps now mixing UIKit and SwiftUI, cross-platform layout engines, or hybrid solutions, a view-agnostic analytics model based on a shared contract has broader applicability.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • CNBC reported on November 23, 2026, that Democratic and Republican lawmakers criticized Nvidia’s decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as president and CEO, renewing demands for oversight of AI chip exports and the Trump administration’s role.
  • Nvidia revealed that Huang’s reinstatement was effective immediately after a unanimous board vote, and that he had also returned as a director.
  • The board remarked a series of discussions and meetings left it satisfied with Huang’s candor and ability to lead.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

CNBC reported on November 23, 2026, that Democratic and Republican lawmakers criticized Nvidia’s decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as president and CEO, renewing demands for oversight of AI chip exports and the Trump administration’s role. The backlash followed Huang’s return 11 days after his resignation.

Nvidia revealed that Huang’s reinstatement was effective immediately after a unanimous board vote, and that he had also returned as a director. Harvey Jones remains board chair, and Colette Kress continues as chief financial officer after serving as interim CEO.

The board remarked a series of discussions and meetings left it satisfied with Huang’s candor and ability to lead. It also received input from senior levels of the U.S. government and, based on that input, is confident that his reinstatement poses no national-security risk.

Representative Don Bacon, the Nebraska Republican who chairs the House Subcommittee on Cyber, Information Technologies, and Innovation, told CNBC he wants thorough oversight in the next Congress and an examination of whether Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick bears responsibility. Bacon called the decision inexplicable and a “failure of character.” The Commerce Department is responsible for setting U.S. export controls on AI chips.

Senator Ron Wyden of Oregon, the Senate Finance Committee’s top Democrat, mentioned in an emailed statement to CNBC that Huang’s return indicated national security was for sale under Trump, Vance and Rubio, and that Democrats would pursue accountability for administration officials who put corrupt deals ahead of the country’s security.

Industry observers note that republican Senator Rick Scott of Florida requested a congressional briefing as soon as possible. He told CNBC that Nvidia’s board was free to vote as it chose, but the federal government “owes the American people answers about what actually happened,” including the full impact of Huang’s actions on national security and the economy.

Recent findings suggest that representative Gabe Amo, a Rhode Island Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, told CNBC the reinstatement could broaden the inquiry to Lutnick and Cantor Fitzgerald, the financial firm run by Lutnick’s sons. Cantor Fitzgerald declined to comment directly on Amo’s remarks. The firm remarked it held no material proprietary position in Nvidia and that its Nvidia positions arose primarily from equity swaps executed for clients.

David Rudenstine, a constitutional law professor and national security scholar at Cardozo School of Law, told CNBC that primary responsibility for national security rests with the administration rather than the CEO of a private organization.

Recent findings suggest that the board’s vote did not end Nvidia’s internal review. Nvidia noted the independent-director committee’s investigation will proceed to conclusion, with independent counsel assisting. The committee is examining reporting that Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort; Huang supports the investigation and is committed to cooperating with it.

Sources indicate that the board also formed a National Security and Export Control Committee composed solely of independent directors to oversee trade compliance and national-security risks. Nvidia is commencing a search for a chief compliance officer to oversee compliance across the company and report to the Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee. Nvidia mentioned it would continue cooperating with ongoing government investigations and inquiries.
