#103920. MicroSD Cards for Raspberry Pi Homelab: What Actually Matters for Reliability

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1377 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

MicroSD Cards for Raspberry Pi Homelab: What Actually Matters for Reliability

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1377 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that microSD cards are the default storage for most Raspberry Pi setups, and they are also one of the most common failure points in a homelab.
  • This post covers what to look for when choosing a card, how to reduce wear once it is running, and what to do when things go sideways.
  • A Raspberry Pi running a home server, a DNS resolver, or an automation hub writes to storage constantly.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that microSD cards are the default storage for most Raspberry Pi setups, and they are also one of the most common failure points in a homelab. The card that ships with a kit or sits in a junk drawer is not necessarily the right card for running a 24/7 service. Picking the wrong one costs you uptime and, potentially, data.

This post covers what to look for when choosing a card, how to reduce wear once it is running, and what to do when things go sideways.

A Raspberry Pi running a home server, a DNS resolver, or an automation hub writes to storage constantly. Log files, databases, container state, and swap all generate write activity. MicroSD flash memory has a finite number of program/erase cycles per cell, and cheap cards hit that limit faster than you might expect.

According to recent reports, the failure mode is usually not a dramatic crash. Cards tend to go read-only first, then start throwing filesystem errors, then stop mounting entirely. By the time you notice, you may have lost days of config changes.

In a recent development, speed class matters, but it is not the whole story. For homelab use, prioritize these attributes in roughly this order.

Sources indicate that endurance rating. Look for cards explicitly marketed as "high endurance" or "endurance" variants. These are designed for dashcams and security cameras, which means continuous writes, which is exactly the workload a Pi homelab produces. Samsung PRO Endurance, SanDisk High Endurance, and Kingston High Endurance are commonly cited options in this category. These cards are usually rated in hours of continuous video recording rather than TBW (terabytes written), so compare the hours figure on the datasheet for the capacity you are buying.

It has been revealed that capacity sweet spot. For most Pi services, 32 GB to 128 GB is the practical range. Smaller cards fill up faster and leave no room for logs. Within the same product line, larger cards usually carry a higher endurance rating: Samsung rates the PRO Endurance at 17,520 hours for 32 GB and 140,160 hours for 256 GB. Pick a size that fits your OS plus your data with at least 20 percent headroom.

Fake capacity is still a thing. Counterfeit cards that report a false capacity are common on discount marketplaces. Always verify a newly introduced card before trusting it with real data.

Step 1: Install f3 on your Pi or Linux machine.

Sources indicate that step 2: Mount the card, then write test files to it (replace /mnt/sdcard with the card's mount point). f3write fills the free space on the mounted filesystem.

Step 3: Read it back and verify.

If f3read reports Data LOST: 0.00 Byte and the Data OK figure matches the free space that was written, the card holds what it claims. If it reports lost or corrupted data, return it.

According to recent reports, A quick sequential read/write test tells you whether the card is going to feel sluggish under load. Use dd for a rough check, or fio for a more realistic workload simulation. The number that matters most for a Pi running services is random 4K write IOPS, because small random writes are what databases and container runtimes generate. The SD Association's Application Performance Class (A1 or A2 on the label) is the rating that guarantees minimum random IOPS, and Raspberry Pi's own microSD cards are rated A2.

Step 1: Test sequential write speed with dd.

Step 2: Drop the page cache with sync; echo 3 | sudo tee /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches, then test sequential read speed. Otherwise Linux serves the file you just wrote from RAM and the result is far higher than the card can really do.

For random I/O testing with fio, refer to the fio documentation for job file syntax, as the flags vary depending on the test profile you want. A UHS-I Speed Class 3 (U3) or Video Speed Class 30 (V30) card should sustain at least 30 MB/s sequential writes. Endurance cards sometimes trade peak sequential speed for better sustained performance over time, so do not disqualify a card solely because it is slower on burst benchmarks.

Even a good card lives longer if you reduce unnecessary writes. These changes are practical on Raspberry Pi OS and most Debian-based Pi distributions.

Sources indicate that move logs to RAM. The log2ram tool writes system logs to a RAM-based filesystem and syncs them to the card once a day and at shutdown rather than on every log line, so a power cut can lose the most recent logs. Install it from its GitHub repository and follow the project instructions for your OS version, since the recommended install method has changed over its release history.

Reduce swap pressure. Swap on an SD card is brutal. Either disable swap entirely if your workload fits in RAM, or move swap to a USB-attached drive. The commands below apply to Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm and earlier. Raspberry Pi OS Trixie replaced dphys-swapfile with rpi-swap, which defaults to compressed swap in RAM (zram) and only occasionally writes idle pages to storage. It is configured through /etc/rpi/swap.conf or drop-in files in /etc/rpi/swap.conf.d/, and changes need a reboot.

Recent findings suggest that use tmpfs for volatile directories. On Raspberry Pi OS Trixie, /tmp is already a tmpfs by default, following Debian 13, so check with findmnt /tmp first. On older releases, add entries to /etc/fstab to mount /tmp and optionally /var/tmp in RAM.

Add noatime to your root mount. Access time updates turn file reads into small writes, although the kernel's default relatime behaviour already limits them. Raspberry Pi OS images already mount the root partition with defaults,noatime, so check /etc/fstab before editing. On other distributions, add noatime to the options for your root partition. Be careful editing fstab: a syntax error can prevent boot. Keep a backup or a second card you can boot from to recover.

If your Pi model supports USB boot (the Raspberry Pi 3B+ and Zero 2 W do out of the box, and the Raspberry Pi 4 and 5 do once USB is in the bootloader's BOOT_ORDER, although early Raspberry Pi 4 boards may need a bootloader patch first), consider moving your root filesystem to a USB SSD or flash drive. You can still use a microSD for the boot partition while running the OS and all writes from USB storage. An SSD tolerates random writes far better than any microSD card.

Industry observers note that the Raspberry Pi documentation covers the USB boot setup process in detail, including the raspi-config option and the bootloader EEPROM patch steps. Check the official docs at raspberrypi.com/documentation for your specific model.

You cannot prevent all card failures, so detect them early and make recovery fast.

Watch filesystem errors. Check dmesg periodically for I/O errors or EXT4 warnings. These often appear before the card fails completely.

Keep a current image backup. Tools like rpi-clone can clone a running Pi to a second card in a USB reader with minimal disruption. The original billw2/rpi-clone repository has not been updated since March 2024, so look at a maintained fork such as geerlingguy/rpi-clone. A weekly clone to a spare card means your recovery time after a failure is the time it takes to swap cards, not the time it takes to rebuild from scratch.

In a recent development, store config in version control. Any config that lives in /etc or your home directory should be committed to a git repo and pushed offsite. This is a safety net that survives even a total card loss.

It has been revealed that microSD cards are not all the same, and the homelab workload is harder on them than most consumer use cases. Start with a genuine high-endurance card, verify its capacity before you trust it, reduce write amplification through tmpfs and log2ram, and keep a current backup so recovery is fast when a card eventually dies.

Sources indicate that if your Pi model supports USB boot, moving the root filesystem to an SSD is the single biggest reliability upgrade you can make. The microSD slot becomes a low-stress boot loader and the rest of your stack runs on storage that was built for it.

Add This Packet Of Seasoning To Pot Roast For A Delicious Southern-Style Sandwich

  • In a recent development, pot roast is one of those simple homemade meals that may take a long time to cook but is pretty hands-off in the Crock Pot.
  • Sources indicate that ranch seasoning is basically an off-the-shelf, ready-to-go spice packet containing multiple seasonings — usually salt, onion powder, garlic powder, and other dried herbs and spices, like parsley and black pepper.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

In a recent development, pot roast is one of those simple homemade meals that may take a long time to cook but is pretty hands-off in the Crock Pot. Just brown the meat, add your ingredients, and let the cooker do its job. There are plenty of ways to upgrade a basic pot roast and some interesting regional pot roast dishes, and this simple trick is a bit of both. To give your pot roast a hint of Southern twang, add a packet of dry ranch seasoning. Similar to a set-it-and-forget-it easy French dip sandwich but Southern, a bit of ranch in your pot roast will give you some delightfully intense flavor and get you darn near a classic Mississippi pot roast.

Sources indicate that ranch seasoning is basically an off-the-shelf, ready-to-go spice packet containing multiple seasonings — usually salt, onion powder, garlic powder, and other dried herbs and spices, like parsley and black pepper. Most brands also contain buttermilk and whey, which will add a bit of a creaminess factor, but you don't have to worry about the roast tasting like a bottle of ranch dressing because the mix will cook down with added beef stock and natural juices to form a nice, thick gravy. It will come out rich, bold, and savory with just a hint of tanginess from the buttermilk. Once your roast is nice and tender, you can simply slice it (or shred it) up and serve it Italian-beef or French-dip style, preferably with some melted cheese on top. The first bite through the bread into the perfectly tender and umami-rich, seasoned beef will make you a believer.

In a recent development, if you want to go for a more or less standard pot roast route, you can simply rub your roast with a packet of Hidden Valley Ranch Seasoning, available online and in stores, or something similar, and cook it how you normally would with beef stock, potatoes, onions, carrots, and whatever other veg you like to use. To go full-on Mississippi roast, you can forgo the veggies and slow cook it with the ranch coating, beef stock or au jus gravy mix, and a half dozen or more whole pepperoncini. Up the spice level with extra hot peppers or use the whole jar. You can even add a bit of the brine for some supplementary heat, plus a zingy kick of vinegar. This will get you closer to an actual Mississippi pot roast, which typically features stated peppers.

Sources indicate that for the bread, something that will hold up to the moisture of the roast is ideal. Toasted French bread adds a crunchy texture, but a toasted hoagie roll works great, and a thick sourdough will add a little extra tang. You'll want a cheese that melts easily, so you can quickly broil it without overcooking the bread. A simple mozzarella is an easy, mild choice, but a nice Gruyère will bring a richer and nuttier flavor with some subtle sweetness.

Ranch-seasoned pot roast or the full Mississippi mix is also great on egg noodles, mashed potatoes, or rice, or you can make a simple open-faced sando with a thick Texas toast. For an even saltier, more savory roast, you can try a three-packet blend with ranch, brown gravy, and Italian-style salad dressing mixes. However, to get that good Southern flavor, don't veer too far off the ranch.

#103912. Tech Report: The 9 Best Chain Restaurant BLTs, According To Customer Reviews

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2056 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foodrepublic ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: The 9 Best Chain Restaurant BLTs, According To Customer Reviews

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2056 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foodrepublic

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A good BLT is elegantly simple, a masterclass in culinary economy.
  • According to recent reports, these details make it hard for chain restaurants to nail a great BLT.
  • Recent findings suggest that cook Out has built a restaurant empire on selling comfort foods that you'd find at a backyard barbecue.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A good BLT is elegantly simple, a masterclass in culinary economy. With this sandwich, nothing is superfluous, nothing is forced. Instead, each ingredient works in unison to create an unmatched harmony of taste, temperature, and texture. Whether you're craving a light nosh or a substantial sit-down lunch, somehow a BLT always fits the bill. And because of its pared-down composition, every element has a chance to shine on its own. However, this also means there's no place to hide mistakes. If the tomato is a bit mealy, the bacon slightly chewy, or the bread a tad soft, it can throw off the entire sandwich.

According to recent reports, these details make it hard for chain restaurants to nail a great BLT. They serve thousands of meals every day, and each individual order exposes them to a world of criticism and critique. To save yourself from a sub-par sandwich, you need to know which chains are executing a quality BLT. And this list hopes to do just that, featuring a handful of fast food chains and restaurants that are dishing up both familiar renditions and inventive interpretations of this classic sandwich. To find the best, I searched social media, roundups, and other online forums to uncover which chain restaurants are doing the BLT justice.

Recent findings suggest that cook Out has built a restaurant empire on selling comfort foods that you'd find at a backyard barbecue. From hush puppies to corn dogs to some of the best fast food milkshakes in the country. But it also offers a fun take on the classic BLT. While most people judge the sandwich's quality by the crispness of its lettuce, the juiciness of its tomato, or the number of grains in its whole wheat bread, Cook Out takes a different approach: speed, price, and efficiency.

These sandwiches are essentially BLT sliders: compact handhelds you can devour quickly and without a tummy ache. Despite their size, photos show you get a decent amount of each ingredient packed onto the tiny hamburger bun. And at a time when value is a particularly tasty quality, the fact that these mini sandwiches cost between $2 and $3.49 (depending on your location) makes them even more delicious. "They are ridiculously cheap," said one customer on Facebook. "Less than two bucks..." On Reddit, the feelings are mutual, with another commenter posting, "The BLTs are the unsung hero of Cook Out." Apparently, not all heroes wear capes; some wear bacon.

In a recent development, sonic is another chain known for its nostalgic, carhop-inspired food. It has all the munchies you crave late at night: tater tots, root beer floats, breakfast burritos — really, the menu covers the gamut. But the restaurant is best known for its selection of classics, including the BLT. While some BLTs are light and dainty, Sonic's BLT Toaster is on the heftier side, perfect if you're craving something not greasy but still substantial enough to keep you full throughout the day. The sandwich isn't such a departure from classic BLTs, but everything just feels, well, bigger. The hand-sliced tomatoes, fresh lettuce, and trio of meaty bacon strips all come sandwiched between two thick slabs of buttery Texas toast.

Sources indicate that customers, say that they love the BLT, with one YouTuber noting it's "crispy, crunchy, and yummy." And speaking of breakfast, Sonic's BLT Toaster is frustratingly elusive. It's not discontinued, but it doesn't always appear when ordering online. A workaround is to get the Grilled Cheese and just add bacon, lettuce, and tomato. Or you can just ask for it specifically if ordering in person.

Industry observers note that potbelly knows how to put together a quality sandwich, and as far as chain sub shops go, it should be in the conversation with Jersey Mike's, Jimmy John's, and Firehouse Subs — at least that's what people are saying on the Reddit threads. However, like most fast food empires, quality varies by location. Still, a good Potbelly sandwich is as solid as any, typically well-stuffed, with a great ratio of condiments and toppings.

According to recent reports, this same formula and attention to detail that make its Italian sub a customer favorite also show up in its BLTA (the "A" stands for avocado). Texturally, it's a terrific blend of creamy, cool, crispy, and crunchy, and unlike the more value-friendly fast food restaurants, the sandwich is assembled with a little more care. Customers note that the avocado is freshly sliced, the bread is crusty and substantial, and the pepper-crusted, applewood-smoked bacon is the best of any sandwich chain. "Potbelly makes an amazing BLT," claims one happy diner on Instagram. "...the lettuce and tomato are fresh and refreshing. The bacon is peppered, which adds a great flavor. The bread-to-ingredients ratio is amazing. Solid BLT 9/10.".

According to recent reports, jason's Deli is more than just a deli. It has more than 200 locations, mostly in the South and Midwest, which is why it probably doesn't get the national acclaim it deserves. But Jason's makes some incredible food that's unlike anything else you'll find at other fast food restaurants and casual chains: giant baked potatoes, massive slow-cooked brisket sandwiches, and a bottomless salad bar that might just be the best in the country.

In a recent development, its version of a BLT — aptly named the Bigger Better BLT — is no slouch, either, although it's sure to ruffle the feathers of BLT purists. Why? Well, the sandwich is stuffed with a few extra letters from the alphabet. Obviously, it includes the standard bacon, lettuce, and tomato — albeit in greater quantity than average —plus slices of avocado and a freshly cracked fried egg, all piled on two slices of multi-grain wheat. In general, customers are impressed by the amount of bacon and the overall sandwich composition. "This is my favorite menu item from here," mentioned a Redditor after posting a glam shot of their sandwich.

From its famous #13 Original Italian to the Substantial Kahuna Cheesesteak, Jersey Mike's knows how to put together a sandwich. The chain takes the same thoughtful approach with its #1 BLT. Our sister site, Chowhound, ranked it the tastiest chain restaurant BLT around, citing the quantity of ingredients and textural harmony as key reasons for its success.

Jersey Mike's doesn't do anything special with its BLT. No bells and whistles or novel additions; it just nails the basics, with a precise ratio of tender tomato, refreshing shredded lettuce, crispy bacon, and a good mayonnaise (and some oil and vinegar or chopped pepper relish if you get it "Mike's Way"). The bread cradles the ingredients so nothing gets too soggy or, worse, falls apart.

On a Facebook post dedicated to the BLT debate, one person commented, "Jersey Mike's is the only place I will go for 'fast food' subs!" Others agree, with another poster noting, "...this was wayyyy good [...] I only wish I got extra bacon, but there was a good amount." And while everyone appreciates a simple sandwich, many customers say their customizations improve the taste, adding everything from tangy banana peppers to spicy chipotle mayo to your standard slice of American cheese.

Five Guys is known for its juicy burgers, thick milkshakes, and an unnecessary abundance of fries, but the fast food restaurant also makes one of the best BLTs of any national chain. However, Five Guys created some confusion among its fan base by formally "launching" the BLT sandwich just a few months ago, even though many loyal customers say it's more of a relaunch, given that it's been available for more than a decade.

Sources indicate that regardless, the sandwich is now available nationwide, which is good news for anyone who loves a BLT that doesn't skimp on the B. The sandwich is served on a sesame seed burger bun, but the applewood-smoked bacon is piled so high that it's about the thickness of a double (or triple) stacked cheeseburger. "They PILE the bacon on those BLTs," commented one Redditor, "...it's unlike any BLT I've ever had because of the sheer volume of meat." Facebook people have similar feelings. Overall, customers view it as an underappreciated alternative to the major sandwich chains, especially for the price, which is a few dollars less than Five Guys' standard burger. On a Facebook post comparing BLTs from other chains, one person commented: "Should have gone to Five Guys. That's the GOAT BLT.".

According to recent reports, cheba Hut has been around since 1998, with its original location satisfying hungry students from the Arizona State University campus. Its menu reflects the playful, somewhat frenzied, college-kid mentality. Sandwiches are bold and inventive, with names and ingredient combinations that would make Panera Bread blush. Its version of the BLT — the Sensi Kush — has a traditional foundation of bacon, lettuce, and tomato, but it also includes a few, dare we say, dank touches that set it apart from your other basic sandwich chain, specifically a drizzle of sriracha honey, fresh avocado, and a buttery blanket of provolone.

Industry observers note that is this genius or BLT blasphemy? Based on customer reviews, it is most definitely the former. "I love a good BLT but I really love the Sensi Kush BLT from Cheba Hut! The honey sriracha sauce is 100," said one Facebook user, along with a pic of their sandwich. Customers on Instagram agree, with one commenter writing, "The sensi kush is fire," while another on Reddit said, "I love Cheba Hut! I think they make the best BLT I've ever had.".

First Watch is a sizable chain with nearly 700 locations across mostly the eastern half of the United States. The restaurant offers a diverse lineup that emphasizes freshness and ingredient quality over speed and cost. At First Watch, there's something for everyone: lemon ricotta pancakes, power breakfast bowls, Benedicts, elaborate, lunch-y salads, etc., but when it comes to sandwiches, its BLT(E) is one of the best.

In a recent development, it pairs your typical BLT with two over-hard eggs (can't have messy yolks getting everything soggy) and Monterey Jack cheese — all on its artisan whole-grain bread. BLT snobs may scoff at the extra ingredients, but the bread, along with the sandwich's overall engineering, is as good as you'll find at a local cafe or diner. The portion is sizable, bordering on two portions-worth. The sandwich's flavor takes people by surprise as well, with it being filling and tasty while not weighing you down. One Instagram post noted, "I enjoyed the BLTE [...]. It was so good. [...] I think I might start orderind sandwiches at First Watch each time I go." For something even more out there, try First Watch's BLT Benedict, which is basically an open-faced BLT sandwich topped with poached eggs and hollandaise.

It has been revealed that celebrity endorsements don't mean everything, but John Oliver (the star of HBO's Last Week Tonight) once publicly stated to his friend Stephen Colbert that his favorite sandwich is none other than a Wawa BLT. But this shouldn't be such a shock. Wawa is famous for its reasonably priced subs and sandwiches, and its BLT doesn't disappoint (at least when the bacon is properly cooked). While a Tasting Table ranking didn't put the BLT at the top of the list, the author still praised the sandwich, saying it was "perfectly built...nicely slathered with creamy mayo and stuffed with strips of bacon, shredded lettuce, and sliced tomato.".

According to recent reports, some chains (even a few on this list) are guilty of — every so often — skimping on ingredients. Not Wawa. Its sandwiches are pretty stuffed. One Facebook user said, "The BLT hyperfixation is in fullllllll effect." Even if you do end up with a thin sandwich, the staff will gladly remake it to your liking. Another ordering tip: Wawa recently moved the BLT from the "cold" to "hot" sandwich section, which has caused some confusion amongst customers over fears that it had been discontinued.

Recent findings suggest that to find the chain restaurants with the best BLTs that delivered on taste, price, and overall value, we dug through dozens of online forums, social media video reviews, and taste tests from within the past year. In the end, this list represents some of the best BLTs you can find, based on photos, reviews, and customer feedback.

Breaking: Modernizing iperf/iperf3 and introducing fireperf

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (673 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Daniel-baumann

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recently I spend some time on modernizing the packaging of the Internet Protocol bandwidth measuring tools iperf and iperf3 in Debian, as well as uploading fireperf to Debian.
  • It has been revealed that previously, src:iperf only built iperf.
  • Apart from tidying the Debian package, src:iperf now builds the upcoming iperf-client and iperf-server packages, the latter contains the systemd and ufw integration.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recently I spend some time on modernizing the packaging of the Internet Protocol bandwidth measuring tools iperf and iperf3 in Debian, as well as uploading fireperf to Debian.

It has been revealed that previously, src:iperf only built iperf. If you wanted to run an iperf server, you had to do it on your own, i.e. there was no systemd service for that.

Apart from tidying the Debian package, src:iperf now builds the upcoming iperf-client and iperf-server packages, the latter contains the systemd and ufw integration. iperf-server runs with a dynamic systemd user and systemd service hardening.

The iperf package is now a transitional package, that also cleans up any leftovers from before the package split into iperf-client and iperf-server (e.g. when upgrading from trixie to forky).

For historical reasons, iperf2 is packaged in debian as iperf, not iperf2. Now the iperf packages have provides for iperf2, iperf2-client, and iperf2-server respectively (so they can be installed by these names too).

Updated iperf packages are available in sid, and backports for trixie are available at Debian Fast Forward.

It might make sense in the future….

given that iperf2 and iperf3 are completely different tools with different advantages and disadvantages depending on the use-case.

therefore the one is not replacing the other (iperf2 in general is the better tool than iperf3, eventhough the common misconception is that iperf3 is supposedly better than iperf2 because the number 3 is greater than the number 2).

…to maybe rename iperf to iperf2 to match both upstream naming and also to harmonize the packaging of iperf2 with other distributions.

According to recent reports, previously, src:iperf3 only built iperf3. If you wanted to run an iperf3 server, iperf3 had a debconf yes/no question which would then start one iperf3 server on the default port 5201.

Apart from tidying the Debian package, src:iperf3 now builds the latest iperf3-client and iperf3-server packages, the latter contains the systemd and ufw integration. iperf3-server runs with a dynamic systemd user instead of the previous local system account, and has systemd service hardening.

Industry observers note that since iperf3 (contrary to iperf, also see here and here for iperv vs. iperf3) does not allow using multiple connections on the same port, you have to run multiple iperf3 servers, each on their own port, in order to serve more than one client at the time.

The old debconf question for enabling a single iperf3 server has been removed as well as the obsolete sysvinit integration.

In order to allow running multiple iperf3 servers at the same time (but on different ports), iperf3-server now contains a systemd service template so you can enable multiple iperf3 servers (e.g. 3 servers on subsequent port numbers, but you can run as many as you want on any ports you like) either manually with:.

or by using debconf interactively to do it automatically for you (which defaults to one instance on port 5201):.

or by using debconf non-interactively to do it automatically for you:.

The iperf3 package is now a transitional package, that also cleans up any leftovers from before the package split into iperf3-client and iperf3-server.

Updated iperf3 packages are available in sid, and backports for trixie are available at Debian Fast Forward.

Image 1: fireperf interactive terminal interface.

Image 2: fireperf non-interactive terminal interface.

fireperf is a modern take on the iperf3 network performance and stress-testing tool under the IPFire project umbrella:.

measures upload or download individually, or concurrent upload and download.

allows to serve many clients in parallel (on the same port).

allows to use many workers in parallel (for maxing out bandwith of servers with LACP instead of ECMP).

allows to use and track many connection sessions in parallel (for maxing out firewalls).

can also be used as a client for both iperf and iperf3 (autodetecting the target).

can also be used as a iperf3 server.

uses less CPU ressources on both the client and the server (io_uring, zerocopy, …).

fireperf packages are in sid, and backports for trixie are available at Debian Fast Forward.
